items.title: V-formation
items.summary: Inspired by migratory birds, this is a technique for sustaining activism for the long haul. Rotate roles to share burdens, and allow members to step back from frontline roles without guilt, and you’ll go far.
items.body:
Migratory birds such as geese that fly in a V-formation, rotating in and out of the lead position that bears the brunt of the wind, can travel over 70 percent further than a goose flying solo. It’s an extremely effective way for a flock to work together, share a burden, and offer rest from the most challenging roles without delaying the journey. 
Activists can learn a lot from this approach.

As a model for distributed leadership, the idea of moving in V-formation is about working together to ensure that everyone gets a chance to rest, and that no one is stuck in a difficult role indefinitely. Adopting this metaphor in your movement means making clear that there is space for members to come and go, and ensuring that if some people need to step aside to rest or recover, others stand ready to take their place and continue the fight. Meanwhile, those that do hang back to rest, recover their energy, and prioritize their wellbeing, can serve the movement in different ways, or later on.
Such an approach is particularly important in moments of heightened risk. Following a military coup in Myanmar in February 2021 that usurped power from the elected government, a country-wide civil disobedience movement emerged. Hundreds of thousands of people across states, regions, and sectors engaged in [civil disobedience](https://beautifultrouble.org/toolbox/tool/civil-disobedience), including mass street protests and ongoing [general strikes](https://beautifultrouble.org/toolbox/tool/general-strike). Years later, the movement persists. 
As the months went by, it became clear that the prospect of success — as with many movements that seek to uproot deeply embedded systems of oppression — was going to be a long-term goal. It is often at this moment of contraction in a [movement’s cycle](https://beautifultrouble.org/toolbox/tool/the-movement-cycle/) that momentum is lost and members begin to [burn out](https://beautifultrouble.org/toolbox/tool/burn-brightly-but-dont-burn-out) and fall away, unable to sustain the same commitment they previously did. It is also here that a misguided perception that to step aside or take a break means ‘giving up’ can emerge, adversely impacting our collective success.
As the age-old adage goes, “you can't pour from an empty cup.” In movements composed of people from all walks of life, juggling many roles and responsibilities, people must rest when they can no longer give to the movement. That is OK.
Going about ‘business as usual’ is another way to step back but keep the line of fight. CDM students in Myanmar who left government universities and refused to return continued to pursue their education by self-organizing makeshift institutions around a range of topics, to study, learn and pursue qualifications by different means. Thousands of people who had to flee the country to neighboring Thailand, set up businesses such as local food and craft stalls or bookstores, pursuing their livelihood, while also creating community spaces that could double up as meeting hubs for revolutionary thought, nourish newly exiled comrades looking for a sense of home, or raise funds to send back home to the movement.
In the meantime, working on bringing in and integrating new members (see: [PRINCIPLE: Make new folks welcome](https://beautifultrouble.org/toolbox/tool/make-new-folks-welcome)) and creating intentional pathways for supporters to be involved (see: [METHODOLOGY: Ladder of engagement](https://beautifultrouble.org/toolbox/tool/ladder-of-engagement)) will go a long way in ensuring there are enough people to keep things going.

learn_more.title: Building Resilience: Self-care and community resilience for the long haul
Practicing individual and collective self-care

items.title: Be Transparent
items.summary: If we can’t talk about it, we can’t change it.
items.body:
People in power withold and misrepresent information as a form of control. It allows them to manipulate our collective perception of reality. That’s one of the reasons why a free press is so important to democracy. Good journalism makes the world more transparent and gives us the information we need to govern ourselves and hold others accountable.

We don’t need to depend on journalists alone. As we build this more beautiful world, we can take steps toward radical honesty in everything we do, including in our communities and workplaces. When a business openly shares its employees’ wages and benefits, the workers can use the information to organize against exploitation. When a community organization writes a report about a project that has failed, people can learn to avoid repeating past mistakes. When neighbors regularly communicate with each other in healthy ways, they are more likely to notice opportunities to improve their community with collective action.

Often, information is hidden because revealing the truth would require admitting imperfection or failure. It is true that transparency can create tensions. But as American abolitionist Frederick Douglass once said, “If there is no struggle, there is no progress.” We must overcome any aversions we hold toward tension and disagreement if we are to build an honest society. The ability to respectfully disagree with one another allows us to have critical conversations about strategy, ethics, and many other topics necessary for societal transformation.

Similarly, we must also overcome a culture of discarding people when they make mistakes. We need cultures of mutual respect and practices of transformative justice, where it is safe for people to be honest with each other. We must create environments where people know that, even when they mess up, it is possible to make amends and restore relationships.

Transparency requires us not only to be honest and share information with others, but also to be able to receive information from others. We must be able to listen and disagree while still holding one another’s inherent worthiness.

items.title: Build for Access
items.summary: We need each other, and so we need to build in ways that meet each other’s needs.
items.body:
We are, each of us, many different things to many different people. We are children and parents and neighbors and teammates and workers and friends, and so much more. The world we are building must be for all of us, and for all the roles we play.

When we build for access, we support each other to live in our communities as complex, whole people. We celebrate and uplift the necessary wisdom that comes from living in systems not designed for us, because that’s where the solutions are. Wisdom from struggles for disability justice, such as the Principles of Disability Justice from Sins Invalid, teach us that a more accessible world is better for all of us.

We need to have access to the knowledge, resources, institutions, and support that allow each of us to offer our unique contributions. We must design for this from the beginning. If access is an afterthought, we’re doing it wrong—and we’re likely doing it for the wrong reasons. We need to build for access because we need to be able to show up for each other and be powerful together. People who dream in languages other than English are leading the way out of a colonial mindset, so we need those languages centered in our planning and organizing processes, not just in our output. People with disabilities are experts at adaptation, so we can’t afford to try to address the climate crisis without their leadership.

Access needs are not always visible. About 14 percent of the global population is illiterate. Many millions of children arrive at school hungry. More than 300 million people are affected by depression. Access means understanding how unjust systems cause these problems and creating solutions that work to end those systems and heal from them, which we can only do with the help of those who have been harmed.

Access looks like community meetings held outside of work hours that offer healthy food, childcare, wheelchair accessible entrances, translation, and a ride home. It is textbooks and classrooms, healthcare, banks, and social services that are created and run by the people who actually use them. It is institutions and movements that love the people inside them, recognizing that they are magnificent, complex people who have specific and necessary medicine that will help us all get free, if they have the support they need. It is time and space for rest, care, and healing so that we can keep going for a long time.

items.title: Choose Collective Courage
items.summary: Our strength lies in what we can do together.
items.body:
There are people and institutions whose drive for profit threatens to destroy everything we have. We can summon the courage to challenge them, to meet our own needs, create our own realities, and defend what we create. Collective courage is about choosing to stick with the hard work of fighting together, even when it may mean giving some things up.

We borrow the term “collective courage” from our friend Jessica Gordon Nembhard and her book, Collective Courage: A History of African American Economic Thought and Practice. It is a phrase that can come to life in many contexts. Whether it’s creating a mutual aid network, campaigning for a policy, protesting discrimination, registering new voters, organizing a community meeting, or running for office, our work cannot be neatly separated into issue areas. It is the work of survival and thriving, and it means innovating and evolving to meet the needs of each moment, and supporting each other when obstacles arise.

A community can hold a vision and an awareness of what could be, but they must choose to bring it into being and respond to the consequences that arise from its creation. Any project that challenges the existing power structure will provoke a response from those in power. Choosing collective courage means leaning into the strength of our communities and preparing to meet that resistance together, despite the odds.

It may be harder to build strength in a collective than retreat into the supposed safety of isolation, but the collective is our power. We can work to trust each other in a society that makes us unsafe, to confront our suspicion and our fears of one another. We can join with other members of the community despite our differences, working and grieving and celebrating together. We can do the hard work of crafting a strategy that integrates different approaches and groups of people in the building of a cohesive vision for our future.

We must be clear about what we’re fighting for and against, so that we don’t end up fighting each other. When those in power try to pit us against each other, we resist because we know that we are stronger when we’re together.

Choosing collective courage means organizing from our roots: being so grounded in our experience and in our place that when we turn toward one another, we can see that we are not alone. It is understanding that we must begin by changing our reality close to home. It is choosing to do the work, together, right where we are.

items.title: Democratize Ownership
items.summary: Our communities practice direct ownership and control of the things that affect our lives.
items.body:
Ownership can have many meanings. owning a house comes with different rights and restrictions than owning a business, or an energy grid, or a patent, or the rights to a song. But one way or another, ownership confers the right to decide how something is managed and how any surpluses are divided and shared. The people who own something are generally also those responsible for stewarding it. If it is a company or organization, its operations are directed by its owners. Most things are owned either privately—by individuals, corporations, or nonprofits—or publicly by governments. But not everything can or should be owned. A solidarity economy seeks to expand the commons that nobody can claim to own for themselves. Capitalism, however, seeks to make as many things as possible into private property. Ownership can be done democratically, but under capitalism it most often is not.

We can change that.

Democratic ownership is when the core stakeholders in an entity control it together—as opposed to just a few people calling the shots. In a solidarity economy, democratic ownership and control allows us to determine the future of our lives, businesses, public utilities, the land, and everything else around us. When we are organizing in our communities, we must ask: Who should have the power to control this project or business? Who should decide how the profits are shared and how much the workers are paid? How should those decisions be made?

Which community members are impacted? How can they be involved in important decisions? What process would allow stakeholders to govern together in the service of our community?

Throughout this book, we spotlight a variety of examples and models of democratic ownership. There are many different ways to do it depending on the situation and the particular needs of the community.

Some forms of democracy are indirect. For example, in the United States, anything that is owned by the federal government is technically somewhat democratic, since US citizens elect their government. However, it’s a stretch to say that many federally-owned projects are democratically controlled; most do not enable the communities they impact to participate in their governance. That’s why, as a general principle, we prioritize local and direct forms of democratic ownership whenever possible. A solution that isn’t accountable to the communities it serves is no solution at all.

items.title: Develop Community Leaders
items.summary: We share leadership and knowledge across communities and generations.
items.body:
This is a long journey. All movements for transformative change require many generations of leaders sharing their knowledge, wisdom, and power.

One of our most important jobs is to build the capacity of the generations that will come after us. This principle is about reproductive labor—the work required to nourish the people who are our future. How do we pass along what we learn? How do we make it easier for the people and communities who will follow in our footsteps?

Developing community leadership means creating the space to share stories, wisdom, and resources with others. It requires the humility not only to share but also to receive. It means asking what elders and youth might add to conversations that people in their 30s and 40s would otherwise dominate. It means asking why people may leave the community, and if we can do anything to support them to stay. If we open ourselves to the possibility that we also have something to learn, we invite the emergence of a deeper truth: regardless of our age, where we come from, or what we have done, we are all teachers, and we are all learners. When we approach leadership development as a two-way exchange, we allow everyone involved to become better versions of themselves.

We should also recognize that leadership development protects us from the system we are up against. Those in power have a long track record of attacking anything they perceive to be a threat to the status quo, including our leaders. That is why a movement full of many capable leaders is more resilient than one that depends only on a few key individuals. If any one person is too essential to a piece of work, it’s a threat to the work itself. We can all create ways for learning to happen across generations of leadership so that our organizations develop institutional memory and so our work can continue for the long haul. Capitalism is a global system. When we share knowledge and skills across borders, we protect each other and speed up the development of solidarity economies as a force that can withstand attacks.

Another way to think about leadership development is in cycles: the cycle of an individual human life, of the planet’s life, and of our movements’ lives. Each of these cycles depends on us to pass along knowledge and wisdom. We should not let individualism prevent us from understanding the ways in which our lives depend on each other and on those who came before us. We are never all alone and we are never starting from scratch.

We are all elders and ancestors in training.

items.title: Practice Freedom
items.summary: We live our lives as acts of resistance to the destruction of land and life.
items.body:
This book is full of powerful stories about new ways of organizing our economies, and there are many thousands of other examples globally. The reason we think it is important to tell these stories is because community institutions and democratic workplaces can be spaces where we can make different choices, choices that are about becoming free.

A beautiful solution is an act of resistance against the systems that dominate our people. Resistance is not just about marches, blockades, and protests; it is also about building the systems we need here and now for our communities to thrive. Resistance is setting up our own schools, our own housing complexes, our own factories in ways that reflect our values. It’s collective liberation in practice.

Living by our values and embedding these in our work doesn’t just happen, though. All of the solutions described in this book, from cooperatives to land trusts to communities of mutual aid, face pressure from existing power structures to perpetuate racism, classism, and heterosexism instead of cultivating relationships of interdependence and mutual respect. Building different structures is not enough. Practicing freedom means we work to understand how systems of oppression operate in all of our groups. We don’t assume that because we are trying to change the system, we are immune from recreating it.

Imagine a growing cooperative enterprise that has to compete with similar sized capitalist businesses to survive. It comes under increased pressure to adopt exploitative practices and take shortcuts in how it sources its materials. The business also becomes large and complex enough that the majority of members are not aware of the cooperative’s practices or of how management makes decisions. To overcome this, the cooperative’s members need to actively work to understand these pressures, come up with creative solutions, and commit to steering the co-op to make decisions that protect workers and the earth.

Working toward our collective liberation must be at the core of everything we do—otherwise, what’s the point? Above the success of any single cooperative project, we must prioritize the broader goal of transforming society for all of us. We must be that ambitious, because our ancestors are counting on us to continue the work they started, and our children will inherit the world we create.

The good news is that everyone—and we mean everyone—can practice freedom in their everyday lives, whether we are raising a family, cooking meals for our religious community, making art, delivering healthcare, or simply surviving in a system that doesn’t want us in it. The choices we make about how we do these things can always move us toward practicing freedom.

items.title: Put Care First
items.summary: Taking care of each other and our home is the basis of the world we’re trying to create—and how we get there.
items.body:
Caring for ourselves and one another is how we stay connected to our humanity, to the source of our power and dignity, and to the web of life. It is the purpose of community. It is the purpose of a solidarity economy.

We want a world in which everyone has what they need to thrive, to be joyful and to be well. Prioritizing quality of life for all human and non-human life means putting care first.

We need to feel safe. We need permission and space to be ourselves and pursue our passions. We need to feel like the rules of the community are fair and applied equitably. We need to have control of our culture—our language, food, dance, music, and history—and our land. And our communities, not just health professionals and politicians, need the power to define what trauma, care, wholeness, and health look like for themselves, because they look different everywhere.

Under capitalism, care—including our health, time, passions, and the environment itself—has been commodified. As we create different kinds of economies, we can measure value in different ways in our businesses and communities, and we can use these measurements to inform how and what we choose to build together. If our economy values care, then it will also include policies and protections such as family and medical leave, minimum wages, overtime, comprehensive benefits, and more. We need to structure our economy so that everyone can access quality healthcare, education, and housing.

Putting care first also means recognizing the labor of caretakers regardless of job title or wage. So much care work is invisible and undervalued in a capitalist economy. The work of caring for an elderly parent, giving birth and raising children, helping a friend in need, or repairing what we have so that we don’t need to buy more new things, is seen as something outside of the economy—something that people should do on top of the “real work” of earning a living. As we build solidarity economies, we know that care work is essential to the health of our communities, and we have to treat it that way.

A society that doesn’t honor and value care is not a society worth building. As the world changes around us, we must be willing to do what it takes to keep taking care of each other even as things get harder and new needs emerge. This is both the basis of the world we’re trying to create—and an essential part of how we get there.

items.title: Share Responsibility
items.summary: We are responsible to each other and have shared responsibility for the whole.
items.body:
How far does your circle of responsibility extend? To your household? Your neighbors? Your country? What is your responsibility to people on the other side of the world? What happens when we extend our shared circle of responsibility to include all of humanity, the earth, and life itself?

If we are to bring about broad social change, our circles must be so much bigger than they are right now. They must include people who have migrated to our communities, people who pray in different ways than we do, and people who hold different values and political perspectives. In a global economy, we have to pay attention not just to the people with whom we interact most directly and most often, but also to those who grow our food or eat what we grow, make the machines we depend on, or feel the effects of our decisions. We are human, so our circles will also include people who have violated community norms and caused harm, and those who they’ve harmed. Shared responsibility means we navigate this reality with practices that don’t throw anyone away.

Mutual aid, or working together to care for each other’s needs, is an expression of shared responsibility. There are times when we respond to the needs of others, and there are times when we are the ones in need. Communities are healthy when they welcome the contributions and value of all their members, not just a few.

When a cooperative business practices shared responsibility, it recognizes its impacts on the entire community and on the supply chain to which it belongs.Yes, it looks out for its members, but it also looks out for the land that it sits on, the community that shares this land, and the workers who extract or produce the materials that its business requires.

Sharing responsibility means that as we organize to build a better world, we don’t look away from the impact of the choices we make along the way. It also means that we pay attention to the choices others are faced with and support each other in making better options available for everyone. Grace Lee Boggs said, “You cannot change any society unless you take responsibility for it, unless you see yourself as belonging to it and responsible for changing it.”

items.title: Take the right risks
items.summary: We all have different boundaries, and we support each other to experiment and take risks while taking care of ourselves.
items.body:
How much are we willing to risk in our fight for a better world? In every situation and at every moment, we each have something different at stake. We each have different things to gain and lose, and different levels of vulnerability to the consequences of our actions and the actions of our community members.

Those who are privileged can take big risks without having to worry much about the consequences; others are seen by those in power as expendable. Collective institutions like unions protect us against individual risk, building the people power to allow us to stand up to injustice as one.

Knowing when and what to risk means being realistic about what is needed. Often, you can try something only once; if it is unsuccessful, the chance may not come again. If you are trying to organize your neighbors to start a food cooperative, but there are already several food cooperatives in the area, then this is probably not taking a “right risk” with your community’s resources.

Taking the right risks also requires recognizing that failure might be more harmful to some people than to others. The consequences of risks are often carried more heavily by people who are more likely to be harmed or criminalized by those in power on the basis of race, gender, class, religion, or sexuality. Those in privileged positions can choose to assume more risk, and privilege can be a valuable tool when leveraged strategically in support of the collective. For example, in a group starting a collective enterprise, those with more money might take on financial risks like guaranteeing a loan.

Taking the right risks can make heroes, but it can also make enemies. For people who hold different beliefs from their family and friends, speaking out and fighting against oppression may mean losing relationships. Or, it could just mean some difficult conversations over dinner. Some people will be celebrated, and some will never have their stories told. These are decisions that can affect our whole lives, so every one of us should be allowed to define for ourselves the risks we are willing to take. This means equipping ourselves and others with the information we need to understand what we are risking.

We need to get better at motivating people to take risks and support and honor them when they do. Our strong relationships can empower us to risk, and so can our own determination to make a better world. We risk for ourselves, for our children, for the planet, and to grow our communities and be whole. We need to recognize where the front lines are, and celebrate those who take risks at the edges of their own comfort and ability. This might involve building ritual around risk-taking—with ceremony, special clothes, or the stories that bring our communities together.

One way or another, we will need to grapple with fear. The political or economic climate will never be perfect for transformation. At a certain point you have to take the leap, to be both ambitious and realistic, and reach for as much as you can. But it is less dangerous to leap when you’ve considered what you are up against. Taking risks usually means facing obstacles. At the end of the day, if your community or your group is committed to facing them together, taking risks can make you even stronger than you already are.

items.title: Travel Many Paths
items.summary: There are lots of ways to get free.
items.body:
There is no one path to a solidarity economy. Creating different economic practices requires creativity, a willingness to experiment, and the humility to fail and try again.

When a solution is working, it can be tempting to think that it is the only way, and to stop believing in or supporting anything else. But there are no easy answers in this work. Just because something is working in one community doesn’t mean that it will work elsewhere. Nor does it mean that it’s the only—or even the best—way to solve a certain problem.

When we elevate one path above others, we can become overly invested in the success of that path and less open to critical feedback. This is a losing strategy. Every solution deserves our loving critique and patience, especially the ones with the most promise. Any beautiful solution should welcome this kind of scrutiny. If not, it will eventually fail to live up to its expectations anyway.

We need to weave many different strategies together to solve our biggest problems. Trying to create one grand solution is more likely to fail. Building multiple solutions that reinforce one another increases the resilience of the whole. As conditions change, diversity creates more opportunities for adaptation.

Part of practicing resilience is learning to be comfortable with seeing others do things differently. This requires humility, respecting that other people may have answers that we don’t. Communitiy approaches to this work will be impacted by local cultures and histories. Some will be more willing to use direct action. Some will be more likely to work with governments or enter into strategic partnerships with large companies. Everyone will use different words. As long as the choices they’re making are not a major threat to our people and our places, many different approaches are worth considering.

Even within a single community, individuals and groups may take different paths to achieve shared goals. This can produce competitiveness, especially in our capitalist context. But we can also recognize that experimentation contributes to the knowledge and experience of the community, which gets passed on and makes it stronger. As long as a path doesn’t actively get in the way of other paths, or oppose our values, we should give it the chance to grow and flourish. Some paths will succeed. Many will fail. The best will make more room for other solutions to be possible. Our job is to learn from all of it and apply that learning to the new paths we travel together.

items.title: How do we acknowledge and repair generational harm, and move toward healing?
items.summary: We can’t build a just world from scratch...

items.title: How do we care for our people as we take action on the side of life and adapt to a changing world?
items.summary: Human civilization is out of balance with nature...
items.body:
Human civilization is out of balance with nature. For centuries, industrialization and global capitalism have polluted the air, burned down rainforests, and wiped-out countless species of plants and animals—warming the climate to levels that endanger much of life on earth. The impacts of this ecological devastation are significant and only getting worse, and they tend to hit hardest in communities least responsible for the damage: people who are forced off of their land; who are living near dirty-energy factories and suffering high cancer and asthma rates; whose agricultural harvests are devastated by drought, flooding, and erratic growing seasons; or whose access to healthcare makes them more vulnerable to global pandemics. Those who justified this destruction in the name of economic growth are learning too late that there is no economy on a dead planet.

In our lifetimes, we will determine the fate of our species and millions of others through the decisions we make about the climate crisis. A lot of choices have already been made, but there are also many others awaiting us that matter.

So what do we do with this responsibility? How do we take action on the side of life, for ourselves and for one another? How do we end centuries of ecological destruction while at the same time protecting our communities from the impacts of a changed climate? Indigenous communities at the frontlines of climate chaos have been leading the way to creative solutions rooted in ancient wisdom. Over and over, they show us that the corporate capitalism and the overconsumption that got us into this mess will not get us out of it, and that change will come from grassroots movements and communities.

“Relentless consumerism is unattached from rationality or from the pursuit of balance between our needs and what nature can provide,” says Ayala Lindabeth Dias Ferreira of the Brazilian Landless Workers Movement. “The sense of time for nature differs from that for capital.” What does this mean for our solutions? How do we reconnect human needs with what nature can provide?

We must also ask ourselves how to govern our communities to navigate unfolding crises locally and regionally, while communicating and coordinating globally. Environmental impacts do not respect borders, and so we must work together across them with a sense of shared responsibility and mutual care and respect for one another, on nature’s time. We must put our support behind those experiencing the worst of the impacts, knowing that their fate is bound up in ours. And we must demand that those responsible for the crises pay for the solutions.

Because the problems facing the earth and atmosphere are so big, change will not happen overnight. The impacts of a destabilized climate are already here and will continue for centuries to come. We can meet the despair that comes with what is dying with the hope that comes with the possibility of new ways of defending life. We don’t know what the future holds, but we do know that solutions grounded in care and cooperation will help us mitigate the crisis, adapt to the impacts, and claim meaning and joy in our lives.

items.title: How do we create and adopt new technologies without deepening inequalities?
items.summary: Technology is often framed as an almost magical, unstoppable force...
items.body:
Technology is often framed as an almost magical, unstoppable force. We’re either told that technology will solve all of our problems, or that technology will take our jobs, robots will rule the world, and all we can do is learn to live with it. How else could we understand this relationship?

Technology is a tool; its value depends on how it is applied and its impacts on society. Humans have created increasingly complex technologies to solve problems. But sometimes one person’s problem is another person’s solution. Whether we’re talking about shovels, tractors, smartphones, or spaceships, technologies can help us or they can work against us. Like everything else, who owns and controls it matters. How can we ensure that technology is driven by community needs and not corporate profits? How do we make sure new technologies include everyone, and not just the wealthy and powerful? Not all technology is necessary. When does it make sense to choose not to develop that next piece of military technology or corporate-controlled AI—and how do we make those decisions together in a democratic way?

Alfredo Lopez, a founder of May First Movement Technology, a cooperative membership organization that advances “the strategic use and collective control of technology for local struggles, global transformation, and emancipation without borders,” considers technology to be valuable when it is controlled by people—not by profit-hungry corporations. Decentralized and democratic ownership challenges the exploitation that we find in tech hubs from Silicon Valley to Singapore. For Roger Baig-Viñas of Guifi.net, a grassroots telecommunications network that brings internet access to previously unconnected communities in Spain, good technology is that which is accessible to a greater number of people while also serving to promote the exercise of other civil and human rights, such as free expression and open access to knowledge. Participation is critical; people and users must be included in decision-making processes and understand the implications and consequences of different technologies.

We can’t expect technology to solve social problems for us. Often technologies that seem to solve problems in one area can create other problems elsewhere. Solar panels and electric batteries, for instance, require mining rare metals and minerals in ways that harm communities and the earth. We must pay attention to the impact that our technological choices have on the world we’re trying to build, and we must ensure that the communities most impacted by technological change have a seat at the decision-making table. When communities control their technology, they can challenge monopolies and the unintended consequences that are rampant in big tech. We can begin by building on the work of organizations that show us that technology can be as diverse and creative as we are, and can be employed to serve the interests of everyone.

items.title: How do we move beyond incremental reforms to real changes that transform the system?
items.summary: Our solutions need to meet the scale of the problems our communities are facing...
items.body:
Our solutions need to meet the scale of the problems our communities are facing. But how? These problems are so immense and interlinked that it can seem like fixing something in one area just creates another problem somewhere else. One of the most frequent critiques of the solidarity economy is that anything we build won’t be powerful enough to contend with the economic power of multinational corporations burning the planet and exploiting workers.

It’s true that a single project—or even all of our projects put together—won’t bring about the solidarity economy our communities need. But the point is not to add up all of our projects or deploy a single global solution. The point is to cause a sea change, a shift in culture that can transform the world. We are not alone in this. As builders and cleaners, teachers and artists, healers and scientists, planners and engineers, we can channel our collective brilliance into imagining and creating a livable future. We are growing our solutions within and alongside powerful movements that are mobilizing millions of people to put an end to oppressive regimes and claim sovereignty over their land and livelihoods. We are connecting and weaving our solutions, creating networks where our cooperatives and community projects can work together and support one another. If we do all this, we can create a whole that is much greater than the sum of its parts.

We feel pressure to compromise and accept policies that improve things for some without addressing root causes. Or we replicate solutions from elsewhere without considering the specific context that allowed the solution to thrive in the first place. How do we resist the impulse to compromise and demand what we actually need? How do we create solutions that are both visionary and designed to confront the root causes of harm in our communities?

We need to discern between what moves us closer to the world we want and what might co-opt or undermine our vision. Some solutions are ready to be tried elsewhere. Some compromises are worthwhile. Some political reforms might not get us to where we need to go but change something about the underlying rules of society, making transformative change more possible. The philosopher André Gorz spoke of “non-reformist reforms”—seemingly small achievements that point toward, not against, more radical change. On the other hand, some projects might have all the right intentions—and even look transformative from the outside—but in reality make problems worse, contributing to gentrification and displacement, exploiting the people they are meant to serve, or setting communities up for disappointment by having unrealistic expectations. We must turn our attention to the details of the projects we are building, while simultaneously thinking bigger. We must get better at learning from the times that our projects don’t live up to their commitments, or even cause harm.

Transformative change requires us to envision thriving local economies in relationships of balance and reciporcity with each other and the rest of the living world.

items.title: How do we relate to government and state power in growing solidarity economies?
items.summary: Governments can support or undermine our efforts to build solidarity economies...
items.body:
Governments can support or undermine our efforts to build solidarity economies. State support for solidarity economies can come in the form of enabling policies and public investment. In some places, the cooperative movement is deeply embedded in government through political parties and tax law. In others, colonial and oppressive governments have repressed solidarity economies because community self-determination weakens top-down control. Almost everywhere, public policy gives advantages to capitalist ownership at the expense of collective power. We can push governments for the policies and resources to support our efforts and we can grow solidarity economies autonomously, without resources or support from the state.

We must relate to government and state power as it is, even as we organize for it to be something else. We can form alliances with governments and the people in them. We can align ourselves with politicians to build our power, and we can cultivate our own people to seek office. We can also work outside of government, designing solutions that do not require its participation or that even escape its notice. If we consider the solidarity economy as part of a “dual power” strategy, which calls for building alternative institutions (like cooperatives) and counter institutions (like political groups and federations) to defend those alternative institutions, we can challenge the state’s control of society and shift power toward new forms of self-governance.

Government is only one kind of governance—which is, broadly, how we make decisions about how to use our collective power and manage our common resources. In the world we’re working toward, democracy happens everywhere, not just in the politics surrounding governments. We decide how powerful and centralized governments should be, and what kinds of democracy we can practice within them. When we practice democratic governance in our daily lives, we have opportunities to learn about how to make those decisions, and to acquire the skills and perspective we need to self-govern.

Finally, the governance of our communities today is shaped by nation-state borders that privilege multi-national corporations and the Global North. We envision solidarity economies in a world organized instead by bioregional and ecosystem boundaries, with governance by and for those affected by the decisions we make—governance that can meet the needs of the land, the water, and all creatures who live here.

items.title: How do we relate to the borders drawn by colonialism and empire, and to peoples’ need to move across them?
items.summary: Borders are enclosures—just like fences or property lines, they impose artificial limits that restrict movement and turn collective resources such as water and energy into commodities that can be bought and sold...
items.body:
Borders are enclosures—just like fences or property lines, they impose artificial limits that restrict movement and turn collective resources such as water and energy into commodities that can be bought and sold. Borders represent claims of power over land and of the right to exploit it. They have been especially useful for colonizers, who invented them to seize and extract land and resources and to divide people who might fight back.

We don’t often pay attention to the things that are allowed to pass through borders with little or no difficulty. The people who create borders usually move freely across them, as do corporate assets and the money of wealthy people. Migrating birds and deadly viruses pass across borders more easily than most people can. Displaced and poor people are often kept from moving freely by force. The hoarding of basic resources inside a country or region—while those outside suffer violence and ecosystem destruction—also creates a need to move. Migration has always been a fact of life, but the scale of forced migration due to war, poverty, and climate change is accelerating and destroying families and communities every day.

Unlike borders, boundaries are not inherently violent. Neither is migration. Boundaries are necessary for individuals and communities to claim their identities and self-govern. The boundaries we want honor life and invite change, while preventing extraction, privatization, and exploitation. Migration is a natural part of that change and creates opportunities for cultural exchange and for expanding our collective understanding of what it means to be human. The migration we want honors and seeks reparations for the theft of land and culture from Indigenous peoples, while also honoring and seeking healing for people living in diaspora.

As Michelle Mascarenhas of Movement Generation says, “Today, our communities are bound by borders created by nation states. As we shift to ways of meeting our needs in right-relationship with the living world rather than by taking it all, the containers for governance will shift from borders to boundaries. We can see the boundaries that the living world creates in Indigenous peoples’ territories that also relate to watersheds, foodsheds, and tradesheds. When those impacted by decisions are the ones making them, our governance will better take into account the needs of the land, water, air, and creatures of that place.”

Can we resist the borders maintained by force and honor the boundaries set by Indigenous peoples and communities? Can we resist forced displacement and support freedom of movement? How can our solutions redraw our maps of the world?

items.title: How do we scale up solidarity economy ideas and solutions?
items.summary: Capitalism says that bigger is better...
items.body:
Capitalism says that bigger is better. What kinds of scale do we really aspire to? Yes, if we want to meet the needs of everyone in our communities, we need our grassroots solutions to grow beyond one place or community. But does scale mean large, powerful organizations with global reach, or does it mean networks of many small projects, powerfully organized? When does it make more sense for projects to stay small or local, and when should they be bigger? How should we support and plan for projects to evolve as they scale?

Nancy Neamtan, a founder of Le Chantier de L’économie Sociale, a membership organization that exists to promote and grow Quebec’s solidarity economy, talks about coordinated enterprise as a crucial aspect of scale—if multiple organizations work toward a collective goal, scaling up our efforts becomes more attainable. In a business that is struggling, owners can easily lose sight of their social mission as they make compromises to stay afloat. But if that project is part of a larger network, it can lean on others for support in hard times, and more easily expand and take risks when there are opportunities.

For Hanan El-Youssef, who served as director of strategy at the International Cooperative Association, including all members in governance processes should be considered a way to achieve scale, not an inhibitor of it. Thoughtfully adopting new digital tools like online voting and discussion can build widespread commitment in ways that closeddoor meetings among elites cannot. Julia Ho, of Solidarity Economy St. Louis, finds that scaling up becomes more possible when an organization repurposes tools that already exist in a community grounded in values and history; participation will spread more easily when it is based on what people already know.

There are a number of tools people have employed to manage the operation of solidarity economies at a larger scale while keeping real power at the local level.

One of these tools is the formation of federations, or umbrella organizations that are owned and run by smaller, more local groups or organizations. This happened in the English cooperative movement during the 1840s, when consumer-owned cooperative stores joined to form a national federation. The federation purchased and even manufactured goods for the stores at lower prices than they would pay on their own. They had national power together, grounded in local ownership. This model has been successful across the world.

Another pathway to scale is through networks. Networks are often democratic and participatory and tend to be less hierarchical and centralized than federations. Groups can usually come and go as they please, as long as they meet the core values and criteria of the network. Whereas a federation works best with a clear, specific purpose, networks excel at connecting diverse independent projects to support various collaborations. Networks are excellent ways for clusters of businesses and organizations to coordinate across sectors of the economy.

Finally, whether we’re talking about federations or networks, it’s important to note that we’re not only talking about economic coordination.Yes, these forms of group governance help our solidarity economy enterprises reach larger economic scales. But they can do much more. Successful networks and federations make it possible to build collective political power beyond the scale that any one project could reach alone. They can also help solidarity economy groups form alliances with other social and political movements. By coming together across sectors and movements, we can assert our power in ways that can change laws in our favor, like changing the tax code to make it easier to convert existing businesses into worker cooperatives. Some cooperative federations even form their own political parties that develop platforms and candidates for office.

Ultimately what’s needed for effective economic and political coordination will differ from community to community, but if we want to change society, we have to find ways to coordinate and share power across locations, sectors, and movements.

items.title: How do we stop depending on violent systems to make us safe?
items.summary: Police, militaries, and prisons were not created to make people safe...
items.body:
Police, militaries, and prisons were not created to make people safe. They were created to protect wealth and property through force. They were created because the only way to maintain an unjust distribution of resources is with violence.

When have you felt safe? What conditions came together to create that sense of safety? For many of us, our imagining and experiences of safety do not include images of armed officers and barbed-wired walls. Safety is the care and support of our families, friends, and communities; it is a nurturing environment in which it is okay to feel all the joy and pain and contradictions of life; it is access to health, food and water, and beauty.

War, policing, and prisons are built on an assumption that people are disposable. Solidarity economies are built on the opposite assumption: that life is inherently sacred, and we can’t throw anyone away. This means we need other ways to resolve conflict and keep our communities safe.

In a world where there is enough to go around, why are we plagued by conflicts over land, water, and power? Many conflicts have at their roots a small number of massively wealthy and powerful people who stand to benefit at the expense of everyone else involved. Millions fight and die for their causes. Could these same millions change the structures of power and find different solutions to our problems? War, policing, surveillance, and incarceration are all tools for expanding and maintaining empires, large or small, by dominating people and pitting them against one another.

So how do we bring about other ways of keeping our communities safe?

There is no one answer. We’re talking about building a different culture, where we actually believe that the lives of everyone around us matter. Even if they have different values. Even if they have different ways of existing in the world. Even if they have caused harm. There are no shortcuts to this culture shift. Our task is the long, hard work of building communities rooted in care and respect for our common humanity. In this, abolitionist movements are leading the way to a world beyond police, prisons, and incarceration. We can learn so much from the long histories of these movements about how to transform conflict, and how to end and heal from violent systems, in our households, neighborhoods, and nations.

The root causes of much of the violence in our world today lie in an economic and political system that needs people to be poor. Solutions that restore economic control and ownership to our communities have the power to attack these roots, and ultimately make a safer world for all of us.

items.title: Abolition
items.summary: Abolition is a political vision, a structural analysis of oppression, and a practical organizing strategy working towards a society that addresses harm without relying on prisons, police, military, or other violent systems.
items.body:
Today, more people are discussing and contemplating prison abolition than ever before. Decades of collective organizing have brought us to this moment: Some are newly aware that prisons, policing, and the criminal punishment system in general are racist, oppressive, and ineffective.

Prison industrial complex abolition is a political vision, a structural analysis of oppression, and a practical organizing strategy. While some people might think of abolition as primarily a negative project—“Let’s tear everything down tomorrow and hope for the best”—prison industrial complex abolition is a vision of a restructured society in a world where we have everything we need: food, shelter, education, health, art, beauty, clean water, and more. These things are foundational to our personal and community safety.

Every vision is also a map. As freedom fighter Kwame Ture taught us, “When you see people call themselves revolutionary always talking about destroying, destroying, destroying but never talking about building or creating, they’re not revolutionary. They do not understand the first thing about revolution. It’s creating.” Prison industrial complex abolition is a positive project that focuses, in part, on building a society where it is possible to address harm without relying on structural forms of oppression or the violent systems that increase it.

An abolitionist journey ignites other questions capable of meaningful and transformative pathways: What work do prisons and policing actually do? Most people assume that incarceration helps to reduce violence and crime, thinking: “The criminal punishment system might be racist, sexist, classist, ableist, and unfair, but it at least keeps me safe from violence and crime.”

Facts and history tell a different story: Increasing rates of incarceration have a minimal impact on crime rates. Research and common sense suggest that economic precarity is correlated with higher crime rates. Moreover, crime and harm are not synonymous. All that is criminalized isn’t harmful, and all harm isn’t necessarily criminalized. For example, wage theft by employers isn’t generally criminalized, but it is definitely harmful.

Even if the criminal punishment system were free of racism, classism, sexism, and other isms, it would not be capable of effectively addressing harm. For example, if we want to reduce (or end) sexual and gendered violence, putting a few perpetrators in prison does little to stop the many other perpetrators. It does nothing to change a culture that makes this harm imaginable, to hold the individual perpetrator accountable, to support their transformation, or to meet the needs of the survivors.

A Black, Indigenous, and people of color survivor-led transformative justice movement has emerged in the past two decades to offer a different vision for ending violence and transforming our communities.

A world without harm isn’t possible and isn’t what an abolitionist vision purports to achieve. Rather, abolitionist politics and practice contend that disposing of people, by locking them away in jails and prisons, does nothing significant to prevent, reduce, or transform harm in the aggregate. It rarely, if ever, encourages people to take accountability for their actions, instead delegating responsibility to a third party—one that has been built to hide social and political failures. An abolitionist imagination takes us along a different path.

None of us has all of the answers, or we would have ended oppression already. But if we keep building the world we want, trying new things, and learning from our mistakes, new possibilities emerge.

Here’s how to begin.

First, when we set about trying to transform society, we must remember that we ourselves will also need to transform. Our imagination of what a different world can be is limited. We are deeply entangled in the very systems we are organizing to change. White supremacy, misogyny, ableism, classism, homophobia, and transphobia exist everywhere. We have all so thoroughly internalized these logics of oppression that if oppression were to end tomorrow, we would be likely to reproduce previous structures. Being intentionally in relation to one another, a part of a collective, helps to not only imagine new worlds but also to imagine ourselves differently. Join some of the many organizations, faith groups, and ad hoc collectives that are working to learn and unlearn—for example, what it feels like to actually be safe or those that are naming and challenging white supremacy and racial capitalism.

Second, we must imagine and experiment with new collective structures that enable us to take more principled action, such as embracing collective responsibility to resolve conflicts. We can learn lessons from revolutionary movements, like Brazil’s Landless Workers Movement, that have noted that when we create social structures that are less hierarchical and more transparent, we reduce violence and harms.

Third, we must simultaneously engage in strategies that reduce contact between people and the criminal legal system. Abolitionists regularly engage in organizing campaigns and mutual aid efforts that move us closer to our goals. We must remember that the goal is not to create a gentler prison and policing system because, as I have noted, a gentler prison and policing system cannot adequately address harm. Instead, we want to divest from these systems as we create the world in which we want to live.

Fourth, as scholar and activist Ruth Wilson Gilmore notes, building a different world requires that we not only change how we address harm, but that we change everything. The prison industrial complex is linked in its logics and operation with all other systems—from how students are pushed out of schools when they don’t perform as expected to how people with disabilities are excluded from our communities to the ways in which workers are treated as expendable in our capitalist system.

Changing everything might sound daunting, but it also means there are many places to start, infinite opportunities to collaborate, and endless imaginative interventions and experiments to create. Let’s begin our abolitionist journey not with the question, “What do we have now and how can we make it better?” Instead, let’s ask, “What can we imagine for ourselves and the world?” If we do that, then boundless possibilities of a more just world await us.

items.title: Baraza
items.summary: Originating in East Africa, a baraza is a kind of large community gathering held to discuss import- ant matters, share information, make collective decisions, and hold leaders to account. It is one of many customary practices of direct democracy.
items.body:
Countless elders, adults, youth, and children converge beneath tents or in the shade of an old tree. The group welcomes those who join. The first agenda item is presented for deliberation.

“Baraza” is a Swahili word for large community gatherings that have been part of the fabric of village life in East Africa long before European colonization. Similar gatherings happen under other names in a variety of forms around the world, especially in the Global South. They provide a space for villages to participate in collective problem solving and can attract hundreds or even thousands of people. Political movements and organizations can tap into these spaces to bring forward critical issues, such as mitigating climate change, curbing domestic violence, or exposing a corrupt local leader. Barazas are a reminder that democracy is about more than voting and elections— it also means creating spaces where people can hear from one another and continue to participate in the issues that matter to them.

While barazas don’t always hold official power, their social power is real. Incompetent civil servants, greedy businesspeople, and dishonest politicians usually refuse to show up at barazas, for fear of being publicly shamed for their actions. Powerful individuals who do attend may feel social pressure to make amends for any harms they have caused to their communities.

Barazas often assemble during crises affecting a whole community, enabling people to propose and discuss possible solutions. Once a solution is agreed upon, participants may form teams to develop plans for implementing it. Barazas are horizontal, directly democratic mechanisms for community organizing.

While it would be reductive to say that all precolonial East African societies practiced collective leadership, baraza-like meetings are ancient. Later in postcolonial history, shared decision-making was an integral component of the early years of ujamaa, a cooperative economics ideology and program championed by socialist Julius Nyerere where approximately 250 families would collectively govern their land and community. More recently in Abim—one of Uganda’s districts most neglected by the state—barazas have been used to evaluate the extent to which civil servants used local tax revenues responsibly. These citizen meetings offered stronger community oversight of local infrastructure, ultimately improving Abim’s roads and bridges.

Inspired by victories like this, the dispersed resistance network Solidarity Uganda organizes fireplace gatherings—the customary “meeting place” in many East African societies—to deliberate on issues like education, governance, and human rights. In 2022, a series of murders of university students in Bushenyi prompted members of one fireplace gathering to create a strategy that would force district leaders to take the matter seriously. They resolved to padlock local government offices, which prompted police to publicly address the matter they had neglected and deploy night patrols. There have been no murders in the area since.

People around the world have organized baraza-like gatherings under various names. Even while living under abhorrent fascism and violence, the people of Kurdistan gather regularly through one of the most intricate systems of direct democracy globally. The Constitutional Movement in Kuwait from 1986 to 1992 employed diwanyat, or local assemblies held at personal homesteads, to organize at a time when street protests were illegal. Due to cultural norms, police would never enter a diwanya. Diwanyat enabled mass mobilization, fueling a movement that eventually achieved the reinstatement of the suspended constitution.

Barazas and equivalent gatherings throughout the world emerge differently in different communities, but they tend to share a few basic steps. A coordinating team of volunteers determines the time, location, and agenda. That team then announces it to the public by tacking a sign to a centrally located bulletin board, posting on social media, or sending announcements home to the parents of school children. When the baraza convenes, the participation of all who show up is valued. Although driven by the discussion and input of attendees, barazas are most effective when they have an agenda to keep them on track. Lastly, if appropriate, coordinators inform participants of the next baraza’s time and location, and encourage them to invite others.

Not merely a mechanism for changing policies and making decisions, barazas practice sharing power and responsibility. They prefigure a world where vast distance between “governance” and “the people” is not inevitable. In the shade of the baraza, neighbors discover new aspects of their collective self-actualization and nudge more formal institutions toward genuine accountability.

items.title: Community Broadband Networks
items.summary: Access to reliable internet service has become a basic need in most of the world, yet many communities either lack service in their area or are priced out by corporate monopolies. Community broadband is a way for people rather than companies to own the means of accessing the internet, securing lower prices and faster service in the process.
items.body:
Households throughout the world often rely on local government to provide them with access to basic utilities such as electricity, gas, and water. In the last two decades, many cities have added another utility to the list of services they provide: internet access.

Community broadband providers offer an alternative to corporate telecom monopolies. In this model, a community-based entity such as a local municipal body, a tribal government, a cooperative, or a nonprofit organization builds and may also manage a network, offering services to residents and businesses. This allows communities to gain control over internet access prices, policies, and critical infrastructure.

In 1994, the city of Glasgow, Kentucky, created the first municipal broadband network in the United States after their cable monopoly frustrated customers with poor customer service and by neglecting to modernize infrastructure in rural areas. When the municipal electric utility in Glasgow began building its own network, the incumbent cable company lowered prices by 75% in an effort to discourage the competition. The struggle gained national attention for the town. Since forming its own internet service provider, the city has been able to adapt the network to community needs and keep prices low.

Rural areas are not the only regions ignored by traditional telecom companies. In Detroit, Michigan, over 35 percent of homes are not on the internet, with a majority of those being low-income households. To expand internet access, community groups came together in 2016 to form the Equitable Internet Initiative (EII), which connected over 150 homes in its pilot year. In addition to providing internet service, the EII offers technology literacy workshops, trains community “digital stewards,” and is in the process of forming a worker-owned utility cooperative to manage internet services. While neighborhood initiatives such as these may not always provide the fastest internet speeds, they can offer connectivity for very little cost to underserved communities.

This kind of model can easily be normalized and applied in neighborhoods across the globe. In Sweden, for instance, where community broadband is widespread, municipalities can choose between enabling a for-profit company to provide fiber access that upholds the community’s agreed-upon broadband standards or creating a local government entity to provide access. Among rural areas in the United States, existing utility cooperatives that provide electricity are increasingly expanding their services to include broadband access.

While local specificities need to be taken into account, there are several possible funding models for community broadband networks. Some cities turn to loans and revenue bonds, which are then paid back through the revenues collected by the network. Alternatively, they can borrow funds from other departments in the city government. Establishing broadband networks gradually, rather than across an entire city at once, can also keep costs low for municipalities. Cities and cooperatives are sometimes able to access public and philanthropic funds to provide for underserved residents.

Community broadband networks are able to keep prices low because, unlike national telecom companies, they aren’t required to generate a greater profit year after year. Additionally, for a municipal provider, a lower cost of service means the city pays less to connect its public libraries, schools, police departments, and government offices. While in the short-term, large telecoms may use their power to lower prices and undercut a community-based option, in the long-term, research suggests that community networks offer improved cost and service. Corporations have, however, fought fiercely to prevent them from doing so. 17 US states have corporation-written laws that restrict community networks.

Reliable internet access is now a necessity for the vast majority of people worldwide. Municipal broadband offers a way to make this crucial service accessible to areas that a traditional provider might neglect—such as rural towns and low-income neighborhoods—and to put its control into communities’ hands.

The Birth of Community Broadband

items.title: Community Land Trust
items.summary: A community land trust is a model of land or hous- ing ownership that isn’t run for profit but for the public good, for the benefit of families and commu- nities. Through collective control of land, a commu- nity can decide how they want to use it.
items.body:
Community Land Trusts (CLTs) are a powerful way to protect affordable homeownership by taking land and housing out of the hands of profit-driven market forces. In societies that view land as something to be bought or sold, CLTs treat it as a shared resource to be stewarded for a social purpose. According to community organizer and scholar John Davis, “What the CLT does better than any other organization … is to preserve affordability when economic times are good and protect its homes and homeowners when times are bad. In the scorched landscape of the [United States’] national mortgage crisis, CLTs are almost alone in reporting few defaults and even fewer foreclosures.”

In a CLT, housing and other buildings are under “dual ownership.” The CLT is a nonprofit entity that owns the land, while families (or a cooperative association, or developers) own the buildings. The CLT signs a long-term lease with the building owners for the use of the land. Through restrictions put on these leases, the land trust puts a cap on the resale price of homes and requires that homes be sold to lower-income families. Government subsidies can be used to bring down the price of the homes and put them within reach of low and moderate-income families. These subsidies are attached to the homes, so they stay affordable for future generations of buyers.

As nonprofit organizations governed by community members on behalf of a social mission, CLTs are more likely to be committed to their community’s agenda and vision—supporting the stability and welfare of their neighborhoods—compared to single-family or investor owners. Most CLTs require that CLT houses be occupied by their owners, meaning they cannot be an investment property.

CLTs can be started as stand-alone non-profit organizations or as programs, subsidiaries, or spin-offs from existing non-profits. Funding a CLT requires a creative combination of government and private grants, loans, and donations. Donations can be in the form of money, land, or legal and technical assistance.

There are over 250 CLTs throughout the United States. They began spreading in the second half of the 20th century, starting with organizers in the Black liberation movement in the late 1960s. Considered by many to be the first community land trust, New Communities Inc. was founded by leaders in the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee to provide for Black families who were getting kicked off their land by white farmers in Georgia. In spite of their effectiveness in stabilizing and empowering communities and protecting low and moderate-income families, CLTs in the United States represent a very small fraction of housing, accounting for only about 10,000 units.

Land trusts can also be found around the globe. In Kenya, the Tanzania-Bodeni Community Land Trust developed in response to local housing needs and seeks to address urban settlement problems. The women-led Maria Auxiliadora housing project in Bolivia adapts the CLT model to build a community for low-income women and families. The Martín Peña Channel Community Land Trust (Fideicomiso de la Tierra del Caño Martín Peña) in Puerto Rico provides housing for a community of nearly 30,000 people. CLTs have also developed in European countries including England and Switzerland.

CLTs are changing with the times. Communities and governments have taken advantage of the flexibility of the strategy. While there are “classic” features to a CLT, it is an adaptable model that allows a community to incorporate the things that are important to them. Issues such as geographic area, how the land is used, affordability, lease provisions, and governance structure can be determined through community planning processes.

With local and national governments establishing CLTs to meet affordable housing goals, there is a risk that some new CLTs are not truly grounded in their communities. CLTs also face the challenge of having to secure funding up-front for land and homes, in addition to getting the support of the families and communities who will use the land and housing. This significant up-front effort to organize people and resources is an important consideration in pursuing CLTs over other forms of affordable housing.

The CLT model calls on landowners to work for the greater good rather than the greatest financial return for the individual. It treats land as a shared resource and housing as a fundamental human right.

items.title: Community Safety
items.summary: People who have experienced violence and abuse from police and within their communities have ad- opted creative ways of addressing their needs for safety. Movements for community safety address violence without relying upon police or prisons.
items.body:
Individuals and groups experiencing systemic oppression on the basis of race, gender, sexuality, disability, and other factors are often the most vulnerable to violence. Many of the systems and institutions that promise safety and security contribute to racial and sexual violence, as well as other forms of domination and abuse. As an alternative to relying on these institutions, people are creating community safety efforts grounded in their own neighborhoods and networks of people they know to help protect and heal from harm.

Around the world, women of color, particularly those who are lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender, have been at the forefront of creating groups and movements to protect their communities from violence, including the violence of police and other government institutions. A growing network has been forming to share experiences and techniques for community safety. Within the United States, the Oakland-based group Creative Interventions collected stories of how people intervened to prevent or stop family violence in their everyday lives. They also supported interventions by friends and family members of immigrant women experiencing domestic abuse, and produced a handbook of resources for anyone to use, informed by what they learned. In New York City, the Audre Lorde Project’s Safe OUTside the System Collective, meanwhile, created strategies based on community building and organizing to prevent racist and homophobic assaults on LGBTQ+ people of color in their Brooklyn neighborhood.

Their efforts often begin with developing ways to respond to interpersonal violence, which expand to strategies for preventing violence, intervening when harm occurs, and transforming the beliefs, patterns, and social and economic conditions that serve as root causes of violence. Some call this approach “transformative justice”—the work of not just addressing a specific instance of harm but also uprooting the underlying causes. Taken together, approaches for responding to interpersonal and state violence have become the basis of comprehensive visions for what it would mean to have truly safe communities.

Efforts to cultivate community safety often emphasize four goals: safety, healing, accountability, and transformation. To pursue these goals, practitioners start from the recognition that people experiencing harm tend to turn first to the people who are closest to them. Community safety can begin with those in relationship with each other, rather than by turning to the police or other government institutions such as the child welfare system. To make this possible, practitioners build their knowledge and capacity to pursue safety outside of state systems using storytelling, collective organizing, and skills trainings, among other methods. Some communities create new structures and cultures for safety by ensuring that they have resources and skills to meet their own needs. In Nairobi, Kenya, young people connected with St. Johns Ambulance have undergone first aid training so that they can administer help in emergency medical situations. This strategy has been especially important for groups in places where calls for medical assistance, including mental health support, could also bring armed police officers.

In addition to developing short-term responses and strategies, fostering safer communities entails a long-term commitment to challenging systems of oppression such as racism, sexism, homophobia, and transphobia that fuel abuse and violence. It involves cultivating value systems and ways of being that affirm the worth and dignity of all people. A community accountability process, for instance, might not only result in protection and support for a survivor of intimate partner violence, but also social, economic and mental health support for the person responsible for the abuse. Community safety is intimately connected to a vision of a world in which freedom from harm does not involve violent institutions like prisons, jails, and detention centers. Grassroots efforts to establish community safety facilitate the building of knowledge and skills so that people have the confidence to participate in liberatory violence prevention, intervention, and response.

Many groups of people who share the same apartment building, place of worship, or workplace have not established values, principles, and commitments to support the safety of their most vulnerable members. But that does not mean it is too late to start. All communities have the capacity to help the people in them experience safety.
