Beyond Survival: Strategies and Stories from the Transformative Justice Movement

items.title: Community-owned Sports Teams
items.summary: Community-owned sports teams share manage- ment responsibilities, ownership, and profit with a team’s stakeholding supporters.
items.body:
Around the world, a combination of mismanagement, lack of regulations, and inequitable wealth distribution has driven sports fans to feel increasingly disconnected from the affairs of their favorite teams. In the UK and elsewhere, football clubs and other sports teams have largely transitioned out of local ownership and into the hands of corporate owners with no real connection to the area and few interests beyond turning a profit. These enterprising, wealth-seeking owners or ownership groups buy a team for its business potential, only to sell it off a few years later at a higher price. As clubs have suffered financial losses under this model, their local supporters feel that this practice is unsustainable and that it diverges from the true interests of the fans. In response, supporters around the world have led efforts to collectively buy back their teams.

Community ownership allows teams to be managed by the people who are most invested in their success. Typically, community ownership structures include both a large membership and an elected governing board. Elections take place regularly to keep the board accountable; each member gets one vote, no matter how much money they’ve invested. In some clubs, board members may appoint a non-elected general member to the primary governing body to fill gaps in the skill set. For example, in a board of older supporters, it might be necessary to bring on a younger person to do youth outreach.

Membership fees and costs involved in becoming an owner of a team are kept low to encourage a broad and inclusive membership. The UK football club AFC Wimbledon, for instance, is majority-owned by a supporters’ trust with approximately 3,000 members. All members can access a website where they can share questions and opinions with other community members and the board. The club reinvests all revenue into itself according to an agreed-on code of ethics.

One frequent criticism of supporters’ trusts is that members equate their team’s success with the fulfillment of their own narrow financial self-interest. But in fact, the individual is not the center of a community-owned club model. Rather, many of these trusts are registered as community benefit (CB) societies, requiring them to prove that they primarily serve community interests, not those of their members. In the UK, an officially designated CB can pay a small dividend to its individual members, but it is usually no more than 2 percent above the interest rate.

Any existing assets are protected by an asset-lock clause, which prevents members from voting to privatize the organization or to distribute wealth outside of it.

In Germany, community-owned club regulation is different. All football clubs are majority-owned by their fans, following a 50+1 model, which stops wealthy corporations and individuals from controlling the teams. Greater regulation prevents clubs from filing for bankruptcy, and a strict licensing system weeds out clubs that are not properly tracking their finances. Similar supporters’ trusts have been implemented in Spain, too.

In the United States, there is a single community-owned American football team: the Green Bay Packers. When the team faced financial difficulties in the 1920s and 1930s, it sold stock to the community to keep itself from going bankrupt. That model persists today, and the team is a publicly owned nonprofit corporation with over 360,000 individual shareholders. Shareholders have voting rights and can participate in annual owner meetings, but their stock cannot appreciate in value and there are no season ticket privileges.

Community-owned teams can struggle with marketing and expanding their fan bases, as well as attracting funding. Another challenge is attracting volunteers on match days—but people are more likely to volunteer for a club that they have a stake in than one that is privately owned. This is just one advantage that this model affords in comparison to private ownership. Having a collective of people who are invested in the club long-term allows it to build better relationships with local partners and ensures greater moral and financial accountability in club governance. Successful supporters’ trusts have core governing policies, delegated authority, business knowledge, and fans who elevate the interests of the collective above those of the individual.

Community-owned sports teams, in contrast to their privately-owned and profit-driven counterparts, contribute to people-powered economies.

items.title: Cooperative Education
items.summary: Cooperative education builds the skills, consciousness, and culture of everyday people to grow and govern social and economic democracy. It teaches us to unlearn dominant values of individualism and greed and uplifts the sacred and interconnected nature of all people.
items.body:
Cooperatives are not a silver bullet, but through member co-ownership and co-governance, they foster skills and culture that build more robust practices of local democracy. Cooperative education is therefore foundational for a more inclusive future. Building democracy requires teaching democracy, and ensuring that all people have access to the lessons of past experience in running democratic economies.

The exclusion of cooperative curriculum from formal business schools around the world pushes the cooperative sector to the sidelines. Of the 30 most prominent business management textbooks, only three mention co-ops, all in negative or neutral light. In some ways, this shouldn’t be a surprise. Most business schools are largely funded by wealthy alumni and multinational corporations, who don’t stand to benefit from the growth of the cooperative sector.

It wasn’t always this way. Before World War II, cooperatives were commonly found in textbooks. In the United States, the Department of Agriculture helped to establish centers to support cooperative development at state colleges, and such centers still exist at Cornell University, the University of Missouri, the University of Wisconsin, and elsewhere. Even Stanford University was founded in part on the premise of advancing education about cooperative economics, although this wish of its founder has been mainly ignored.

To address the lack of cooperative education, Saint Mary’s Business School launched the first cooperative business program in North America. Approved in 2002, Saint Mary’s Masters of Business Administration (MBA) allows students to enter business education through a cooperative lens, gaining fluency in mainstream business content while simultaneously critiquing it and cultivating an ability to build and run alternatives.

Full-fledged university programs in cooperative business are new to North America, but they draw inspiration from a global network of co-op educators. Kenya, India, and the Canadian province of Quebec all boast meaningful co-op sectors backed by formal cooperative education in universities. As a growing movement, new voices are helping to evolve and mature the field of cooperative education. Cooperative education can look different in different settings. Many universities in the United States still offer a cooperative center within a business school or a certification program that allows students to learn strategies for cooperative workplaces and collaborate with local co-ops. Some schools, like EdVisions Cooperatives and the Friends Institute, are run as cooperatives. Other organizations, like the Rocky Mountain Farmers Union, offer children’s summer camps that teach cooperative leadership skills.

Cooperative education is also happening through efforts to form or reorganize universities as cooperatives. Operating a university as a cooperative allows students to live and experience values of democracy and civil participation, and, in this way, contribute to one of the purposes of higher education. Cooperative universities recast students and faculty as active participants in democracy, increase their personal investment in the institution, and challenge the modern university’s profit motive. Mondragon University, for example, operates as a workers’ cooperative. Students earn their tuition through working within co-op businesses within the university, which together enable the university to operate, while faculty invest in the university and receive surplus funds as a salary.

In addition to fostering social and economic democracy, cooperative education matters for a variety of practical reasons. One example is accounting. Traditional accounting systems are built to help managers and owners track, manage, and maximize profits for shareholders. But cooperatives serve the needs of their communities and are expected to balance financial sustainability with other goals like job creation, access to quality goods and services, and ecological restoration. Without protocols to track these broader goals, narrow systems for capitalist accounting can easily distort the core intentions of a coop. An unfortunate trap is that the MBA graduate with the wrong accounting tools can destroy the culture and value of a cooperative because they aren’t tracking and accounting for the right things.

The field of marketing is also an evolving discipline within cooperative education. Investor-driven businesses are structured to “buy low and sell high,” using cheap materials and labor and selling at the highest prices that customers will pay (voluntarily or not). At the same time, mainstream marketing trains consumers to connect personal identity and value to the things they buy, while ignoring harm to workers, the environment, or even to themselves. This kind of marketing doesn’t make sense for the co-op sector. If you’re part of a community-owned grocery store, what does marketing look like? Do you mimic traditional grocery stores that place candy at children’s eye-level so parents can’t check out without a fight? How might marketing for cooperatives create healthier and more responsible consumer patterns while ensuring customer loyalty and sales? Marketing and accounting, along with new approaches to human resources and governance, are among the most exciting innovations that cooperative education can bring to the private sector.

While Saint Mary’s University’s MBA program has now gained international recognition and attracted students from several countries, it faced notable challenges as the first program of its kind. It took years to secure a student pipeline to meet the school’s financial needs. The sector faces a vicious cycle: without co-ops, cooperative MBA programs struggle for viability. And without formal cooperative education, co-ops struggle to reach scale and market-share.

As the viability of formal cooperative education depends on market and regulatory conditions, the broadest task ahead is to inspire public belief and demand in a vision for a cooperative, just, and democratic economy.

items.title: Debt Abolition
items.summary: Over centuries, popular uprisings and indebted poor people have advocated for the abolition of debt and won. At a time when billions of people are harmed and oppressed by debt, the time has come for an international “jubilee” of debt forgiveness.
items.body:
In most mature capitalist societies, people are required to go into debt in order to access basic education, housing, and healthcare. Borrowers become beholden to lenders, who then use debt obligations to control and coerce whole communities. The same process that happens on a community and individual level also happens at national and global levels. Wealthier nations wield debt obligations over poorer nations, compelling them to sell public utilities to private companies, slash social services, and enable the exploitation of their natural resources.

Today, global debt equals more than 3.5 times the value of the entire global economy, and it is growing.Yet history shows us that unjust debt can be abolished.

Movements calling for the cancellation of debts are growing. After the 2007–2008 foreclosure crisis and recession in the United States, a group called Strike Debt (now The Debt Collective) organized a “Rolling Jubilee,” which raised donations by crowdfunding, bought $32 million in outstanding debt for a fraction of its value, and forgave all of it. In recent years, mass protests against systemic racism and police brutality have led to calls to buy back debt in Black communities. During the 2020 global pandemic, social movements worldwide called for a mass cancellation of rent.

These movements have deep roots. The idea of periodic debt forgiveness appears in many religious traditions—most famously the Hebrew Bible’s “jubilee,” a law stipulating that all debts be canceled every seven years. Islamic law has long held that charging interest on debt is immoral, and it strictly forbids usury.

The tactic of buying back debt can yield results. By 2019, the group behind the Rolling Jubilee won $600 million in student debt discharges for 28,000 former students of Corinthian College through its debtors’ union. The Debt Collective found that these debtor organizing tactics to dispute and ultimately cancel debt were highly effective at making meaningful change in debtors’ lives.

Sonya Renee Taylor, a Black author and activist in the United States, spearheaded the #BuyBackBlackDebt initiative in July 2020. This decentralized mutual aid campaign is a way of “mending the relationship between Black people and white people,” she said. “It is about ending the relationship of extraction and benefit at the detriment of Black people’s lives, opportunity, wealth, and resources. It is about balancing karmic debt, spiritual debt, energetic and relational debt—so that we can figure out how to be in a right relationship with one another.” The mechanics of the project are simple: Taylor calls on white individuals to reach out to Black friends, colleagues, and family and offer to buy back some or all of their debt. To date, the project has bought $100,000 in debt through the participation of nearly 200 contributors.

Political movements are also aiming to challenge the global inequities created and sustained through debt. One grassroots effort, the Jubilee Debt Campaign, calls on the Global North and powerful global financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank to support a debt amnesty that would eliminate debts owed by countries in the Global South, especially those whose wealth was stolen through colonization. This campaign recognizes that exploitative policies by institutions and nations that benefited from colonization have continued to oppress post-colonial countries by subjecting them to predatory indebtedness.

The Jubilee 2000 movement took important steps to shed light on one of colonialism’s current manifestations: the injustice of high-interest debt owed to countries and corporations in the Global North by countries in the Global South. Between 1998 and 2015, the campaign won $130 billion of debt cancellation for 18 lower income countries, including Ecuador, Burkina Faso, the Philippines, and Argentina. Already, those countries and others had resisted paying the debts owed to the IMF and World Bank for decades, and audits later revealed that much of the debt was illegitimate and violated international law.

What does abolition mean for people and countries forced to live with the burden of debt? The urgent health and economic crisis caused by COVID-19 pushed countries in Latin America and Africa into impossible decisions: pay back debt owed to the Global North or provide healthcare for their populations. People in the US faced similarly dire choices, often forced to decide between paying off their mounting debt from medical bills and education or affording food and housing.

Debt isn’t just about money. Debt is a power imbalance— often along racist and classist lines—that can mean the difference between life and death.

Debt Justice
Black Debt, White Debt

items.title: Design Global, Manufacture Local
items.summary: The rise of the internet age has seen the cre- ation of a digital “design commons”: a vast pool of knowledge and blueprints—for everything from farm equipment to malaria drugs—that is freely accessible to communities around the world, for use in local production and economic development.
items.body:
Imagine a community of farmers trying to find more sustainable and effective ways to produce. Through prototyping, they begin to develop equipment specifically suited to low-cost organic farming. As they experiment with designs and test equipment, they refine their knowledge of what yields results for their community. Instead of keeping the fruits of their intellectual labor to themselves, they decide to share them with the world, publishing their designs online for any internet-equipped farmer to adapt to their local context.

“Cosmolocal production” is a term for the process in which globally shared knowledge and designs enable communities to meet their needs locally. The growing knowledge commons includes designs for farm equipment, medicine, food-processing tools, and renewable energy tech. The three main motivations that drive cosmolocal production include livelihood, problem-solving, and sustainability.

First, cosmolocal production has the potential to catalyze a livelihood revolution. For instance, L’Atelier Paysans is a cooperative that conducts farm equipment prototyping and design workshops throughout France, then shares its designs freely. Farm Hack is an association started in the northeastern United States that does similar work. Shared designs for tools like irrigators and cultivators can dramatically lower the costs of equipment that might otherwise be too expensive for small-scale entrepreneurs. This model, applied not only to farming but also to other industries, can revolutionize how people earn a living and provide for one another.

Cosmolocal production is also about problem-solving through production at a small scale. The international humanitarian relief organization Field Ready uses portable molds and 3D printers to support the recovery efforts of disaster-hit communities across southern Asia. Here, specialized medical equipment—or even basic tools like buckets to fetch water—can take weeks or months to arrive at a disaster zone. Field Ready’s approach moves production to sites of disaster to address the problem without delay.

Similarly, Open Source Malaria uses shared knowledge and community contributions to develop malaria-fighting drugs, which can otherwise be prohibitively expensive for people in poor countries. The Open Insulin Project in Oakland, California has adopted a similar approach to insulin production in the United States, where the drug is exorbitantly expensive due to price gouging and predatory patenting. What if these and other medications, once proven effective, could be produced by any sufficiently resourced lab in any country?

The third main contribution of cosmolocal production concerns transforming the destructive logic of industrial production into something regenerative, something that can drive a transition to emission-free production, carbon drawdown, and local control. Netherlands-based company Precious Plastics, for instance, designs machines that recycle and upcycle plastic waste into new products. It has cultivated an international community of designers and volunteers to develop the systems, and its machine blueprints can be freely downloaded so that any locality can build its own solution to the plastic crisis. In the Maharashtra area of India, Solar Urja freely distributes its design for a cheap, repairable solar lamp that can replace dirty-burning kerosene lanterns. In conjunction with Solar Urja’s rollout of the new lamps to villages, repair centers have been established to fix broken ones, creating local employment opportunities. Additionally, a cooperative run by local Indigenous people produces solar panels for the lamps.

Global challenges like the climate crisis are too urgent to allow profit-oriented intellectual property regimes to hinder progress. Patents on critical technologies can take decades to expire, and most people cannot afford to pay excessive royalties for the technologies that are fundamental for planetary survival. Open access to knowledge and design can enable communities to adopt low- or no-carbon technologies with minimal obstacles. When designs are shared, anyone can be a participant, a contributor, and an agent of change in creating a better world.

items.title: Food Sovereignty
items.summary: Food sovereignty is the right of communities to access healthy and culturally appropriate food and to have control over agricultural and food production systems. More than just access to food, it means being able to choose our food and to participate in producing it.
items.body:
More and more communities today have little or no say over how their food is produced. With the rise of multinational agribusiness corporations, farmers are locked in a race to the bottom, competing to sell their products to middlemen at ever lower prices, while consumers continue to face rising food prices. Additionally, with more than 50 percent of the world’s population now living in cities, growing and gathering food is no longer part of daily life for most people. Many people around the world depend on aid for their food, which is often of poor nutritional quality and culturally inappropriate.

The concept of food sovereignty concerns communities’ rights to have autonomy and control over their food consumption, production, and distribution. But there are barriers to accessing food, like cost and availability, and the ability of people to produce food, which relies on having land and knowledge. The food sovereignty movement first gained popular attention in the mid-1990s through the efforts of La Via Campesina, an international network of farmers formed to defend peasant agricultural practices and to address the insecurity that farmers experience globally. The movement gained greater momentum in 2007, when the International Forum for Food Sovereignty was held in Mali. There, the Declaration of Nyéléni establishing a definition of food sovereignty was written and signed by representatives from over 80 countries. From the beginning, the concept was political. Then and now, it challenges widespread trade and agricultural policies, as well as the powerful interests that benefit from them.

There are many examples of initiatives that show us what food sovereignty looks like. Community-supported agriculture (CSA) programs, for instance, are based on a mutual commitment between producers and consumers to share the risks and rewards of agriculture. The CSA concept exists around the world under many different names and arrangements, shaped by the unique needs of the local farmers and consumers.

In Japan, the CSA model first emerged as the teikei system. Teikei, which means “cooperation,” is a system in which community members contract a farmer to grow for them for a season. The payment given to the farmer is not based on the crop yield, but rather reflects what the farmer needs for the season. For instance, a group of 100 community members had each member pay 1 percent of their annual income in exchange for 1 percent of what the farmer was able to produce that season. Teikei members also contribute the labor to the farm, including doing intensive tasks such as weeding, harvesting, and delivering produce to members’ homes.

As the concept has grown and spread around the world, CSA programs have drifted away from their original ideal of food sovereignty and toward consumer demands, with farmers often offering customized share sizes and making consumer participation in growing, harvesting, and distribution optional.

Another powerful initiative that supports food sovereignty are the cooperatives of small-scale farmers who band together to pool marketing, administration, and logistical labor and costs. At their best, these cooperatives enable farmers to reduce their costs and challenge large corporations head-on, while retaining local ownership, culture, and values.Yet these cooperatives, like CSAs, run the risk of compromising with the market and losing their community focus in pursuit of large-scale production.

At the national level, the battle for food sovereignty has brought together organizations and individuals to lobby governments to adopt holistic food policies. Food Secure Canada was formed as a coalition of local initiatives in 2001 under the banner of food security. In 2009, the coalition’s framework shifted to food sovereignty, which led to a national campaign to lobby the government for more inclusive food policies.

Food sovereignty must be grounded in local practice, but effective organizing and collaboration between grassroots organizations has led to the formation of international organizations such as the International Planning Committee on Food Sovereignty (IPC). The IPC has successfully introduced reforms and brought food sovereignty principles to the table of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. The IPC has changed how food security is discussed at the international level, bringing stakeholders to the table, such as peasant farmers, who were previously excluded in these policy meetings.

In the face of frequent temptations to compromise with the status quo, the principles of food sovereignty provide an essential North Star for the farmers producing our food, the communities striving to nourish their families, and everyone in between.

items.title: Free/Libre and Open-Source Software
items.summary: Transparent software written by and for the people can help us avoid corporate exploitation of our pri- vacy, data, and money.
items.body:
In a world where so much of the economy is based on private ownership, the rise of free/libre, opensource software (FLOSS) as a central part of the digital economy represents a striking act of resistance. At the core of FLOSS is the belief that people should control the technology they build and use, and that technology is a commons that works better when shared. The underlying code must be “open source”—meaning that anyone can access, examine, and verify it. For example, when developers claim a piece of software is secure or does not surveil its users, others can inspect the code and come to their own conclusions. FLOSS is also typically available free of cost, so it opens doors for communities that cannot afford to pay for expensive corporate software.

With FLOSS, users can “fork” the code—copying it and creating their own tools out of it. Some licenses, particularly those that go under the banner of “free software,” require that all adaptations of the code be shared under the same kind of license. The result is a non-proprietary digital commons—a pool of interrelated tools that no single company or person can claim exclusive ownership over and in which no single entity can constrain innovation by limiting access to the software’s code. An example of how this works is that, while Microsoft and Apple tightly control the releases of their operating systems, there are hundreds of free GNU/Linux “distributions,” customized to various user preferences and needs through diverse FLOSS communities. The competitive influence of FLOSS also helps to drive down the price of proprietary software. In Latin America, where FLOSS is widely used, a legitimate, licensed copy of Microsoft Office only costs $10, down from hundreds of dollars previously. Further, activist-led cooperatives (like MayFirst.coop) and collectives (like Riseup.net) can use FLOSS tools to provide services to movement groups without relying on corporate services.

Proprietary software generates profit not only through sales and subscriptions but through controlling user behavior and extracting user data. For example, while Facebook may be free to use, its terms of service allow it to use or monetize any content a user generates on its website without compensation or consent. Uber profits from the labor of drivers who have no way of knowing how the underlying algorithms that calculate payment for that labor actually work. In contrast, FLOSS projects disclose their algorithms and data collection practices, making companies that build products using FLOSS much less likely to engage in questionable business models. Although FLOSS began largely among hobbyists working during unpaid time, developers can increasingly earn income from the work they do, including by providing technical support, customization, and computing power to the people who use their software. They may also receive income from the crowdfunding, grants, or investment that are given to a project in good faith before it begins. With crowdfunding, people are often happy to lend their support when project developers can clearly explain a compelling vision of meeting a community need. This means that crowdfunded projects are more likely to be designed to meet community needs from start to finish. Grant funding works well for projects that serve the public interest. Increasingly, software companies are also paying their employees to contribute to FLOSS projects that their products rely on.

Still, many FLOSS projects experience challenges with sustainability over the long term. Although the FLOSS movement is well established, corporations undermine FLOSS projects in many ways, such as by encouraging features and improvements that suit their own needs and preventing efforts that could compete with their proprietary products. In some cases, such as Google’s Linux-based Android operating system, FLOSS tools have been used to enable widespread corporate surveillance. There are also frequent legal challenges to FLOSS; most often, this occurs when proprietary software uses FLOSS components and violates the license when they charge people for that software. Finally, relying on corporate hiring practices and hobbyists with free time means that FLOSS projects have struggled to attract contributors with diverse backgrounds, identities, and income levels. Keeping the commons truly shared and accessible requires constant vigilance and intentional effort.

As corporations increasingly use FLOSS software in products for clients engaged in surveillance, policing, and weapons development, many FLOSS contributors are organizing to demand higher ethical standards. The Ethical Source Movement seeks to build on the achievements of FLOSS by requiring users to adhere to international labor and human-rights standards. Others feel that such restrictions would ultimately harm the software commons by adding overly complex constraints.

Given its subversive ethos with respect to the dominant capitalist logics of privatization and profiteering, it is easy to mistake FLOSS for a small or marginal movement within the software world. But more than 90 percent of the software that runs the internet is FLOSS. Much of this software is well-known and widely used, like the Firefox web browser, the Android mobile operating system, and GNU/Linux, which itself has hundreds of different spinoffs. The power of a digital commons has become clear. Increasingly, the struggle underway is about whether FLOSS will ultimately serve ordinary users or corporate interests seeking to co-opt it.

FLOSS has many layers. It is a legal definition that challenges copyright. It is a method of open, transparent, and collaborative innovation. Most importantly, it is a culture for creating trustworthy software that respects its users and contributes to a digital commons for all.

items.title: Informal Settlement Networks
items.summary: Residents in informal urban settlements are form- ing organizations and networks to demand their human rights and improve their quality of life.
items.body:
The industrialization of cities in the global South has spurred economic growth. But that growth often does not appear in the incomes of the poor and working-class people whose work makes industrialization possible. Governments, both local and those providing aid from abroad, consistently fail to address the needs of these groups. Refugees, survivors of environmental disasters, and people who have been displaced due to discrimination by race, class, and other identities find shelter in informal settlements in countries including India and Kenya.

While informal settlements, or slums, are characterized by overpopulation and a lack of basic amenities like sewage systems, they are home to vibrant communities. When these communities organize themselves into networks at the local, national, and international levels, the settlements are able to share knowledge, collaborate, and create strategies for building power and meeting their needs.

Savings groups provide one of the building blocks for these networks. Here, community members pool together their money to form a fund that can be drawn from to support projects and meet needs in the community. In South Africa, one fund has loaned money to more than 2,000 members for business and livelihood projects, and it has a 95 percent repayment rate. But these savings groups do more than just pool money. As one member of a Liberian informal settlement network reported, “They collect people and build a critical mass. When the savings groups are networked, federations are born.”

For example, in Kenya, 15 to 20 women might form a network, supported by a small amount of funding that enables them to train and work together. Their network would then become part of a city-wide federation of other small networks. Each local group or settlement chooses its leaders—chair, secretary, and treasurer—and then creates teams: a finance team, a data team, and a documentation team (which trains young people to collect data through GIS, gather stories, and contribute to a blog). The leaders of each of these local networks congregate every three months in city and county forums to discuss challenges and decisions. Reports from local meetings are delivered by a representative of each county at the national level. At the national level, a working group of 12 people are selected according to their skills for partnering with governments and officials.

Informal settlement networks raise the voices of people living in slums, making their lived experiences and realities the basis for change. Instead of a top-down approach, the residents of the settlements decide what projects are most important for addressing their needs.

One of the primary needs facing informal settlements is secure housing tenure. Just about every informal settlement around the world is dealing with constant evictions and the immense harm these cause to residents. By organizing together, informal settlement networks can fight back.

In Nigeria, large-scale evictions in Lagos and Port Harcourt inspired the Nigerian Federation to support community-led mapping and profiling of informal settlements. They collected data from every informal settlement in both cities and used GPS boundary maps and geo-tagged information about the utilities (water, electricity, etc.) to make the informal settlements visible and support community members organizing to prevent evictions. At the same time, an allied NGO called the Nigerian SDI Alliance used multimedia to shine a public spotlight on the crisis.

Women are at the center of many of these settlement networks—negotiating for space, organizing for the right to stay, and building necessary infrastructure. Women often organize the savings groups and hold leadership roles that reflect their knowledge as shapers of their communities and as those who are most negatively affected by poor conditions in the settlements. The data they gather is used in negotiations with local governments, and the money and resources they pool are used to meet acute needs in emergencies. Peer-to-peer learning occurs as one group of women trains the next on savings collection, data aggregation, and negotiation tools.

These networks connect settlements locally and around the world. One of the primary connectors of settlements globally is Slum Dwellers International, an organization made up of more than 30 federations (or networks) of informal settlements in Latin America, Africa, and Asia which supports learning and collaboration across national and regional borders. Federations working to stop evictions in India compare their experiences with those of federations in Kenya. Data collection methods are adapted from one settlement to another. Local leaders attend meetings with government officials in different parts of the world to share strategies for success.

Informal settlement networks are an important example of the grassroots power that poor people can have when they come together to provide for one another and demand what they need.

items.title: Land Justice
items.summary: All people have a right to permanent and secure land tenure as the source for many of our most basic needs. Through tools such as reparations, rematriation, easements, and land trusts, we can share the land fairly among the human and non-human citizens of planet Earth.
items.body:
The theft and private hoarding of land is part of the DNA of racial capitalism. Around 60 million hectares of the Global South is gobbled up by transnational corporations annually. In the United States alone, over 95 percent of the farmland is white-owned and increasingly corporate-controlled. This is the result of the violent expulsion of Indigenous people from their homelands, as well as the systematic exile of Black and Brown people from their land through government discrimination, lynching, redlining, and corporate land grabs. Colonial powers have imposed private property throughout much of the world, changing people’s relationship to land to one of property, as opposed to Indigenous understandings of land as a family member and a shared commons.

“To us in Africa, land was always recognized as belonging to the community,” said Julius Nyerere, the first president of Tanzania. “Each individual within our society had a right to use the land, because otherwise he could not earn his living and one cannot have the right to life without also having a right to some means of maintaining life. But the African’s right to land was simply the right to use it; he had no other right to it, nor did it occur to him to try and claim one.”

Millenia-old Indigenous land sharing tools like the huza cooperative system of the Krobo in Ghana and the matrilineal clan-based collective land ownership outlined in the Kayanerehkowa (Great Law of Peace) of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy demonstrate that private enclosure is not an inevitable phenomena. This essay discusses five legal tools that build on Indigenous wisdom and can support the work of land justice.

A land trust is an organization that holds land or conservation easements to protect properties for a public or environmental purpose. The first community land trust, New Communities Inc., was founded in 1969 by Black civil rights activists who had been violently attacked for their voter registration work. They purchased 5,700 acres of land shared among 500 families and established residences, cooperative farms, and a community center.

Building on this legacy, the Northeast Farmers of Color Land Trust, established in 2017, has been working to purchase 2,000 acres of land over the next five years to return to Indigenous, Black, and Brown farmers and land stewards. This land will be permanently protected through the legal mechanism of agricultural and cultural easements.

A property easement is a legal agreement where the title to a parcel of land remains with the landowner, but another person or organization is given use rights for a distinct purpose. While easements for conservation, agriculture, and utilities are most commonly known, the Native Land Conservancy (NLC) of the Mashpee Wampanoag is pushing forward the newer idea of cultural easements. Indigenous peoples’ rights to use their homelands for gathering, ceremony, burial, fishing, and wildcrafting can be restored using a cultural respect easement, which guarantees permanent access to the land even if ownership changes hands.

After recognizing where land has been stolen, rematriation is profoundly and simply an act of giving the land title back, with particular attention to the leadership of Indigenous women and trans people. The Sogorea Te’ Land Trust rematriated its first property in Huchiun territory, Bay Area, California, a traditional village site named Lisjan, which is now home to ceremonial grounds, gardens, emergency water catchment, and youth programs. Settlers can give their property deeds to native land trusts or directly to tribal entities, as in the case of the Ponca tribe accepting the return of their land along the Trail of Tears in 2018.

Near the end of the US Civil War, Rev. Garrison Frazier and 20 other Black Baptist and Methodist ministers met with Union General William T. Sherman to request allotments of 40 acres of land for each freed Black family in an area independent from whites. Fazier and the ministers explained, “We feel it very important that we obtain HOMES, owning our own shelters, and the ground, that we may raise fruit trees, concerning which our children can say, ‘These are ours.’” The Union agreed to give these allotments, but the famous promise of “forty acres and a mule” as reparations to former slaves was broken, and reparations were instead given to the plantation owners for their lost “property.”

The call for reparations continues today, through the work of the Movement for Black Lives and the Truth and Reparations project. Reparations has the potential to return 36 million acres of land to dispossessed Black people via public trust, and would guarantee cessations of harm, compensation of damages, and the restitution of livelihood and dignity.

Land justice, however, is not just a matter of changing who owns the land—it means recognizing that the earth cannot be owned by humans. We are guests on this planet, the younger siblings of creation, and we need to infuse our relationship to land with commensurate humility.

items.title: Legislative Theater
items.summary: Legislative theater is a participatory, community- based tool for proposing and enacting legislative and policy changes at any level of government.
items.body:
In 1992, Augusto Boal, the creator of Theatre of the Oppressed—a set of practices that empower people to change society using theater techniques and games—was faced with a dilemma. His theater work was an international sensation. Centers for the Theatre of the Oppressed were up and running in both France and Brazil, and people all over the world were practicing his ideas. At the same time, he was facing pressure at home in Brazil to run for city council in the city of Rio de Janeiro. Faced with a choice between the two, Boal decided not to choose. Instead, he combined the two possibilities and passions into one—and legislative theater was born.

To those who say that theater is nice but has no tangible outcomes, legislative theater may be the answer.

Legislative theater involves a short play about a particular issue or set of issues that ends in a crisis that the audience is invited to help solve by taking the place of one of the characters on stage. Audience interventions are followed by a brainstorm and discussion of policies or laws that could solve the problems that came up in the performance, or that could help bring about some of the solutions “spect-actors” (the engaged audience) had offered during the performance. In some iterations of legislative theater, mock legislatures debate bills drafted based on the laws or policies previously suggested in the theater exercise.

Boal’s election campaign literature explained his rationale: “I want to make politics but I don’t want to change my profession—I am a man of the theater! For me, this was always possible and now it is necessary: Theater is political and politics is theater.”

Boal was one of 42 city councilors elected from a field of 1,000 candidates. Over the next four years he developed the methods of legislative theater, forming 19 permanent Theatre of the Oppressed companies in Rio, which led to the introduction of 30 pieces of legislation, 13 of which resulted in legal changes.

The version of legislative theater Boal developed while he was a city councilor was an ideal arrangement that has proven difficult to match since. In his case, the elected official was the main convenor of the process, and was therefore in a position to act on the recommendations that emerged. In other cases, without one or more elected officials directly involved in the project, or without a firm and genuine commitment to the project from elected officials, it may be harder to achieve such results. Therefore, it is advisable to seek out legislators who are willing to play a role throughout the process, including fighting for the resulting recommendations in the actual legislature.

Like all Boal’s Theatre of the Oppressed practices, legislative theater trusts the wisdom of the audience, and provides them an opportunity to try out their ideas on stage to see how they might work in real life. Legislative theater simply takes that process one step further, making a direct connection between the ideas generated in the theater and the legislative process, which so desperately needs creative approaches to problem solving.

learn_more.title: The Courage to Be Happy: Augusto Boal, Legislative Theatre, and the 7th International Festival of the Theatre of the Oppressed
Experiments in Legislative Theatre
Drama Out of Crisis: How Theatre and Improv Teach Lessons in Sexual Consent

items.title: Limited-Equity Housing Cooperatives
items.summary: A limited-equity housing cooperative is a form of shared housing in which many individuals or fam- ilies jointly purchase housing, often a multi-unit home. Instead of owning a particular unit within it, each party owns a share of the property as a whole, which expands access to home ownership for lower-income people.
items.body:
In many countries, home ownership is a time-tested path to financial security. But today, rental costs in urban centers across the globe continue to rise at a rate faster than income, making it nearly impossible to save enough for a down payment on a house. Expensive down payments and the skyrocketing cost of urban real estate have pushed home ownership further out of reach for many on low to moderate incomes. Communities need a model which serves the housing needs of these income groups over time. There is an accessible alternative to a lifetime of high rent payments to landlords: limited-equity housing cooperatives (LEHCs).

Buying housing as a group presents many advantages. The most obvious is that buying a share in a housing cooperative costs less than buying an individual unit. Members of a housing cooperative have joint control over the governance of common areas like green spaces and playgrounds, and in the US, owners of a share in a co-op are entitled to the same tax deductions as homeowners.

Housing co-ops have a board of directors composed of member-residents which is responsible for overseeing the management of the property and planning for future renovations, much like a homeowner association.

A limited-equity co-op is one in which the resale value of shares is limited. This means that if someone decides to leave the co-op and sell their share, they will receive the purchase price plus interest which is capped at a certain amount. Limiting equity helps to keep homeownership accessible to low- to moderate-income families by protecting share prices from the speculative market. Most members end up paying the equivalent of 5 to 10 percent of the unit’s total cost for their initial share as opposed to the 20 percent down payment generally required to get a mortgage.

Not all housing co-ops impose restrictions on resale value. In fact, most co-op housing units are sold at the market rate. Some only restrict resale value until the first mortgage is paid off, which normally takes 30 to 40 years. Limited equity allows co-op residents to reap the benefits of home ownership, while also keeping housing affordable for generations to come. Many limited-equity co-ops have income restrictions, where membership is restricted to lower-income applicants to prevent wealthier buyers from crowding others out. Laws and regulations supporting LEHCs vary from state to state and country to country.

In the 1960s and ’70s, LEHCs experienced explosive popularity in major US cities like New York, Washington, DC, and San Francisco, thanks to a broad range of financing options including low interest rates and affordable loans for prospective builders of new co-ops. However, after their first mortgages were paid off, many LEHCs transitioned to market-rate cooperative housing. The number of accessible, limited-equity co-ops in the United States has dwindled.Yet the model still shows its promise. In 2005, a building slated for demolition in the Chinatown district of San Francisco became the center of a long, difficult fight for a limited-equity housing opportunity. The San Francisco Community Land Trust, Asian Law Caucus, and Chinatown Community Development Center teamed up to buy the building and transform it into a cooperative. The tenants were able to avoid eviction and are now owner-residents of their limited-equity co-op.

Establishing a LEHC entails a lot of heavy upfront costs and efforts such as buying land, funding new construction, and navigating housing code and laws. The journey from idea to occupancy is normally about five years, which can deter those who might benefit the most from being part of a co-op. To make matters worse, traditional banks often refuse to finance blanket mortgages to groups of lower-income people because they perceive them to be high-risk borrowers.

In the United States, when the size of a LEHC is above 20 units, it usually requires a professional management company. In larger co-ops, the board members need training in governance, financial planning, management oversight, and conflict resolution. In effect, the resident board members are overseeing a sizable ongoing business and stewarding a multimillion-dollar asset. The turnover of board members means that the latter need continuous training to ensure their capacity keeps up with the organizational and corporate needs of the cooperative.

The limited-equity model is most common in the United States, but housing cooperatives with many different structures and models have developed and proven viable all over the world. Furthermore, this idea of established institutions creating housing opportunities can be seen in several other countries such as the Philippines, India, Turkey, Egypt, and Singapore. In Italy, housing cooperatives are managed by four national groups. Social housing cooperatives throughout the country provide accessible homes for the elderly and for people with disabilities. Over 200,000 people in the Emilia Romagna region of Italy live in housing cooperatives.

In some places in Scandinavia, 15 to 20 percent of all homes exist in some form of housing co-op. Two national organizations in Sweden, HSB (founded by consumer cooperatives) and Riksbyggen (founded by the construction trade union movement) leveraged their access to land and assets to become the two main developers of the nation’s co-ops. Prior to 1991, national and local government policies enabled the development of municipal or limited-equity housing cooperatives in Sweden through the provision of land at below market price and loans below market interest rates. By having prospective members fund capital accounts, HSB and Riksbyggen raised the capital to provide their members with access to affordable housing. With their resources, these national organizations set up housing units and then transferred management responsibilities to the cooperative. In Sweden, applicant members of HSB must fund a deposit account with the organization to be in line for a new co-op apartment. The funds of these 120,000 non-housed members are a key supplier of funds for HSB to build new cooperative apartments.

In Uruguay, Federación Uruguaya de Cooperativas de Vivienda por Ayuda Mutua (FUCVAM) brings together over 500 mutual aid housing cooperatives comprising more than 25,000 families across the country. Their model is built on five core principles: solidarity, democratic participation, self-management, mutual-aid, and collective ownership (i.e. limited-equity). Founded in 1970 to unite and build the power of the housing cooperative movement, FUCVAM has shaped housing policy across Latin America, supported the formation of housing federations, and, most importantly, provided access to housing for hundreds of thousands of people across the continent.

With the support of funding entities and government policy, LEHCs could bring the dream of permanently affordable home ownership to many more people. Coops like these also transform the dream itself from one of individual ownership, to co-owned and co-managed communities.

items.title: Media Cooperatives
items.summary: Corporate consolidation has combined catastrophically with the rise of targeted online advertising to degrade the quality and independence of journalism. In the resulting tectonic shifts, there are opportunities to build democratic media outlets that channel power to communities and workers.
items.body:
Seismic shifts in how news is funded have plunged journalism into an extended crisis. As a result, movements and civil society have an opportunity to create a news ecosystem that is aligned with popular priorities. But this chance won’t last.

As tech platforms have cut deeply into advertising revenues, news organizations are more dependent on reader revenue, and this has given audiences more power. They now worry relatively less about corporate advertisers and relatively more about anything that could cause a wave of mass unsubscriptions. While this trend is broadly positive, the power of subscribers and donors remains mostly unrealized. A corporate representative can still influence coverage by conveying mild discomfort in a meeting about a multi-million-dollar ad buy. To match that, thousands of monthly donors would have to threaten to leave in unison.

The fact that these publications are for-profit means a big chunk of reader revenue is paying shareholders, not journalists. While no publication would exist without its readers, investors make the big decisions: hiring, firing, editorial mandates, and budgeting.

A truly accountable media economy needs readers to be actively involved in democratically shaping the news institutions they rely on. Media cooperatives, where workers and audience members collectively, proactively and democratically determine the direction of the organization provide an important example.

Cooperatives can take many forms, depending on their membership structure.

Worker cooperatives like Mexico’s La Jornada or Uruguay’s Brecha are democratically controlled by the workers. Consumer cooperatives like Germany’s Taz, England’s Bristol Cable or the NB Media Co-op in Canada are owned and funded by readers, who employ journalists to carry out the mandate. Multi-stakeholder cooperatives like Scotland’s The Ferret and Canada’s Media Co-op (of which this writer was a co-founder) bring reader-members, worker members, and sometimes contributors together on the board of directors.

In each case, members are involved in the big decisions. And when the model is successful, each media institution is more connected to the creativity and energy of its workers and readers. That can mean better coverage overall, resilience in times of crisis, and the ability to change leadership that is out of step with members’ needs. But a cooperative isn’t the only way for readers and workers to be represented.

In 2022, the Guardian pulled in nearly $100 million from online reader revenues—mostly monthly donations. A non-profit like the Guardian could, and should, have board seats reserved for representatives elected from its reader-donors. Readers should have a forum to discuss the priorities and standards of that institution.

Despite hopeful entrepreneurial rhetoric, reader-funded outlets are not growing fast enough to make up for the wreckage left behind by corporate media. To restore an economic basis for journalism—and create for the first time a vibrant and truly democratic media—bigger investments are needed. Government funding is a fraught subject, but it is possible to design such programs in ways that keep control in the hands of voters instead of bureaucrats or corporate actors.

On the scale of an individual reader, journalism is expensive. But if we think of it as a social institution on the level of schools or health care, it’s exceptionally cheap—about $20 per year, per person could double the number of journalists in any given country.

The challenge is to keep the interests and desires of each person connected to the value they create—whether by funding, reading or creating the news.

Saving the Media

items.title: Participatory Budgeting
items.summary: Through a local democratic process, community members directly decide how to spend part of a public budget. Participatory budgeting enables residents to work with their government to make decisions that affect their daily lives.
items.body:
In 1989, the workers’ party implemented participatory budgeting in the city of Porto Alegre, Brazil, making it the first city in the world to have this. Participatory budgeting was intended to directly include citizens in government decision-making, after years of military dictatorship had excluded them. For nearly 20 years, as many as 50,000 people participated annually in making decisions on how to spend up to 20 percent of the city’s budget. In 2017, the practice was suspended by the newly elected Brazilian Social Democracy Party, which cited a lack of resources and a need to reform the process.

Despite the setbacks in Porto Alegre, participatory budgeting has spread to over 3,000 cities in Latin America, North America, Asia, Africa, and Europe since 1989. Most participatory budgeting processes involve the municipal budget in cities of all sizes, from ones with less than 20,000 inhabitants (e.g., Icapuí and Mundo Novo in Brazil, and Grottomare in Italy) to mega-cities like Buenos Aires, New York, and São Paulo. Participatory budgeting has worked in both rural municipalities (like Governador Valadares, Brazil) and completely urban ones (like Belo Horizonte), and in cities with both scarce and plentiful public resources. The process can be applied at any level of governance, including counties, states, housing authorities, schools and school systems, universities, and other public agencies.

Though each participatory budgeting process is different, most follow a similar basic structure: residents brainstorm spending ideas, volunteer budget delegates develop proposals based on these ideas, and residents vote on the proposals. The government implements the top projects and then begins planning and revising the process for the next time. For example, if community members identify recreation spaces as a priority, their delegates might develop a proposal for basketball court renovations. The residents would then vote on this and other proposals, and if they choose the basketball court, the city uses the funds they allocated to renovate it.

In fact, in the Kadutu community of the South Kivu province of the Democratic Republic of Congo, participatory budgeting led to renovations of basketball and volleyball courts in 2012. There, much of the process relies on mobile phone technology and SMS voting to ensure widespread participation. Throughout the province, participatory budgeting also led to the construction of nearly 60 new classrooms, a public health center, and public restrooms, along with the repair of a dangerous bridge.

Participatory budgeting relies upon both the political will of officials and community support. Someone with control over budget money (an elected official, agency head, or department director) must participate in the process and agree to let the public decide how to spend part of the budget. Participation from community organizations, particularly those working with marginalized groups, is necessary to engage people and push the process forward. The result is a process that is both top-down and grassroots.

Participatory budgeting does not require a new pot of money but a change into how funding decisions are made. Some resources are necessary to carry out the process, but this investment saves money down the road, as participants discover new ways to make limited budgets go further.

As with any kind of public participation, there is a risk that the individuals and groups with the most power will dominate the process. But this risk can be minimized by setting low barriers for participation, encouraging community members to both plan and lead the process, and doing targeted outreach to ensure inclusion of underrepresented communities.

Budgeting is a large part of what governments do. When community members decide spending through a public process, there are fewer opportunities for corruption, waste, or backlash. Ordinary people have a real say—and they get to make real political decisions. As a result, participatory budgeting tends to engage many people who are otherwise cynical about government. Politicians build closer relationships with their constituents, and community members develop greater trust in government. Participants become more active and informed citizens. Community members, staff, and elected officials learn democracy—by doing it together.

Porto Alegre: Participatory Budgeting and the Challenge of Sustaining Transformative Change
How to Control the Budget? An Experiment in Social Democracy

items.title: Participatory Guarantee Systems
items.summary: Participatory Guarantee Systems (PGS) facilitate the building of closer relationships among food producers and consumers involved in short sup- ply-chains by enabling for quality certification to take place on a local level. Organic producers and consumers use PGS to create healthy and resilient local food systems, to make organic certification more affordable and accessible, and to build trust and relationships.
items.body:
The modern organic movement started as a response to industrial agriculture systems, with independent small-scale farmers choosing to sell their products locally and build direct relationships with their consumers. As organic began to grow as a sector, supply chains lengthened, meaning that the number of people and processes between the farmer and the family eating the food increased. Private, for-profit, third-party certification of foods became the norm. In many countries, including the United States, the use of the term “organic” is now regulated by the government and can only be used by producers with accredited third-party organic certification.

The organic sector is increasingly dominated by largescale agribusinesses that only produce one type of crop and long supply chains. Many small farmers are not able to manage the costs and paperwork requirements of third-party organic certification, and people living in areas where organic food is produced are often unable to access or afford that food.

Participatory guarantee systems (PGS) provide an alternative to third-party certification schemes that are specifically suited to local markets and short supply-chains. In a PGS, the producers, consumers, and distributors can define and enforce their own certification, based on the standards that are most important to them. Since each PGS is created by farmers and the communities they serve, the model is adaptable to local cultural values and community needs. For example, some PGS go beyond conventional organic certification standards to include a greater focus on issues like soil health, biodiversity, food access, or working conditions.

The International Federation of Organic Agriculture Movements (IFOAM) maintains a directory of PGS initiatives worldwide and advocates for governments to recognize them. While many different forms are possible depending on the context, an initiative must contain the following elements to be recognized as a PGS: a shared vision, stakeholder (farmers and community members) participation, transparent standards and processes, mechanisms for building trust, non-hierarchical democratic structures, and an ongoing learning process. In 2020, the directory included 223 PGS initiatives in 76 countries serving more than 500,000 farmers.

Organic PGS initiatives are often linked to local market opportunities. In 2012, for example, a group of volunteers in Sri Lanka started a weekly market called Good Market, at which all farm products for sale had to be organically grown. One of the most common questions from early visitors to the market was: “How do I know this is organic?” Large organic exporters had third-party certificates for their tea, spices, coconuts, and tropical fruits, but small-scale farmers who grew organic rice, legumes, and vegetables couldn’t afford export-level certification. This imbalance worked against creating more sustainable, sovereign food systems.

In 2013, a local farm hosted a weekend retreat for producers and consumers who were interested in making organic certification more affordable and accessible. The group used the IFOAM Organic Norms and experiences of other PGS initiatives as a starting point, and then over time added additional standards and processes based on their requirements. For example, they decided that consumers should be able to participate in all farm visits, and they developed an assessment form with a “star system” so they could distinguish between farms that just barely met the organic standards and farms that were adopting regenerative practices to build soil and increase biodiversity. All materials were translated into Sri Lanka’s three local languages.

Farmers who are verified under the PGS are able to sell through marketplace events, local retail outlets, and organic delivery services. Local consumers tend to prefer PGS over third-party certification, not only because the products tend to be more affordable, but also because the process is transparent. They can find out what farm a product comes from and can partake in farm visits. Everyone involved feels a collective responsibility for maintaining this trust in, and the reputation of, the PGS. The consequences for non-compliance are clear. Farmers lose their organic-certification and are no longer able to supply through organic market channels.

While PGS initiatives are most common in local food systems, they can provide a low-cost, community-owned alternative to private third-party certifications in other sectors as well. PGS works in any context where community stakeholders agree on a core set of standards, a process for verifying those standards, and a transparent recordkeeping system.

items.title: Policies for Cooperatives
items.summary: Public policies are often designed for the benefit of profit-focused businesses and disadvantage co- operative enterprises. But legislation can—and in many places around the world already does—sup- port cooperatives and enable them to flourish.
items.body:
Member-owned companies around the world are achieving great success in certain industries, from insurance and software to dairy and textiles. Studies repeatedly find that co-ops are as productive as—or even more productive than—their investor-owned counterparts. And they have proven more resilient than capitalist businesses during periods of systemic financial crisis. However, in most regions of the world, cooperatives comprise just a small fraction of all businesses. If co-ops are so beneficial, why aren’t they more widespread?

Government agencies, financial institutions, and the laws that spell out how enterprises must operate can help or hinder the cooperative sector, depending on how they are designed to understand cooperatives and promote their growth.

In many places, co-ops encounter financial and administrative obstacles that their investor-owned competitors don’t face. In markets designed to serve wealthy investors, co-ops can struggle to access the funding they need to flourish and grow. Conventional banks are often reluctant to give loans to co-ops that have a few members or have unconventional business models. To them, shared ownership can appear confusing or excessively risky. So-called impact investors rarely know how to work with cooperative startups and may demand a right to vote on and veto decisions in a manner that is incompatible with the interests of members. Therefore, co-ops often must seek alternative means of funding like subsidies, grants, tax exemptions, preferential procurement by public authorities, and more. Even regions that have laws allowing the formation of co-ops can make the process unnecessarily hard. For cash-strapped founders looking to create a business that prioritizes its social mission over its profit margin, these hurdles can be onerous enough to deter them from forming a cooperative.

Carefully crafted policymaking can help make co-ops a more accessible and attractive business structure. For instance, Italy has pioneered several strategies that make it easier to establish and grow co-ops. Italian law requires most co-ops to contribute a portion of their profits to solidarity funds, which are then used to support growth within the sector. There is also a separate legal framework that enables employees to pool their unemployment benefits and savings to buy shares in a traditional business when it is on the verge of closure and convert it into a worker co-op.

In the United States, a federal loan fund for rural electric co-ops in the 1930s enabled consumer-owned utilities to power most of the country’s farmland within a decade. In the 1970s, US Congress began providing tax advantages for owners who sold their companies to employees. During the same decade, the Swedish economist Rudolf Meidner proposed a model where a portion of corporate profits would go toward expanding employees’ ownership of companies and the economy at large. While not fully realized, his proposal—and the support it garnered from unions—galvanized the development of a more robust social safety net for workers in Sweden.

Other countries, such as Brazil and South Africa, take a more targeted approach to supporting co-ops through laws that require governments to prefer cooperative suppliers when buying certain things, like food and clothing for schools. In Bangladesh, national policies concerning rural development, women’s empowerment, and cooperative entrepreneurship seek to encourage women to form and contribute to cooperatives. To do this, the government disburses loans to members of women’s cooperatives and encourages saving through cooperatives. These policies have strengthened over 115,000 cooperatives with over 7.5 million members. In the US city of Cleveland and the UK city of Preston, “anchor institutions” like hospitals and universities enter into procurement contracts with co-ops, after competitive tender processes, which provide significant sources of regular income for the co-ops in the city.

Governments can also ensure that it is possible to incorporate cooperatives flexibly and creatively. Laws in Italy, Quebec, and France allow co-ops to have multiple stakeholders as members, pursue broad social interests (like employing folks from disadvantaged groups), and accept investment money from “supporter” members who don’t use the co-op’s products or services.

On the other side of the globe in South Korea, a law was passed in 2012 reducing barriers to co-op formation, most notably by reducing the number of required founding members to five. Within three years of its enactment, more than 7,000 new co-ops were registered—mostly by small entrepreneurs like freelancers and informal workers. Without this reform, thousands of people would not have benefitted from even the limited degree of job security that such co-ops provide.

A robust cooperative policy agenda need not be limited to cooperative law reform, but should also include economic policy on procurement, labor, securities, and competition. Governments can encourage business advisers, lawyers, and accountants to be educated about how co-ops work, so that they can help potential cooperative entrepreneurs navigate the financial and administrative hurdles to formation. Whether a co-op gets started through the pooling of worker or community member resources, or whether it is started with the help of funding from formal institutions and government support, policies have an important function in creating a favorable environment in which cooperative enterprises can thrive.
