items.title: Popular Education and Folk Schools
items.summary: Folk schools and popular education processes provide opportunities for people most affected by injustice to build skills, participate in democratic learning, and gain tools for organizing.
items.body:
Liberatory education supports people to build connections, learn freely, and organize to make change in their communities. Examples of liberatory education have arisen around the world out of peoples’ struggles—in the folk schools of Denmark, out of political repression across Latin America, in African liberation struggles, and during the Great Depression in the United States. Two related approaches to liberatory education are the methodology of popular education and the folk school.

The term “popular education”—and its early development in theory and practice—comes from Paulo Freire, a Brazilian intellectual and activist active in the mid-twentieth century. Popular education is a group process that brings people together to share and analyze their experiences, and come up with strategies for change. In the simplest terms, it means people getting together to learn something they need to know. Popular education rejects the system of experts and teachers transferring knowledge to students, only for that knowledge to be regurgitated for an essay or exam. This more rigid system confines even the most creative of teachers, who are held back by standardized curriculums and testing. In popular education, everyone involved is both a teacher and learner.

Folk schools, which originated in Denmark during the nineteenth century, were designed to provide people in rural areas with educational spaces to learn skills relevant to their lives. Inspired by the ideas of Danish poet, thinker, and pastor Nikolai Frederik Severin Grundtvig, these schools also taught citizenship skills that aided Denmark’s transition to democracy and encouraged lifelong learning outside of formal educational institutions.

Today, folk schools are located around the world and often provide both educational spaces and living and cultural spaces that allow people to gather and learn from each other, in a spirit akin to popular education. Their missions depend on the needs and culture of their local communities, so they often look and behave very differently from one another. Music and other cultural expressions are often central to how they share stories and raise spirits.

One of the most famous examples of a folk school is the Highlander Research and Education Center, located in New Market, Tennessee, in the United States. Founded in 1932 as the Highlander Folk School, inspired by Denmark Folk Schools, its mission was to “provide an educational center in the South for the training of rural and industrial leaders, and for the conservation and enrichment of the indigenous cultural values of the mountains.” Over the years, it has offered a variety of programs such as supporting labor organizers working across racial lines, civil rights leadership training in the 1960s, and intergenerational workshops. Its location at the intersection of the Appalachian region and the American South has led to a focus on regional issues such as efforts to protect the land from strip-mining and organizing against toxic polluters.

The methodology of popular education is central to Highlander’s approach, and generations of movement leaders in the US South and elsewhere have received training from Highlander to transform how their communities and movements learn and take action together. Interwoven with their commitment to popular education, Highlander practices related methodologies of cultural organizing, integrating community based art and cultural expression into everything they do; participatory action research, in which communities shape the methods and analysis of research that affects them; language justice, so that people can lead changemaking whatever language they speak; and intergenerational organizing. Highlander shares the theory and practice of these methodologies to encourage widespread use.

Highlander hosts community workshops, leadership and fellowship programs, and children’s justice camps. They support liberation struggles like the immigrant justice movement and the Movement for Black Lives. The work of Highlander can also happen in communities far away from Tennessee. One example is Project Upstream, which enabled unhoused people to become fellows in a program where they met, discussed their conditions with other unhoused people, and then worked to bring that information to government officials. The first year, the program identified the need for improving access to restrooms.

Other folk schools may operate differently, with a student demographic that aligns more closely with the ages of traditional university students. It is common for Danish folk schools—more than seventy operate independently throughout the country—to offer on-campus housing as well. But despite differences in target populations and course design, the basic tenets of folk schools remain the same. There are no traditional grades. Learning is rooted in students’ own motivation and interest. By providing a space for popular education, where everyone is an expert on their own life experience, folk schools allow people who experience oppression to gain tools for leadership and making change. Schools that empower their learners create more empowered communities.

learn_more.title: The Global Folk High School Movement
Training for Transformation: A Handbook for Community Workers
The Highlander Research and Education

items.title: Public Pharmaceuticals
items.summary: By removing the profit motive, democratic and pub- lic ownership of pharmaceutical companies can lead to healthier outcomes for society and reclaim medicine for the common good.
items.body:
The global medicines market is dominated by large private drug companies responsible for a decline in meaningful innovation as well as skyrocketing prices, recurring shortages, troubling safety issues, and corruption in the institutions that are supposed to regulate them. These trends are harmful to our health, economies, and democracies—and they are inevitable outcomes of an industry driven by profit-maximization.

So-called “Big Pharma” companies spend less than onefifth of their revenue on research and development, but half of their revenue on marketing. Many also regularly distribute more than 100 percent of profits to shareholders by selling off assets, taking on more debt, and downsizing production—inefficient and extractive practices in an industry we depend on for our health and wellbeing.

To get different outcomes, we need a different design. Democratic, public ownership of pharmaceutical institutions at scale would remove the profit motive and help reclaim medicine for the common good. Public ownership of pharmaceuticals can exist at any or all points in the supply chain, from research for new medications to manufacturing and distribution services. Since they are not beholden to shareholders and have some insulation from market pressures, they can focus on goals other than maximizing profits—like contributions to public health, scientific advancement, and local economies.

From Massachusetts to the UK, Thailand, India, and beyond, there are many existing examples of states turning to public ownership of pharmaceutical companies in efforts to combat high prices, medicine shortages, and political interference by multinational corporations.

Since 1960, Cuba’s entire pharmaceutical sector has been public. It produces both low-cost generic drugs and first-in-class discoveries, while providing thousands of good jobs and educational opportunities in the national economy. Known principally for its innovations—like the world’s first lung cancer and meningitis B vaccines—the industry also manufactures most of the domestic supply of medicine and shares its technology with numerous low and middle-income countries, lessening those countries’ reliance on Big Pharma to meet healthcare needs.

When properly resourced, Public Pharma can lower drug prices, reduce inefficiencies, and ensure broad, equitable access to new drugs. Public control of manufacturing, wholesale distribution, or retail pharmacies can serve as the basis for large-scale investments in public health, creating educational opportunities and decent jobs and increasing resilience in supply chains. South Korea, for instance, supports small and medium pharmaceutical companies with publicly owned manufacturing facilities, which generate local jobs and purchasing power that broadly benefit the economy.

Public Pharma can also assure that medications most essential to public health are prioritized for development. State-owned pharmaceutical companies in both Cuba and Brazil operate with explicit mandates to develop medications ignored by the market, like those for neglected tropical diseases, while Big Pharma companies prioritize medications that generate the most profit—often copies of existing products.

Public Pharma can contribute to the creation of a biomedical commons in which life-saving technologies, and the information needed to produce and improve upon them, are treated as collective resources for all of humanity. Large-scale public ownership and control of the benefits of pharmaceutical innovation, for instance, could help facilitate programs in which the wealth created by the industry could prioritize serving historically marginalized communities, rather than perpetuating neglect in the name of business imperatives. Public Pharma is a vital tool for reorienting the purpose of health care from profits to human needs.

Successful examples from around the world can inform the design and development of a robust Public Pharma sector for any country. Sweden’s state-owned Apotek Produktion & Laboratorier AB has found a niche in specialty pharmaceutical manufacturing, selling products to dozens of countries, and directing any profits it earns to its only shareholder: the Swedish state. China and India’s stateowned drug companies have long produced a significant portion of the world’s supply of active pharmaceutical ingredients. Brazil’s state-owned labs produce more than 100 essential medications that allow its national health service to offer free and reduced-price medications to low-income patients.

Around the world—even in the United States—public sector labs were historically responsible for the development of most vaccines. Insulin as a treatment for diabetes was developed in a public lab in Canada and the subsequent sale of the rights to produce insulin to private US manufacturers remains a powerful cautionary tale about the harm that can happen when privatizing public goods. Despite being a century-old drug, insulin prices in the US have skyrocketed in recent years as the three companies that control virtually the entire insulin market make small tweaks on their products in order to take out new patents and continually raise prices. This trend has produced a uniquely American epidemic of cost-related deaths because of people rationing insulin.

Because of the US’s outsized role in global trade talks and the utter dominance of its Big Pharma firms in the global medicines market, developing a public pharmaceutical industry in the US in particular would be decisive in global efforts to roll back Big Pharma monopolies and reclaim medicine as a public good. It would reduce regulatory capture and shrink corporate lobbying, opening up political space for much broader input into the priorities and outputs of this critical industry. With democratic, public-sector institutions innovating and producing medications at scale, Big Pharma’s interests would no longer dominate, and public institutions would have incentives to cooperate instead of competing in times of public health crises.

learn_more.title: Medicine for All: The Case for a Public Option in the Pharmaceutical Industry
Insulin: A Case Study for Why We Need a Public Option in the Pharmaceutical Industry
It’s Time to Socialize Big Pharma

items.title: Recuperated Factories
items.summary: Worker-led campaigns have seized the means of production, made decisions democratically, prevent- ed unemployment, and revitalized communities in the process.
items.body:
Recuperation refers to when workers take control over their workplace and transform it into a worker cooperative, with decisions made democratically and profits shared among all. Although often motivated by national economic crises and the resulting abandonment of businesses by capitalists, recuperation can arise from a range of situations affecting a workplace, such as strikes or bankruptcies. Unlike owner-led conversions to employee ownership, recuperation is a process that comes from the bottom up, often against the wishes of the owning class. Recuperated factory takeovers have happened all over the world.

During Argentina’s economic crisis that began in 2011, workers prevented the permanent closure of dozens of businesses—from ceramics factories to luxury hotels. One of these businesses, the towering Hotel Bauen, opened in the late 1970s in the heart of Buenos Aires. It held status as a meeting place of the ruling class during Argentina’s ruthless military dictatorship. After the hotel’s indebted owners fired the staff and permanently turned off the lights in late 2001, a few dozen ex-employees and cooperative activists banded together to reclaim it. They staged an occupation of the hotel in early 2003, and immediately began talking about how to reopen it—only this time, under democratic control. They wanted to replace the hotel’s previous culture of competition, suspicion, and chronic instability with one of solidarity. Despite continuous harassment by powerful state representatives, the worker-owned Hotel Bauen grew to become a hub for progressive politics—providing space for community organizers, discussion groups, and artists.

In 2008, during the global economic recession, workers at the Republic Windows factory in Chicago protested layoffs by staging a sit-in strike—one of the first since they were made illegal in the United States in 1939. To the surprise of many, they won. But only four years later, the new owners laid them off. This time, a group of the now jobless workers decided to do something different. Working with an organization called the Working World, they bought their old factory and started their own business, New Era Windows Cooperative.

Meanwhile in Thessaloniki, Greece, workers began occupying a factory in 2013 after the owners declared bankruptcy and stopped paying wages. With the overwhelming support of their members, the workers’ union decided to repurpose the factory’s machinery to make ecological soap products for a new business, Vio.Me, which would be run by the workers. For nearly a decade, the workers have had to defend the property with physical blockades and nightly security shifts. They also have had to defeat annual attempts to auction the property to new ownership. Meanwhile the government refuses to acknowledge the workers’ attempts to formalize their ownership of the factory and has shut down electricity to the property in an effort to drive them out. Nonetheless, Vio.Me continues. As one of the workers said in a 2019 article in Unicorn Riot, “This factory is a factory that mainly produces dignity.”

For workers, recuperating a workplace usually begins by occupying it, but that is just the first step. A lot of learning and planning is often necessary before the business can get going again. Workers who were previously employed at the factory understand parts of the manufacturing process. But because former managers will have withheld certain information from them and separated workers into isolated assembly-line roles, workers often need to combine their experiences to reconstruct an understanding of what is involved along the production chain. In cases where the owner moved or sold essential equipment, new worker ownership must replace that equipment and establish relationships with suppliers of raw materials and anticipated customers. Unless members of the previous management team are part of the takeover, the workers might need to pursue training or find trusted advisers in the areas of bookkeeping, financial analysis, sales, human resources, and more.

As a group, it is important for the workers to collectively develop an understanding of entrepreneurial risk-taking, when to delegate tasks or grant authority, and how to define success. In situations where the business is embroiled in a wider economic crisis, the workers will need to be creative problem solvers, because banks often freeze accounts. If payments in the national currency are jeopardized, workers may need to organize compensation in ways that meet their needs without relying on money. Whether or not business is good, the workers must consider how much money to save for purchasing future raw materials and equipment.

Typically, legislation protects the previous owners of recuperated businesses, and authorities may forcibly evict, imprison, or repress workers attempting to occupy and operate them.Yet factory takeovers can mobilize support from surrounding communities, as well as from academics, activists, and pragmatic lawmakers. After all, an empty factory does not produce value in the form of jobs or taxes for the local municipality.

Existing labor unions and cooperative developers can help support the process whenever the opportunity to recuperate a factory presents itself; they should prepare ahead of time for how to do so. Additionally, policymakers should consider proactively establishing legislation that facilitates recuperation, especially to safeguard manufacturing jobs in their communities. But most importantly, workers must understand that they have the power to take back any community asset that lies empty, remains idle, or does not serve them.

learn_more.title: The Take
Recuperated Enterprises in Argentina: Reversing the Logic of Capitalism
Occupy, Resist, Produce: Inside the Self-managed Factory of Vio.Me.

items.title: Reggio Emilia Preschools
items.summary: Emerging after World War II from one of the most war-ravaged regions in Italy, Reggio Emilia is a teaching style and philosophy that enables young children to grow into complete people and develop the core capacities to participate in radical democracy throughout their lives.
items.body:
Reggio Emilia is a system of education—a pedagogy—focused on preschool students. It embraces and encourages the unique curiosities of each child, grounding education in the needs and conditions of the surrounding community. Teachers, parents, community members, the classroom, and the local environment are all integral components to how a child learns to participate in the world in the Reggio method. But it goes one step further—recognizing how teachers and parents learn from their observations of and interactions with children.

The pedagogy gets its name from where it first arose: Reggio Emilia, a small city in Italy’s Emilia-Romagna region. One of the wealthiest regions in Europe, almost a third of its economy flows through cooperative businesses, in industries such as agriculture, manufacturing, and finance. But it was not always this well-off. Immediately following World War II, Emilia-Romagna was one of the poorest, most devastated regions in the country.

Educator Loris Malaguzzi developed the system in response to the war’s devastation, as a way to inoculate children against fascism and similar nationalistic, depersonalizing ideologies. The original Reggio Emilia preschools were funded by local women, and as a result the community was highly involved in how the schools operated.

Today, there are many Reggio-inspired schools around the world, making this style of preschool a regional export. Naturally, their interpretations of the core ideas vary, since Reggio Emilia schools should be flexible and adaptive to the needs of the locality, its families, and the individual students.

According to Malaguzzi, Reggio-inspired schools should be organized to foster strong relationships among “three central protagonists”: children, teachers, and parents. These relationships allow them to influence and learn from each other, continuously. “Our aim is to make a school that is a place of research, learning, revisiting, reconsideration, and reflection,” he wrote in 1993. “We strive to create an amiable school where children, teachers, and families feel a sense of well-being.”

Reggio schools train students to participate in democratic and cooperative structures throughout their lives by turning the classroom into a radically democratic place. “Ensuring that every child feels a sense of security and belonging within the school enables each child to accept and participate actively in transforming situations that are part of learning experiences,” wrote Malaguzzi. “The group becomes self-sustaining, developing its own conversation, its own ways of communicating, acting, and thinking.”

The role of the teacher is different from more conventional schools as well. In Reggio-style schools, teachers behave as facilitators for learning, and a significant part of their role is focused on documenting the behavior of children and tailoring teaching styles accordingly. By documenting and thinking deeply about the progress of students, and then discussing broader observations among themselves, teachers practice an iterative process rather than an inflexible and repetitive one.

A popular book about Reggio Emilia preschools, The Hundred Languages of Children, explains that teachers “need to redefine their roles so that they are more than conveyors of knowledge and supporters of children. They are creators and sustainers of relationships; they are researchers; they must learn to follow children’s time and interests; they must sometimes think ahead, be the chief protagonist, invent, prompt, design, create, be the audience and the listener, the arbiter and judge, the author and scribe, the listener and recorder.”

Reggio Emilia preschools turn the classroom itself into an environment where children internalize the values of collaboration and democratic society even before having the vocabulary. These experiences prime children to be active participants in the world around them.

learn_more.title: The Hundred Languages of Children: The Reggio Emilia Experience in Transformation
For an Education Based on Relationships
Reggio Emilia Education

items.title: Remunicipalization
items.summary: Remunicipalization is when the management of utilities is brought back under public control. Some of the most important examples concern water, but remunicipalization encompasses regional and na- tional-level services from energy and transportation to internet access and education.
items.body:
The remunicipalization of utilities is often a community response to dysfunctional governance by privatized utility suppliers and public-private partnerships between governments and private industry. The factors leading to water remunicipalization, for instance, are similar worldwide: poor service performance, under-investment in infrastructure, disputes over operational costs and price increases, soaring utility bills, environmental hazards, and lack of financial transparency. Their experiences of these common problems have motivated many communities and policy-makers to take services back into public control. Between 2000 and 2015, 235 cases of water remunicipalization occurred in 37 countries around the world, including in major cities from Kampala to Kuala Lampur and Bogotá to Berlin.

Though each case differs, remunicipalization brings benefits to local governments and citizens alike. Since remunicipalizing its water supply in 2007, Houston, Texas has saved $2 million annually while Paris, which remunicipalized in 2011, saved €35 million in the first year alone. Without the obligation of generating profits for shareholders, the publicly owned utilities companies don’t have to fight to reinvest revenues in improving the water systems—as have governments in both Dar es Salaam and Berlin.

Remunicipalization efforts can increase access to water for low-income households by making water policy more accountable to community needs. Arenys de Munt, a small town in Spain, has promoted social policies to guarantee the right to water for all its citizens since 2011, when the town successfully remunicipalized water services. The newly established municipal company Aigües de Arenys/ GUSAM reformed the tariff structure by providing a discount on the first 100 liters of water per person per day. The most vulnerable families—those earning less than a single minimum wage income—are guaranteed access to water.

Similarly, Medina Sidonia—another Spanish city with remunicipalized water services—has developed an innovative approach to ensure the provision of a minimum amount of water (three cubic meters per person per month) to residents experiencing financial difficulties. After remunicipalization, the city council has not only declared water a human right but is implementing a policy to make it an accessible reality.

Most cases of remunicipalization around the world have involved terminating private contracts, either before they were due to expire or directly after the expiration date. However, challenges can arise with the premature termination of a contract. If the contract is terminated before it expires, private operators can obtain compensation for the profits they would have generated. If municipalities claim a breach of contractual obligations, private operators often contest this in court. The government of Castres, France, for example, was forced to pay €30 million in compensation to private water empire Suez, even though its contract had been illegally signed by former Mayor Jacques Limouzy without proper consultation with the town council.

Beyond national litigations, investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) provisions, which allow multinational companies to sue states, increase the risks for governments and citizens wanting to remunicipalize utilities. Multinational water companies use ISDS provisions to claim significant amounts of public money in compensation for canceled service management contracts, despite failing to meet their own obligations.

Many of the successful remunicipalization efforts around the world would not have been possible without the tireless mobilization of committed citizens. Berliners organized a referendum to demand that secret water privatization contracts be disclosed. In Uruguay, a referendum calling for a nationwide end to privatization eventually led to the remunicipalization of water and sanitation services.

Remunicipalization is about building better public services—more transparent, more accountable, more efficient, and more focused on people’s long-term needs. If citizens are willing to fight for remunicipalization and against privatization, it is because they believe that the public sector is better equipped to meet broader social and environmental goals than profit-driven private companies.

Remunicipalization strategies can be applied to other essential services such as energy, transportation, healthcare, education, and more. Hundreds of cities in Germany have remunicipalized energy services; several cities in Sweden have reversed private contracts in elderly care; and numerous cities in France have remunicipalized waste collection, transportation, and school meal services. In Spain, many services from public park maintenance to funeral services have recently been remunicipalized.

These efforts reflect a global recognition of the need for cross-sector strategies and alliances among citizens, workers, and local authorities to de-privatize essential services. People are rediscovering the value of public ownership for the common good.

learn_more.title: Remunicipalisation by The Transnational Institute
Reclaiming Public Services: How cities and citizens are turning back privatisation
Remunicipalisation: Putting Water Back Into Public Hands

items.title: Social Cooperatives
items.summary: Through social cooperatives, people can care for each other within a framework of democratic con- trol and shared power.
items.body:
In the 1980s, the Italian government implemented a range of austerity measures. These included reductions of government services in response to financial crises and the rise of an ideology that favored private business over the public sector. This left devastating gaps in the provision of critical services like healthcare and shortages in opportunities for people with disabilities. The country’s cooperative movement responded by adapting old models of economic democracy to new challenges. Cooperators created a new type of cooperative, one designed specifically to serve a public mission.

Many kinds of social cooperatives have emerged across Italy in recent decades. Coopselios, for instance, is a large co-op in the Emilia Romagna region that provides health and social services. InGalera is a Milan restaurant run by incarcerated people, while the Girasoli restaurant in Rome mainly employs members with Down syndrome. Social co-ops are engaged in a wide range of initiatives, from recycling to fostering relationships between native Italians and immigrants. Some specialize in supporting people struggling with drug dependency, while others provide home-based care for the elderly.

Whereas cooperatives traditionally have just one type of member—such as their workers or their consumers—social co-ops can be multi-stakeholder. Care providers and their patients, for example, can co-govern the organization together. And governance is key. Unlike other kinds of nonprofit organizations, social co-ops are controlled by the people who participate in them directly, not just the people who fund them.

The government of Italy formally embraced social cooperatives in 1991, when it passed a law that established the model as a distinct kind of legal entity. Most of the revenue for social co-ops now comes from government contracts. But operations are managed by the people providing and receiving services, not a distant government bureaucracy. This way, public services can involve a deeper sort of democracy than government elections. Over 10,000 social co-ops are operating in Italy today.

When social co-ops work the way they should, their workers and those they serve in the community have a seat at the decision-making table, either through direct assemblies or elected board members. This is especially important for groups of people who tend to be ignored or dismissed by traditional service providers and government officials. In social co-ops, they are at the center.

Social co-ops have spread beyond their roots in Italy. Governments in France, Canada, the United Kingdom, and elsewhere have passed legislation to support the formation of social co-ops following the Italian model. But even in places that lack supportive legislation, the ethos can still take root. For instance, charitable nonprofits can organize their governance so that workers and other participants are in control, not just funders. Businesses can do the same, ensuring that they are accountable to the public good, not just to private investors. And governments can prioritize cooperatives when they grant healthcare and public service contracts.

For all of us, the social co-op tradition can serve as a reminder that we can take care of each other without sacrificing democratic participation. The work of care need not be paternalistic; it can and should empower everyone involved.

learn_more.title: Humanizing the Economy
The Rise of Social Cooperatives in Italy
Worker Self-Directed Nonprofits

items.title: Tandas
items.summary: A tanda is an informal finance circle that is based on trust and community relationships. It is used by people all over the world and allows its participants access to cash that they can use to improve their lives.
items.body:
Many communities around the world don’t trust financial institutions and governments. Many people, especially in the Global South, do not even have a savings bank account. Instead, communities have developed other ways to save money and take out loans. One method is through a community-based practice called *tanda* in Latin America, *susu* in West Africa and the Caribbean, *jam’eya* in much of the Arab World, *paluwagan* in the Philippines, and hundreds of other terms across different parts of the globe.

A tanda is when a group of friends, family, neighbors, or even colleagues pool their money together to help each other either save or borrow. For example, a group of six people might commit to paying $200 every week for six weeks, and then each receive a lump sum of $1,200 once during a six-week period. A tanda may also be organized if a community member is in a sudden need for cash due to a medical emergency, an upcoming event, or a purchase beyond what they could normally afford. Those in need will get access to a cash loan upfront and repay it later through their contributions. Others use it as a saving opportunity.

To organize a tanda, you first need to decide on who the participants are and how many. Then, as a group, you will decide on the amount that each person will pay and the frequency (which might be weekly, monthly, yearly, or otherwise).You will also decide the order in which people will get paid; it could be through a random draw or by order of urgency and need. Finally, you need to pick someone who will coordinate the tanda, which involves collecting and distributing payments.You can also add any additional rules that the group agrees on, such as that money will be pooled at weekly meetings or processes for exiting a tanda and swapping turns.

Traditional banking services often require credit history, monthly fees, lengthy forms, and identity screenings. These can be barriers to low-income communities, immigrants, or people who work in the informal economy. Tandas offer a flexible, transparent, and simple banking alternative to many community members who don’t have access to formal financial services.

When you participate in a tanda, you are also participating in a trust-building exercise. Oftentimes, people participate because they trust the organizer, and gradually they build trust with each other. Because of this, tandas offer a more comfortable space for a collective financial experience when compared to banks, given the participants work directly with their peers rather than with bankers, who have more power and authority and an incentive to exploit.

The beauty of this communal practice is that the space and trust created through a tanda encourages people to have vulnerable conversations about their finances and support each other in planning and budgeting. It helps break the taboo that many communities have around financial planning or discussing money. Additionally, technologies like video chat and mobile cash payments enable people to organize tandas across borders.

One criticism of tandas is that there are no mechanisms to prevent people taking advantage of each other. However, this criticism ignores the weight that relationships and societal expectations have on people’s behavior. Studies show that it is rare that tanda participants miss payments, likely because tandas are rooted in trust and relationships—this communal aspect serves as a form of accountability.

Many people find it easier to be disciplined with their savings if they are committed to a group or know that people are depending on their contribution. Also, some people will spend money if it’s laying around, so keeping it held in a communal fund can prevent needless spending. More importantly, the collective nature of the tanda offers an economy rooted in community, rather than in individualism, and in relationships rather than transactions.

learn_more.title: Tandas And The Informal Economy of Mexico
Mission Asset Fund
SUSU - How to Start & Use It Correctly

items.title: Zero Waste
items.summary: Communities around the world are finding alternatives to corporate waste management that demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of zero waste systems, wherein materials that are not needed are either repurposed, composted, or recycled.
items.body:
Conventional waste management systems are damaging to the health of communities and the environment. The more waste that we send to landfills or incinerators, the more we pollute our air, water, and land, and the more cancer, asthma, and other adverse health consequences we create for those living nearby. Dump sites are often built in or around low-income residential neighborhoods, meaning that poor communities and people of color are much more likely to suffer the effects of dangerous environmental conditions created by waste processing. The need for zero waste is, therefore, an issue of social and environmental justice.

The scale of environmental injustice resulting from waste management practices is global. North Americans consume over 326 pounds of plastic per person per year, while for Southeast Asians the figure is about 53 pounds. Yet the negative health and environmental impacts of waste are not as visible in the Global North as they are in the South, because more money is invested in hiding waste through landfills, incinerators, and exporting. Though recycling is an important component of transitioning to zero waste systems, it doesn’t address the underlying problems of overconsumption and disposability. What’s not buried, burned, or recycled in the North is exported through the waste trade. Canada and the United States ship vast quantities of plastic waste to other countries, mainly in Asia, under the guise of recycling.

The Philippines, for instance, has had to contend with the consequences of waste from wealthier countries, as multinational companies based in the Global North have saturated the Philippine market with products in single-use plastics. Those companies and their home countries shirk the burden of managing their waste, and the hazards that the waste brings, particularly for the low-income communities that live near the dumping grounds. Some impacts include increased risks of flooding from clogged storm drains, threats to the livelihoods of people who rely on fishing, toxic emissions from burning plastic, dangers for wildlife that ingest plastic, and health hazards from small pieces of plastic entering human food systems. Meanwhile, the production of plastic requires fossil fuels that exacerbate climate change, the effects of which are felt disproportionately in the Global South.

In response, Fort Bonifacio, a village-sized district in Metro Manila, decentralized its waste management system and completed a material recovery facility in 2011 that composts food and stores recyclables for resale. This reduced waste by 95 percent and created new jobs locally. The new waste workers earn three times more than they would have as informal waste pickers by getting a fixed minimum income from the city, in addition to any revenue they receive from selling the recyclables and compost. Waste workers still face many hardships—such as social marginalization and the lack of a social safety net. But it makes a real difference when governments formalize these workers, pay them a living wage, and engage with them to help steer the governance of a zero waste system.

This effort is part of a global zero waste movement that seeks to extend the lifecycle of products and eliminate the injustices in prevailing waste disposal systems. Zero waste doesn’t mean that there won’t be anything to throw away; the goal is to reduce waste wherever possible by reducing the production and consumption of materials that turn into waste. It also means that discarded materials will either be reused, repurposed, repaired, composted, or recycled. Zero waste is about rethinking the usefulness of waste materials and organizing their circulation differently.

Also in the Philippines, the city of San Fernando in Pampanga has over 100 small-scale material recovery facilities. Before implementing a zero waste program, the city spent 70 million pesos (approximately $170,000) in waste hauling and tipping fees alone. Since the program began, waste has been collected from all residents and costs have dropped to just 12 million pesos per year, leaving more funding for education and health services. Cleaner canals have also reduced the mosquito population, resulting in a steep decline in dengue fever cases.

While zero waste practices do not depend on state regulation, legislation can influence industrial choices over products and packaging and can prompt action toward better waste management practices. Further, when initiatives are built and managed by communities, rather than imposed upon them by governments, power shifts into the hands of locals and away from waste-promoting companies.

No single person can challenge corporate waste systems alone, but when community groups come together, they can create shifts. Zero Waste Boston in the United States, for example, is a coalition of environmental groups that developed a worker-owned waste management cooperative, Cooperative Energy, Recycling, and Organics (CERO). CERO collects food waste from restaurants and other establishments and transports it to local farms outside of Boston for composting. In Baltimore, what started as a youth-led campaign to stop the installation of a new incinerator near their school is now a collaboration with the city to move toward zero waste.

Many companies have distorted the concept by claiming to be a zero waste organization while failing to enforce basic zero waste precepts like a prohibition of trash incineration. The success of zero waste efforts requires creative, grassroots solutions to manage waste and move power to the communities most affected by failing waste management systems. Amplifying local stories from all over the world is crucial in changing false narratives, preventing harmful waste management practices, and avoiding community health and environmental catastrophes. From policy to grassroots action, in the Global North and South, everyone’s efforts can move us toward a zero waste future.

learn_more.title: CERO Cooperative
Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives
Zero Waste Masterplan

items.title: Artist and Freelancer Co-ops in Europe
items.body:
*1980s–Present, Europe*

Artists are some of the original gig workers. The word “gig” comes from “engagement,” a performance associated with a single contract—one-off and occasional. Working in the fields of arts and entertainment means dealing with multiple clients, inconsistent employment, and multiple workplaces. Because of these conditions, artists often face economic challenges. They have difficulty accessing health insurance, retirement, family and sick leave, unemployment benefits, and other benefits and protections that standard employees might receive.

Starting in the 1980s, artists in various countries across Europe who had precarious working conditions chose to cooperate to obtain professional recognition and more predictable contracts. They formed worker-owned cooperatives that allowed them to gain access to social protections and strengthen their sense of community.

One of the longest running artist cooperatives in Italy is Doc Servizi. It was founded in 1990 by musicians seeking to obtain decent work, share job opportunities, create working teams, and organize training to increase their expertise. Since its birth, Doc Servizi has formally employed its members, who are also its owners. They are thus able to maintain the independence associated with freelancing but can also receive social protection due to their status as co-op employer. Doc Servizi offers digital platforms and other services to support members’ self-management. Today, the cooperative remains focused on entertainment but is also part of Rete Doc, a bigger network of Italian cooperatives that covers all sectors of the cultural and creative industries and comprises more than 8,800 worker-members.

In the late 1990s, similar experiments began in Finland and Belgium with two cooperatives: Lilith and Smart. In order to guarantee its worker-members the status of employees and provide them with a safe and secure work environment, in 1997, Lilith was created in Helsinki by a group of musicians and producers. Today, Lilith is the biggest Finnish cooperative of workers in creative fields with more than 400 members. Smart, or the Société Mutuelle des Artistes, is a multi-stakeholder cooperative founded to support artists to develop their activities through the provision of shared services and a digital platform that makes it easier to invoice for their work. In the beginning, Smart was created in 1998 as a nonprofit association, but it became a multi-stakeholder cooperative in 2016. At first it was aimed at artistic and creative workers, but it later opened up to all freelancers and, recently, to platform workers. In the cooperative, the workers are shareholders, co-investors, and salaried employees through either fixed-term or open-ended contracts. Smart is now a network of cooperatives and companies that stretches across nine countries in Europe and has about 32,000 workers in its membership.

More recent examples of cooperation among musicians are DiGiDi and Resonate. The Danish DiGiDi was founded in 2003 as a cooperative digital music distribution service and today counts more than 6,500 members, including labels and artists. Resonate is an Irish multi-stakeholder cooperative that since 2015 has offered streaming music services with the purpose of bringing together the core stakeholders of the music economy. Both cooperatives are designed to offer more sustainable careers for their members and to value the creative work of musicians.

Contingent and unreliable working conditions are not only common in the arts and creative industries but, especially with the spread of casualization and automation, also characterize employment in other sectors. In many parts of the world, self-employed workers in industries ranging from software development to food delivery, and from education to journalism, have turned to cooperatives for fairer contracts and greater control over their time. As the cooperative sector grows, it is increasingly able to shape public policy.

In 1994, a French activist named Elisabeth Bost helped to formalize a new cooperative model, the Business and Employment Cooperative (BEC), to address the needs of isolated, self-employed workers in any field, enabling them to share common resources and services. Each BEC supports the “employee entrepreneur” in many ways: legal, administrative and accounting management, business administration, job creation, training, and peer-to-peer exchange. In France, about 155 cooperatives with 12,000 employee-entrepreneurs are organized on the BEC model. The model has been adopted in Switzerland and the Czech Republic, and similar forms exist in Morocco and Tunisia.

As ever more jobs are absorbed by the gig economy, worker-owned cooperatives represent a viable means of mitigating the isolation and unreliability faced by increasing numbers of workers. Working together instead of working alone, artists and cultural workers can gain more control over the market and the future of work as a whole.

learn_more.title: All for One: Response of Worker-Owned Cooperatives to Non-standard Employment
Platform Cooperativism in Italy and in Europe
Smart Coop

items.title: Association of Recyclers of Bogotá
items.body:
*1980s–Present, Bogotá, Colombia*

They have been known as scavengers, reclaimers, recicladores, and waste pickers. They exist in the informal sector, often in low- to middle-income countries where formal work can be nearly impossible to find. In consumerist societies, waste pickers find opportunity where others only see garbage: they earn income by sorting through what would otherwise linger on the streets or get sent to landfill, collecting anything that can be processed and reused.

Waste is a particularly pressing issue in Bogotá, Colombia, a city of nearly 10 million people. In 2011, the city government proposed auctioning $1.7 billion in contracts to private waste companies. This threatened the informal sector of recicladores who, for decades, had been working to keep their city clean by sorting through waste, diverting reusable and recyclable materials from landfill.

This proposal also posed environmental threats. For private waste management companies, it is more profitable to send waste into the landfill than to repurpose it, since companies do not pay to use public landfills. Once there, waste pollutes the air and water, and emits methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Failing to recycle also drives up the demand for raw materials like wood and petroleum, which leads to deforestation and oil drilling.

The work of recyclers and waste pickers is vital to reducing the ecological impact of cities. In parts of the world where people have little economic power, informal work like waste picking is widespread. There are 20 million recyclers worldwide, many of them in China and Brazil.

In Bogotá, recicladores work long hours in rough conditions, sorting through many tons of waste and selling what they reclaim to processors or middlemen. Their lack of recognition in the formal economy means that employment protections don’t apply to them, and they often experience abuse by police and sexual harassment at worksites. While mature capitalist countries may look at this as an obsolete industry, many recicladores don’t necessarily want new jobs. To begin with, they want safer working conditions.

The city of Bogotá did not pay recicladores for their work until 2013, when the mayor of Bogotá acknowledged their environmental contribution. At the time, he announced a payment system for recicladores, so they could be paid for their work and not just for the resale value of collected waste. Today, these workers get paid by the city government for every ton of recyclable materials they collect. This compensation is in addition to any other payment recyclers might receive from selling materials they find.

This victory was in large part due to the efforts of the Asociación de Recicladores de Bogotá (ARB), which has fought for—and won—rights for waste pickers for over several decades. Nohra Padilla Herrera, a third-generation recycler, organized the association in the 1980s in response to the poor working conditions she faced. Individuals like Herrera frequently inherit informal recycling work because there aren’t money-making alternatives for them or their families. Organizing into cooperatives, trade unions, and associations is crucial for informal workers in Brazil to be able to fight for their rights. This organization aids them in gaining formal recognition of their work and participating in decision-making processes.

The association aims to improve the economic and social conditions for the marginalized recicladores and to provide recognition through cooperative associations. It represents 24 cooperatives, made up of about 3,000 recyclers. The kind of mutual support that the recyclers practice in ARB emanates directly from their daily experiences; they have limited capital to form businesses, so they rely on community.

When Herrera and her crew of recyclers began organizing themselves, they didn’t expect their efforts to turn into a decades-long movement with many victories along the way. They just hoped to be able to earn enough to support their families. Now, recicladores have official recognition and rights, their own recycling centers, and company agreements. Waste pickers’ organizing has also gone global, with groups worldwide learning from their counterparts in other cities about organizational models for securing their rights. Herrera serves as a leader in the Latin American & Caribbean Network of Recyclers. In 2008, ARB hosted the first International Conference of Waste Picker Organizations with representatives from 40 countries, including Brazil, China, and India.

The Brazilian waste pickers’ cooperative Amanecer de los Cartoneros has grown to become the biggest in the world. Its workers go door-to-door to collect recyclables and process more than 300 tons of recyclables per day. The SWaCH cooperative in Pune, India has secured the right for women to drive the trucks that collect community waste. This cooperative has expanded to process organic waste too, contributing to the building of zero waste systems.

Around the world, recyclers like Herrera are organizing to demand dignity and recognition for the work they do. In societies where many refuse to view recyclers as workers, this organizing has led to real solutions, paving the way for more effective, ecological waste systems led by those who work on our streets.

learn_more.title: Asociación de Recicladores de Bogotá
Bogotá Recycler Nohra Padilla Praised on World Stage
Global Alliance of Waste Pickers

items.title: Autonomous Self-Defense in Cherán
items.body:
*2011, Cherán, Michoacán, Mexico*

Armed guards stood at every entrance and exit of Cherán, an Indigenous P’urhépecha community within the Mexican state of Michoacán. These watchers were local volunteers who protected their pueblo from unwelcome cartels, politicians, and others deemed dangerous, working to ensure that the violence that shook the town in the late 2000s and early 2010s would never return.

The small urban center of the rural community was surrounded by expansive mountains, which formerly teemed with lush old-growth pine forests. By 2008, however, deforestation rates were accelerating across the region, leaving behind large swaths of dead stumps—scars representing years of people’s struggles against the activities of talamontes (illegal loggers). The loggers and their hired mafia gunmen cleared dozens of hectares per week: first, to sell timber for easy money and, second, to establish lucrative avocado plantations to capitalize on surging global demand. Endless caravans of trucks, stacked high with stolen wood, rumbled through Cherán on a daily basis.

Community members attempted to reason with the loggers. Many local farmers and activists were abused, murdered, or disappeared. Others sought help from the police or military, to no avail. The people of Cherán, finding themselves on their own, had to fight back.

By 2011, about 70 percent of Cherán’s territorial forests had been destroyed. A group of Cherán mothers and grandmothers, tired of feeling powerless, met in secret to form a plan that would protect their life-giving woodlands. Unlike the pockets of young townspeople who had been rising up against the loggers wearing masks, the women wore no face coverings. “They were braver than us,” says Cherán resident Ricardo Torres, “so we started taking our cues from them.”

On April 15, 2011, the señoras took five loggers hostage. Seeing what was happening, community members ran to furiously ring the downtown church bell while others ignited fireworks—making any commotion they could to get the people of Cherán into the streets and actively defending their land.

Townspeople erected makeshift barricades to monitor traffic and, along the roadways, positioned the torched mechanical remains of seized logging trucks. Neighbors lit fogatas (bonfires) on street corners. Traditionally the place where families would meet to share a meal and conversation, people moved their kitchens from inside the home to out in the street so that neighbors—fearful of retribution—could come together to care for one another, keep an eye out, and feel safer.

After the townspeople succeeded in driving out most of the loggers through their actions, they took their struggle to the mayor and police force—considered enablers and colluders by many—who had sprung into action only to demand the release of the hostage loggers. “We had gone to the major political parties, seeing what they could do to help,” Torres says, recalling how politicians were accustomed to visiting Cherán. “But they were only interested in us during election campaigns, for our votes.” Recognizing the futility of appealing to authorities, the townspeople declared that no national political party or politician would ever be welcome in Cherán. All electioneering would be banned, too.

The town’s focus turned to building shared community governance. With the support of scholars from Mexico and abroad, the people of Cherán waged a lengthy legal battle in federal court to have their Indigenous sovereignty recognized and to govern themselves under a customary law system based on ancestral governance models. In doing so, they sought to revive their traditional Indigenous model of governance.

“On November 2, 2011, the Federal Electoral Tribunal, Mexico’s maximum authority on elections, ruled we had the right to choose our own leaders as per our own customs,” Torres says. “They ordered the state congress to reform the law in our favor and the electoral institute to facilitate this change.” The mayor was replaced with a democratically elected, 12-person council. Under this system all prospective councilors must first be endorsed by their respective neighborhood assembly—symbolically called fogata, in honor of the street fires first lit for safety after the expulsion of the loggers. An assembly can include 20, 30, or even 50 families, and it is the forum where neighbors discuss issues, seek consensus, and make decisions.

The assemblies also act as a “first filter,” a screening process for people wanting to access political power. “We select our representatives this way,” Torres says, “because when people are nominated and vetted aloud by those who truly know them, they are evaluated for their past actions—not mere political promises.”

Among its duties, the council controls the community security force, made up of independent volunteers that run the town’s security checkpoints and conduct daily patrols of the forest. Thanks to this protection, García says, Cherán’s residents do not fear being out after dark—as is common in other areas of the state—and they not only have some of their beloved forest still intact, but also continue regenerating it by planting new saplings. “Today, at the edges of where our territory meets those of neighboring communities, there is a defined border: on our side, verdant forest,” Torres says, “and, on the other, industrial avocado plantations.”

In its role as the commercial and academic hub for the nearby villages, Cherán is losing its language. Torres laments that his own and younger generations barely know their ancestral tongue. “I understand it somewhat but cannot speak it—my kids even less so,” he says. “But that doesn’t mean we’re not P’urhépecha, that we don’t think Indigenously.” Little by little, the community’s renewed solidarity and honoring of traditions are getting townspeople of all ages in touch with their roots.

The realities of Cherán’s self-defense and organization have continued to evolve since the residents’ initial coup, and profound challenges have arisen along the way. But the town remains a testament to what can happen when people have the courage to imagine and live out what safety really means to them.

“Historically, our community has had a great ability to organize itself, to practice jaropikua,” Torres says, using a local word that roughly means “mutual aid.” “P’urhépecha is not just a language; it’s a lifestyle, a vision.”

learn_more.title: The Mexican Town that Kicked Out Politicians and Started Over
Cheran: The Town That Threw Out Police, Politicians, and Gangsters
One Mexican Town Revolts against Violence and Corruption. Six Years in, Its Experiment Is Working

items.title: Berea College
items.body:
*1855–Present, Berea, Kentucky, United States*

Founded more than 150 years ago with a mission to make higher education accessible to poor white and free Black students, Berea College was the first school in the US South to be sexually and racially integrated. Founder John Fee was an abolitionist who started an anti-slavery church in 1853, which also served as a one-room school. Fee and his colleagues were expelled from Madison County, Kentucky by pro-slavery factions in 1859, but they returned after the Civil War and officially incorporated the college, named Berea after an open-minded town in the Bible. Its first class, in the 1866–67 school year, consisted of 96 Black students and 91 white students.

Berea’s mission has adapted to changing times. Its 2022–23 student population of 1,450 boasted national and international learners alike, but the private, liberal arts college has remained committed to educating diverse students from the Appalachian region. In the fall of 2022, 27 percent of the student body identified as Black, 15 percent as Hispanic, and 40 percent of the student body came from Appalachia (including 33 percent of all Black and 34 percent of all Hispanic students). Additionally, 8 percent of all students are international, representing 71 countries. Berea has gender-inclusive housing, and the recently founded bell hooks center equips students with ways “to imagine and enact new relationships” beyond gender and racial hierarchy.

What unites students is their academic potential and economic need. Berea College covers all students’ tuition—valued at roughly $44,300 a year per student— with federal grant money for low-income families, ardent fundraising, and its $1.4 billion endowment. A “financial eligibility requirement” means that 97 percent of students are undergraduates who have significant financial need. The cost of housing, meals, and books are prorated based on family income, with average family income estimated at $29,296 in 2019. In the same year, 59 percent of students in the incoming class had their costs fully covered. Nationally, the average Class of 2020 graduate in the United States carries $32,731 in student-loan debt. In contrast, 49 percent of Berea students graduated debt-free. As the average amount of student debt increases across the United States, it is decreasing at Berea. Over half of Berea’s students are of the first-generation of their families to attend college.

The school fiercely and innovatively breaks the mold of today’s elite colleges in both cost to its students and its community and service-oriented approach. In the mid1960s, Berea initiated programs for students to engage in community service in the Appalachian region and beyond, a legacy that continues through the college’s Center for Excellence in Learning Through Service. In 1970, Berea created the Appalachian Center, which established a curriculum in Appalachian Studies that informs and empowers students both from and outside the region. With the motto “Tradition, Diversity, Change,” the Center’s work embraces all of Appalachia’s diverse peoples, celebrates their cultural richness, and explores tangible ways for students to work with these communities.

Berea regards students as regional and international investments, not as revenue streams. Student organizations at Berea are active in different religious, gender, environmental, and social justice movements—in the spirit of the college’s motto, drawn from the Book of Acts: “God has made of one blood all peoples of the Earth.” Community-service initiatives sponsored by the college are plentiful, such as Berea Kids Eat. In the city of Berea, over 85 percent of youth enrolled in school participate in the free National School Breakfast and Lunch Program. Through coordinating resources from local farmers, the college, and state and federal programs, the Berea Summer Food Service Program ensures kids in the region receive food year-round. Meals are free for youth with no income requirements, registrations, or limits on the number of meals.

Unlike other private institutions with robust endowments, Berea does not funnel funds to build extravagant amenities to attract prospective students. Instead, it maintains a careful budget and internally produces much of what it needs. To offset the cost of operating the college, all Berea students work at least 10 hours per week in over 120 different departments. They serve as teaching assistants, groundskeepers, information technologists, staff at the college-owned hotel, artisans in the workshop that produces and sells mountain crafts, and more. Students also tend to the 250-acre organic farm situated on campus, producing beef, goat, chicken, pork, and vegetables for the school’s cafeteria.

Students receive a Labor Transcript upon graduation that chronicles their work experiences. The Labor Program is guided by five learning goals and expectations that illustrate the program’s commitment to developing both hard and soft skills, critical thinking and problem solving. The program also supports students to gain experience in work roles that are relevant to their fields of study. Roughly half of all students do internships as well. In short, students are para-professionals who help operate all aspects of the college, an experience they recognize as preparing them to get things done. Berea is one of only nine federally recognized Work Colleges in the United States, which are subject to special regulation by the Department of Education.

Although graduates find jobs around the nation and are successful in national graduate and professional schools, Berea College’s attention to learning about and serving the region helps students see the value of long-term local commitment. Although educated youth are known to leave the region, 67 percent of all Berea’s graduates from Kentucky and elsewhere in Appalachia since 2010 have decided to stay.

Faculty and staff salaries at Berea are lower than at other colleges, but professors are no less qualified. Over 90 percent of the full-time faculty hold the highest available degree in their field. These professionals are deeply dedicated to the college’s students and ideals. To help faculty and staff better understand the lives of their students, Berea offers continuing education, including a pair of week-long tours. One brings staff and faculty into Appalachia to learn about the history, economics, politics, religions, and stereotypes of the region. Another is a civil rights tour through Tennessee, Alabama, and Mississippi. With a ten-to-one student-to-faculty ratio at the college, knowledge and understanding of students’ backgrounds is crucial for professors.

Despite pressures to commercialize and standardize, Berea College strives to realize its roots and reason for being: the values of inclusion, equity, and impartial love.

items.title: Carolina Textile District and COVID-19
items.body:
*2020, Western North Carolina, United States*

Western North Carolina has long been a center for manufacturing, especially of textiles and furniture. Despite free-trade agreements, which stripped jobs from communities on both sides of the US-Mexico border, one in four people in North Carolina’s Western Piedmont region still work in manufacturing. Many Guatemalan Mayan immigrants have settled in the area to work in textiles and furniture production. Over the years, they have shaped the region by campaigning for dignified workplaces. Organizer Molly Hemstreet witnessed their struggle to unionize a production facility in Morganton, North Carolina, and began to wonder: Could workers own and operate their own companies?

In 2008, Hemstreet and leaders from the Mayan community co-founded a sewing cooperative, Opportunity Threads. They drew on inspiration from Frank Adams, an early architect of the Highlander Folk School (now the Highlander Research and Education Center). Opportunity Threads has become one of the largest immigrant-led sewing co-ops in the United States, with more than 50 workers as of 2020.

Aiming to expand cooperativism across the textile industry and strengthen local supply chains, Hemstreet collaborated with the area’s economic development association and a textile research and development center to establish the Carolina Textile District (CTD). Fueled by its mantra, “be big by being small together,” CTD is a network that brings together over 30 small manufacturers, including Opportunity Threads, and is led by nine partners, representing 1,500 workers in total. Members cooperatively govern, train new workers, share contracts and contacts, develop strong ethical standards for the industry, and share their struggles and joys.

When the COVID-19 pandemic struck the United States in early 2020, CTD was well-positioned to produce personal protective equipment and cloth face masks. Pivoting its textile and furniture member-companies to manufacture medical supplies was a challenge with many moving parts. It required consulting with doctors and public-health professionals, navigating ever-changing federal guidelines, prototyping masks and gowns, sourcing medical-grade materials, organizing the cohorts of manufacturers, connecting with markets and sponsors, developing a cohesive warehousing and distribution center, upscaling production, and overseeing quality control. As factories in Western North Carolina were shuttering, CTD was not only safely keeping open their plants, but hiring as well. The pandemic underscored the need for CTD and accelerated the network’s growth.

Opportunity Threads was the hub for CTD’s sewn goods during the pandemic. Worker-owners responded quickly, putting their technical skills to use in developing market-ready goods. Other CTD members came on board to help. Since CTD members had several years of “coopetition” under their belts, the network rapidly developed new products and increased production. At one point, they were producing 50,000 units per week, which kept over 60 mills humming. “We have achieved so many things that we probably would not have been able to accomplish in a company owned by one person,” says Maricela Lopez, a worker-owner at Opportunity Threads.

Through this project, CTD supplied 190,000 sanitary gowns to North Carolina’s Department of Health and Human Services and over 500,000 facemasks and other personal protective equipment to frontline workers. Additionally, it generated $2 million in revenue for its textile and furniture manufacturers. According to Sara Chester, CTD co-founder and Industrial Commons co-executive director, “When weekly mask production hit 40,000 units, [we] realized something tremendous was being achieved.”

Instead of communities having to wait for companies to come in and to solve economic, health, and social problems, cooperative industry networks can solve critical problems quickly and creatively. This model is one replicable example of how rural communities can actively build an industry ecosystem where workers own a secure supply chain, collaborate in mutually beneficial ways, and solve their communities’ most pressing problems.

items.title: Chitsvachirimurutsoka Cooperative Society
items.body:
*1982–Present, Hatfield, Zimbabwe*

After the end of Zimbabwe’s war of liberation in 1980, 22 ex-freedom fighters came together to start a new life by founding a cooperative farm called the Chitsvachirimurutsoka Cooperative Society. For them, this was a new battle: “a battle for economic independence.” The founding members of Chitsvachirimurutsoka were able to raise the money to buy land, equipment, and farming tools by combining their demobilization allowances—sums of money given to former fighters by the government, amounting to approximately $128 in US dollars a month per person. Using traditional skills, members began crop and livestock production. They grew maize, sugar beans, and sunflowers.

The first three years were challenging. The members did not have the business skills to efficiently manage the farm. To make matters worse, bad droughts ruined the crops, leaving little to harvest and the farm in debt. This made life very difficult, and the cooperative lost three members who abandoned the project.

Chitsvachirimurutsoka made it through these challenging early days, living up to the meaning of its name: “There is no gain without sweat.” Management of the cooperative was improved through business training given to the members. While drought is an ongoing issue, Chitsvachirimurutsoka has learned to manage it. As a result, it has had many profitable years and has invested proceeds in improving the living standards of members and developing of the wider community. For Chitsvachirimurutsoka, contributing to the community is an essential part of being a cooperative. Over the last few decades, members have dug boreholes to provide clean water, built and repaired roads, started a preschool on the farm, paid for funerals, and supported sick and orphaned people in their community, in addition to many other contributions.

A key pillar of the cooperative’s mission is to solve food insecurity. Every day at the farm, from seven in the morning to seven at night, members sell poultry, vegetables, and other products at affordable prices. Most of the customers come from nearby Epworth, a settlement of about 300,000 people, many of whom are poor. Chitsvachirimurutsoka also supplies food to several community institutions including a cafeteria, some schools, and local clinics.

Chitsvachirimurutsoka’s general meeting, which occurs three or four times a year, is the supreme authority guiding the cooperative’s actions. Here, members make major decisions such as approving by-laws, regulations, codes of conduct, and the action plan and budget for each year. The general meeting elects the Management Committee, the policy-making body of the cooperative which oversees budgets and plans to ensure the cooperative is on track to meet its goals. The committee members serve for three years (but can be removed if they are not performing well).

The chairperson of the committee appoints a coordinator to implement resolutions passed at the annual general meeting held in December. This coordinator reports to the Management Committee and must be approved by a majority of members. Once appointed, it is the coordinator’s responsibility to ensure that the cooperative brings in enough revenue and keeps costs low enough to reach the net profit goals set by the committee. The coordinator manages all other cooperative members. In this way, Chitsvachirimurutsoka has a traditional business structure with the coordinator as the boss, except during general meetings when the members are collectively in charge.

However, Chitsvachirimurutsoka is not like a private company where a small number of shareholders make major decisions and control all the profit. Every member of Chitsvachirimurutsoka Cooperative Society holds shares in the enterprise, so that each receives dividends when the co-op profits or shares in its losses. Members actively participate in decision-making and work in positions that make sense for them. Women are treated the same way as men, and there is much consideration for children, dependents, and disabled people.

The success of Chitsvachirimurutsoka and other cooperatives of the early 1980s has encouraged the formation of hundreds of cooperatives in Zimbabwe. In keeping with one of the international cooperative principles, “cooperation among cooperatives,” these cooperatives started to organize themselves at the district level, where they came together to share information, ideas, experiences, and resources, including a revolving loan fund, a machinery pool, and bulk buying and marketing arrangements. The same happened at provincial and national levels, with cooperatives pooling together transportation and group insurance, as well as standardized accounting and auditing to assist the members and their initiatives. Though later economic and political crises would hit the cooperative movement hard, these early advances should be celebrated for their democratic and grassroots development model.
