items.title: Community Media Association of Honduras
items.body:
*2013–Present, Honduras*

In June 2009, the democratically elected president of Honduras, Manuel Zelaya, was arrested and forcibly removed from the country on the order of the Honduran Supreme Court by the Honduran Army. In the months and years that followed the coup d’état, thousands of journalists, opposition politicians, human rights activists, and others were detained, disappeared, or murdered by the new regime. Media coverage of this violence was virtually non-existent, since even during Zelaya’s presidency, Honduran media was solely controlled by a few wealthy conservative families and intentionally excluded voices critical of the government installed by the coup.

This tumultuous political landscape led to the formation of the Community Media Association of Honduras (AMCH, or Asociación de Medios de Comunicación Comunitarios de Honduras in Spanish). The AMCH is made up of approximately forty groups and organizations throughout the nation, including alternative media groups, activists, indigenous groups, young people and more. It aims to facilitate conversations with the National Telecommunications Commission of Honduras (CONATEL) to challenge the limited broadcasting landscape in the country.

In Honduras, one must purchase a license to start a media company. After the coup in 2009, licenses could only be acquired through an auction system controlled by parties loyal to the government. This arrangement prevented large portions of the Honduran people from starting media companies, specifically excluding peasant groups, human rights organizations, young people demanding democratic change, and Indigenous and Garifuna peoples (descendants of 18th-century African shipwreck survivors). The result was that a small number of companies owned most of the radio and TV stations in Honduras—a broadcast monopoly.

A 2011 report on the events surrounding the coup, created by the government as part of the Accord for National Reconciliation and Strengthening of Democracy in Honduras, concluded that the broadcast monopolies bore significant blame for the social crisis, and recommended democratizing access to the radio frequencies, television, and the internet.

In response to the wave of national discussion that followed, the AMCH brought together local and regional collectives to demand change. In August 2013, the regulating authority approved the AMCH’s proposal to make it possible for community groups to acquire media licenses. As of January 2017, 25 community radio stations in different parts of the country are in operation, and two television stations have been approved. Prior to this, only five community radio stations existed in the entire country.

Community media grants visibility to decentralized grassroots resistance and social change. In the San Antonio neighborhood of the town of El Taragual in western Honduras, a Lenca indigenous community has been fighting a law passed by the government that would divide up their land into plots. For them, radio is a necessary tool for educating the community about the adverse effects and conflicts that this parceling would cause. Emeterio Pérez, the leader of the neighborhood where the radio station originated, joined a group of coffee and grain farmers between the ages of 80 and 100, who committed to donating a portion of their wages to the radio station’s Steering Committee. They donated one work day per week, and a group of women sold homemade bread, nacatamales and other treats to support the station. On May 3, 2015, with a year’s savings and the technical support of AMCH, the Taragual community put a radio transmitter on air with the Voice of Life program on 106.7 FM. One year after speaking into their microphones for the first time, the station’s management committee had built alliances with key players in the neighboring cities of Gracias, San Rafael and La Union.

Today, the committee is attempting to legally register with the Indigenous Association for the Integral Development of El Taragual, which would grant them governmental recognition of their community radio frequency. The AMCH is providing technical training and legal support for this effort.

Through supporting community efforts and providing resources to formalize local broadcasting, the AMCH slowly works towards building a democratized media landscape that provides a variety of cultural and educational listening options throughout the country.

items.title: Comprehensive Sexuality Education in the Philippines
items.body:
*2014–2019, Philippines*

Youth in the Philippines face many challenges regarding their sexual wellbeing. Rates of teenage pregnancy and HIV/AIDS are rising, and high rates of violence and extreme poverty prevent youth from making healthy choices and completing their education.

85 percent of the Filipino population is Catholic, which means that Catholic teachings provide the dominant discourse on sexuality. An 18 year, highly politicized struggle led to the national Reproductive Health and Parenthood Act in 2012, which guaranteed access to contraception, maternal health, sex education, and fertility control. Since then, continued opposition from both religious leaders and politicians has prevented adequate funding of reproductive-health programs and severely limited their implementation across the country. Many Filipino youth have limited exposure to and experience with issues of sexuality, human reproduction, and anatomy. They’ve had little to no education about how to protect themselves from sexually transmitted infections and unwanted pregnancy. When unplanned pregnancies happen, young people face a great deal of pressure to marry. This often ties them into a cycle of poverty that can be very difficult to overcome. Sexual abuse, exploitation, and incest are infrequently discussed and, for the most part, young people lack the knowledge and tools for sexual safety and negotiating sexual relationships.

In 2013, Aimee Santos-Lyons, a Filipina immigrant to the US, and her husband Rev. Joseph Santos-Lyons from the US Universalist Unitarian Association (UUA) began holding a series of sexuality education workshops for Filipino youths with the national Unitarian Universalist Church of the Philippines (UUCP) team based in Dumaguete, Negros Oriental, in the Visayas region. The program was developed to be culturally relevant, utilizing local examples, popular education methods, and interpretation and translation work in Tagalog and Visayan languages. This work built on the sexuality education program of HASIK, a feminist organizing group based in Metro Manila that works with urban poor women and girls.

In an effort to expand the workshops nationally, the Rev. Jory Agate from the UUA collaborated with Rev. Rebecca Quimada Sienes from the UUCP to design and lead a Filipino adaptation of the Our Whole Lives (OWL) program. The OWL program first began in the US during the 1960s, when the UUA realized that the youth in its congregation needed guidance around sexuality. It created a secular, science-based curriculum that spoke to the sexual realities youth were experiencing. It provided sexuality education guided by ethics, safety, and responsibility to the community. Over time, with the help of the United Church of Christ, the OWL program has expanded to serve people of all ages. There are thousands of OWL trainers in the United States, and the curriculum is used by religious and secular groups alike.

To bring OWL to young people in the Philippines, the UUA raised money through international networks, relying upon the groundwork laid by the Santos-Lyons’s earlier workshops. Local workshop leaders aimed to center Filipino culture and norms, carefully adapting the OWL curriculum to ensure its relevance to the cultural and economic context of Filipino youth today. Trained peer facilitators assisted with delivery of the material and small group facilitators fostered conversations in participants’ own languages. Workshop leaders created mechanisms to circumnavigate traditional Filipino deference to authority figures in order to encourage more input, feedback, and questions from youth.

Since Filipino Unitarian Universalist congregations are small and rural, a week-long workshop was held at the church’s headquarters in Dumaguete, to which youth from various congregations were invited. To mitigate the privileging of white, Western views of sexuality, the program included guest speakers from the region. Local leaders from the health department led a presentation on contraception, three community members identifying as LGBTQ participated in a panel on sexuality, and an external agency led a day of gender equity and non-violence work with the male participants.

One goal of the workshop was to enable youth to take home and into their peer communities key principles of sexual health. Leaders encouraged the students to remember seven core components of a sexually healthy relationship, which represented the foundational values of the program. When the workshop’s success was later evaluated using a survey, these tenets were participants’ most significant takeaway, along with newfound acceptance of the LGBTQ community and a commitment to using contraception.

Leaders recognized the limited reach of this one-week workshop. The young participants could only absorb so much information from their first experience of comprehensive sexuality education. Additionally, the workshop only reached a tiny fraction of the Unitarian Universalist youth in the Philippines. For greater change to occur, these programs need to be available much more widely. In the process, however, they must retain their cultural specificity, connecting a global effort to the languages, norms, and concerns of the places where they spread.

items.title: Conflict Kitchen
items.body:
*2010–2017, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States*

Believing that the quickest way to a person’s heart is through their stomach, Conflict Kitchen sought to promote peace and build cross-cultural understanding by introducing people to the food and culture of places with which their government is in conflict. Based in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and the brainchild of artist-activists Jon Rubin and Dawn Weleski, Conflict Kitchen used a simple takeout window framed by a colorful facade to serve up the cuisine, and celebrate the culture of a succession of countries, including Iran, Afghanistan, Cuba, North Korea, Venezuela, Palestine, and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy.

The takeout window functioned as a platform for public dialogue, and the food line became a space for hungry Pittsburghers to engage with people and places the media consistently distorts and misrepresents. The takeout counter was staffed by chefs and public artists trained to facilitate conversations about the featured country. Each food wrapper was printed with personal profiles of people who live in the country being celebrated, as well as articles on the country’s food, art, religion, culture, and government.

To extend the experience beyond the takeout line and further encourage cross-cultural dialogue, Conflict Kitchen also organized public events that centered around food. Pittsburgh locals and Iranians in Tehran shared a meal via webcam in a virtual, city-to-city dinner party. Both groups made the same Persian recipes, then sat down to eat together. Other events have included informal lunch hour discussions on food and politics, dinners with invited speakers, and live cooking lessons through Skype.

In November 2014, a series of death threats forced Conflict Kitchen to close down for nearly a week. In response to the threats and allegations of being anti-Israel, the directors of Conflict Kitchen emphasized that their purpose is to hold a loudspeaker to the voices and historical experiences of people from across the world—Palestinians and Palestinian-Americans included. The backlash they received is proof that this type of work is necessary.

Conflict Kitchen offered the public many points of entry, from the taste of a new dish, to interactions with employees or fellow customers, to the interviews printed on the food wrappers, and the intimate meals with people far away. Cultural exchange was central to the project; the organizers prioritized facilitating a space for locals and people overseas to express their respective point of view.

The webcam meals between Pittsburgh and abroad provided a temporary glimpse of what it can mean to share cultures, politics, and, of course, food. By creating a zone of open dialogue and cross-cultural understanding for at least one meal, Conflict Kitchen made a world where we listen to each other and draw our own conclusions seem possible. It used food as a vehicle for cross-cultural understanding—and also provided delicious takeout.

items.title: Energiewende
items.body:
*1979–Present, Germany*

On April 15, 2023, Germany shut down its last nuclear power plant. For over six decades, Germans had been getting up to a quarter of their energy from nuclear plants. Over the years, the political will to phase out nuclear power often waffled, highly dependent on popular pressure. The 2023 phaseout was not inevitable: it was a hard-won milestone in Germany’s transition toward a safer, more democratic energy system.

In 1971, Germany’s government adopted its first environmental policy program and formed the German Advisory Council on the Environment. Environmentalists in the early 1970s had pushed for holistic changes in the system, including an overhaul of nuclear energy efforts as the implications of nuclear power became part of public conversation. Activists and farmers occupied a site intended for a new nuclear reactor in 1973, drawing much public attention to the movement. The occupation proved successful, but oil shortages caused by the Yom Kippur War—and, later, the Iran-Iraq War—created a renewed interest in nuclear energy.

Germany’s Green Party, founded in 1979, won its first parliamentary seats in West Germany’s lower chamber in 1983. Its elected members brought with them the notion of “Energiewende”—literally meaning energy transition or energy change—which called for a transition to a renewable energy system controlled by local communities.

A newly popularized understanding of climate change brought about a 1987 Green Party proposal to drastically reduce carbon emissions in the decades approaching the 2000s. At the same time, renewed opposition to nuclear power developed in 1986 following the Chernobyl nuclear plant disaster in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, and this opposition successfully pressured the German government to agree on a nuclear phaseout date. But, just when it seemed that the phaseout would happen, a conservative government rolled back plans in 2010.

Then came the Fukushima meltdown of 2011. The anti-nuclear movement surged once again, and the government responded to the massive pressure coming from the people, again re-establishing a nuclear phaseout date.

Today, the fight for clean energy continues in Germany. Nuclear is out, but in the face of new crises, the German people, the German government, and industry interests are again engaged in the push and pull of deciding the fates of fossil energy sources like coal and natural gas.

The Energiewende calls not only for green energy but also for a democratized energy system. Renewable sources can be owned by individuals, municipalities, and communities. This redistributes power over the grid through a bottom-up approach led by energy activists and community leaders.

Opposition to the Energiewende primarily stems from the coal industry, particularly mining trade unions. As a stable and relatively cheap form of energy, coal is widely supported by Germany’s industrial base. Jobs in the renewable sector are far less protected by unions and tend to lack reasonable worker contracts, and the transition requires an energy surcharge for consumers.

For the Energiewende and German climate activists, there have been significant setbacks. After the COVID-19 pandemic began in 2020, the clean energy movement took a hit in its ability to organize demonstrations and campaigns. Then, when Russian President Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine in early 2022 and Europe mobilized to pull away from Russian energy sources, there was a renewed effort for increasing development of new gas contracts and infrastructure. As Europe and Germany in particular face an energy shortage, in large part due to the invasion and sanctions on Russian energy, there has been a big push from powerful institutions like the European Commission to transition to natural gas as a bridge technology.

But the crisis is an opportunity. “Energy policy is a highly controlled, elite controlled policy field,” says Tadzio Müller, longtime climate activist, political scientist, and researcher. It took time, but it was public pressure from the German people that resulted in the nuclear phaseout. Despite setbacks and delays, “we re-established the principle that social movements can demand phase-out dates for dirty technologies,” says Müller, referring to a 2038 phase-out date for coal in Germany.

The Energiewende lives on, aiming to curb carbon emissions and create a carbon-free, renewable grid by 2050. But its implications run deeper. It stands for a future of decentralized, community-owned power as people claim ownership of renewable energy sources.

learn_more.title: Energy Democracy: Germany’s Energiewende to Renewables
Germany’s Energiewende: The Easy Guide
Inside Germany’s Power Struggle Over Nuclear Energy

items.title: Equipo Maíz
items.body:
*1983–Present, San Salvador, El Salvador and throughout Central America*

El Salvador’s civil war and state-sponsored death squads terrorized the nation during the early 1980s. Among the atrocities were the mid-Mass assassination of Óscar Romero—the Catholic archbishop of San Salvador who loudly condemned poverty, torture, and other rampant injustices—and the subsequent murders of 42 civilians at his funeral. Spurred by those events, a group of educators founded Asociación Equipo Maíz in April 1983.

Although many civilians were involved in armed conflict, the Equipo Maíz team believed that education, information, and analysis were needed to understand and challenge the social, political, and economic forces that led to the country’s unrest. The group, using minimal resources and meeting in community settings, started teaching poor Salvadorans about the issues affecting their daily lives, thereby providing a route for people to transform their social realities.

When the group was initially formed, its founders struggled to agree on a name. After a few years operating as Equipo de Materiales Educativos Populares (Popular Educational Materials Team), the liberation-focused members craved a name that encompassed the mission’s breadth. In practice, the group was not solely issuing instructional documents; it was teaching and mobilizing the Salvadoran people. Names like Cebadera (a common shoulder bag carried by peasants that is filled with animal feed) were considered before someone suggested honoring maíz (corn), the life-giving crop for the Mesoamerican peoples that is the building block for traditional tamales, tortillas, and economies.

Because Equipo Maíz arose during the civil war, its outreach and educational efforts were concentrated within El Salvador. But over time, word of the group’s popular-education methods spread and gained traction throughout Central America. This led Equipo Maíz to collaborate with numerous organizations, sharing its printed materials, workshop outlines, and training guides with organizations in Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Mexico.

Equipo Maíz’s founders aimed to promote inclusion, foster creativity, and provide a path to liberation through knowledge. “Popular education is about using the wisdom of the people for community transformation,” said María Elsie Orellana, a Salvadoran women’s activist who has participated in Equipo Maíz workshops. It is not about one-off training sessions; rather, it is a process, brought about by necessity, that encourages the wholeness of participants while also building communities and their capacities. “Organized communities find the solutions to their own problems,” added Zulma Tobar, a coordinator for Sister Cities International. These communities, in turn, create a larger network of solidarity and creative resistance against oppression and human rights violations.

Equipo Maíz ensures all of its teachings are accessible and relevant. During the war years, some of the earliest workshops focused on themes from the Bible as a way to analyze social realities. This enabled members of the general public, most of whom were familiar with the Bible, to draw upon their existing knowledge as a path to complex discussions about topics of common interest. Popular education takes many different tangible forms, inspiring theater-style programs and other hands-on activities to engage learners of all levels.

Today, Equipo Maíz continues to hold educational workshops for communities about locally important topics. Additionally, it acts as a folk-academic publisher, authoring and releasing educational books on more than 60 topics, including climate change, ecology, gender equality, neoliberalism, peaceful protest, national history, and more. By providing its services to community groups that advance public power and social justice, Equipo Maíz counters the resurgence of far-right authoritarianism in El Salvador and across the region. While many citizen groups access its educational services free of charge, some entities—such as local municipalities or their international sister cities— are asked to pay.

Equipo Maíz’s outstanding achievement is its ability to produce publications in a language accessible to the people it serves. It creates educational and communication materials that democratize knowledge for different communities, such as historical and cultural documents and informative posters on sexuality. The publications seek to better understand the fundamental goals and effects of the economic and political decisions made by governments in the region, which has allowed human rights defenders to expand their political participation.

Equipo Maíz is governed by a representative democracy, in which the board of directors is elected every two years by an assembly comprised equally of workers and supporters. Those leaders are tasked with shepherding the organization, setting priorities, strategizing, and overseeing the four employee teams: education, sales and marketing, design, and printing.

Today, Equipo Maíz strives to incorporate younger generations, especially students, into its efforts of educating and empowering communities. Through accessible study of pressing challenges, Central Americans have the tools to sow greater equity and justice.

items.title: GreenWave Regenerative Ocean Farming
items.body:
*2014–Present, North America*

In 1992, at the height of industrialized fishing in Newfoundland, the cod stocks collapsed and 30,000 people were out of work overnight. Boats beached. Canneries emptied. As a commercial fisherman, I was face-to-face with the reality that there would be no jobs on a dead planet, and went on a journey of ecological redemption.

After oyster farming on Long Island Sound for almost a decade, it all came to a screeching halt in 2011 and 2012 when Hurricane Irene and Hurricane Sandy destroyed my farm. My farm and livelihood had become a canary in the coal mine for a climate crisis that arrived a hundred years ahead of schedule. Our fishing community needed another way forward.

Ocean farming is a trade both old and new, a job rooted in thousands of years of history, dating back to Roman times and Indigenous clam walls in the Pacific Northwest. It is also a way to synthesize the good and refuse the bad of industrial practices. We desperately needed a strategy based on one hard and fast rule: grow only zero-input species that won’t swim away and don’t need to be fed.

The design morphed into a vertical underwater garden: hurricane-proof anchors on the edges connected by horizontal ropes floating six feet below the surface. From these lines, kelp and other kinds of seaweed grow vertically downward, next to scallops in hanging nets, mussels held in suspension in mesh socks, oysters in cages on the seafloor, and then clams buried in the mud bottom.

These crops are regenerative—they breathe life back into the ocean. Shellfish and seaweeds are powerful agents of renewal. A seaweed like kelp is heralded as the culinary equivalent of the electric car. Oysters and mussels filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, removing nitrogen, a nutrient that is the root cause of the ever-expanding dead zones in the ocean. And these farms function as storm surge-protectors and artificial reefs, both helping to protect shoreline communities and attracting a range of aquatic species that come to hide, eat, and thrive.

This regenerative ocean farm design is replicable, affordable, and easy to build—it requires $20,000-$50,000, access to 20 acres of ocean, underwater rope scaffolding, and a boat. Once finished, it churns out a lot of food: up to 250,000 shellfish and 65 tons of seaweed on a mature 20-acre farm.

The regenerative ocean farm model is scalable. There are more than 10,000 plants in the ocean and hundreds of varieties of shellfish—we’ve barely begun to scratch the surface of what we can grow. And the demand for these crops is not dependent solely on food; seaweed can be used as soil amendments, animal feed, biomaterials, and more.

These crops hit the climate sweet spot—requiring no fresh water, fertilizer, or feed while creating economic opportunities for coastal communities. Ocean farmers can partner with the ocean to simultaneously create jobs, feed the planet, and fight climate change. According to the World Bank, a network of ocean farms equivalent to less than 5 percent of US waters can have a deep impact with a small footprint, creating 50 million direct jobs, producing protein equivalent to 2.3 trillion cheeseburgers, and removing the carbon equivalent to 20 million cars.

In 2014, I co-founded GreenWave with Emily Stengel to replicate and scale regenerative ocean farming. GreenWave works to spur collaboration and innovation with a global network of farmers, entrepreneurs, and researchers, all hell-bent on building community-based climate solutions out at sea.

GreenWave works with ocean farmers to replicate the model throughout North America and beyond to build a blue economy that ensures we all make a living on a living planet. The goal is to train and support 10,000 ocean farmers by 2030 to build community-based climate solutions out at sea that yield positive environmental and economic impact at scale.

When more than 8,000 aspiring farmers signed up for GreenWave’s training program, the organization pivoted their strategy to expand their reach and jumpstart the industry. GreenWave launched the Regenerative Ocean Farming Hub in April 2022, a free online resource including a suite of seed-to-sale courses, more than 80 how-to videos, interactive farm design tools, and an online community for aspiring and active farmers to connect and propel the industry forward.

In addition to training and technical assistance, GreenWave supports small- and medium-scale seaweed farms through climate subsidies; market cultivation across food, agriculture, biomaterials, and other industries; as well as the development of farmer-owned kelp seed hatcheries, dock-side processing, and storage infrastructure.

With ocean agriculture still in its infancy, we have an unprecedented opportunity to build a food system from the bottom up. Together we can avoid the mistakes of industrial agriculture and aquaculture, farm for the benefit of all, not just the few, and weave economic and social justice into the DNA of the blue-green economy, all while creating millions of jobs and feeding the planet.

items.title: Guifi.net
items.body:
*2003–Present, Catalonia, Spain*

In the rural mountain communities outside of Barcelona, Spain, fiber optic lines run across the land— from east to west and north to south. These lines supply internet access to the region’s farmers and villagers. The access they provide is thanks to Guifi.net, a telecommunications network that is governed democratically by the members it serves.

Guifi.net began in late 2003 to solve a specific problem in the village of Gurb in Osona County: little to no internet access. While urban centers in Spain were already connected, most rural villages lacked access. In Gurb, the only place in town with the internet was the town hall. This was because, under Spanish law, internet service providers (ISPs) are required to provide service to every town. For-profit ISPs could fulfill the minimum legal requirement by providing internet to only the town hall in rural villages like Gurb. Facing constituents who were angry that their representatives had internet access while they did not, elected officials welcomed the Guifi.net solution with open arms.

Starting as a single connection across rooftop antennas, Guifi.net then expanded and installed more nodes that could send and receive WiFi signal among them, sharing connectivity throughout the network. Eventually, in 2009, the network added fiber optic lines. Now, it has established over 36,000 working nodes, connecting not only Gurb but many other villages to WiFi. The network creates a common pool of bandwidth to which neighbors can contribute and from which they can draw, and this continues to grow as more participants join. Members receive bills that separate how much of their payment goes to construction and operational costs and how much gets reinvested into the network.

Guifi.net is explicit in its anti-capitalist motives. Its model disrupts the traditional telecommunications economy by fostering a collaborative economy and a commons. It rejects exploitation of user communities and favors a sustainable, mutually beneficial network infrastructure. The project sees internet and telecommunications access as a human right and aims to provide connectivity for groups who are traditionally excluded.

The infrastructure and services provided by Guifi.net are funded by donations, loans, subsidies, and member payments. The project also brings in money through the Guifi.net Foundation, which was founded after Guifi.net received the National Telecommunications Award from the Catalan government in 2007.

Unlike many for-profit companies, speculative and extractive practices are explicitly forbidden by the organization. To protect the network against exploitation, Guifi.net is a direct democracy where governance occurs through participatory meetings. It has three groups of stakeholders: public interest, altruistic, and in-return. The public interest group comprises the administrative bodies; the altruistic group is made up of volunteers and donors who do not seek repayment; the in-return group seeks some benefit for themselves either by offering services for fees, or fees for services.

Guifi.net isn’t the only network of its kind. Similar telecommunications networks include the Freifunk network in Germany, or FunkFeuer in Austria, a citizen-led provider that taught Guifi.net how to use its technology. Beyond this, there are other communities in diverse locations, from Slovenia to rural villages in Mexico, who are actively developing their own wireless networks.

In today’s world, internet access is not simply desirable but is essential for exercising other important rights and for accessing a wide range of further resources. It supports freedom of expression, education, communication across boundaries, and connects people to the information they need to defend their rights around housing, land, energy, and so much else. The countless rural communities who, under capitalism, lack internet access because supplying it is not profitable for ISPs, do not need to wait any longer. Like Guifi.net, communities can take steps to understand how these networks work, reach out to community members and international partners, and build mesh networks of their own.

items.title: Health Mutuals in Mali
items.body:
*1996–Present, Mali*

More than two decades ago, the chief physician of the Center for Community Health in the rural community of Nongom-Souala in Mali noticed the center’s services were largely unused by the region’s over 10,000 inhabitants. Nongom-Souala is primarily home to agricultural workers in the cotton industry, who struggle to afford healthcare, especially in the winter after harvest season when they are short on cash. To remedy this, the center’s chief started Cotonniers de Nongon Souala (MUT-CO NONGON), a healthcare mutual that was the first of its kind in rural Mali.

The idea is simple: a mutual is a form of community insurance where members pay a regular fee with the understanding that the funds will help any member who falls ill. Membership fees are between 1,000 and 2,500 CFA francs a month (equivalent to $2 to $5) plus an annual fee of around 3,000 francs, depending on the mutual, and cover 70-80 percent of healthcare costs.

In the last 25 years, healthcare mutuals in Mali have grown exponentially as a mechanism for providing universal access to care. In 1998, the Malian government established the Union Technique de la Mutualité Malienne (Technical Union of Malian Mutuals), a federated structure for mutuals. Presently, it includes 115 mutuals of which 108 are exclusively health mutuals that together provide for 35,000 people.

Most health mutuals arise for reasons similar to MUT-CO NONGON: people living in poverty suffer disproportionately from health problems, which in turn exacerbate poverty through lost wages and the costs of care. Mutuals attempt to intervene in this cycle by improving poor people’s access to healthcare and being responsive to local needs. In Mali, health mutual members can afford to utilize twice the amount of health services as the national average.

Unlike private health insurance companies, health mutuals only serve one community and are run by their members. All members are part of a general assembly that elects the board of directors to make decisions. Mutuals often have no employees, ensuring all fees go to the membership. While corporate insurers prioritize profits, mutuals can put their members first. The rise of the mutualist movement in Mali has increased access to healthcare for workers in agricultural and informal industries, which represent 78 percent of the population. In 2010, the Malian government began co-funding 50 percent of mutual membership fees for these workers and continues to support mutuals through government grants. Mali remains the only country in Sub-Saharan Africa to have a legislative and regulatory framework for mutuals. Mutualists hope that eventually they will be able to provide access to healthcare for everyone in the agricultural and informal sectors, and they continue to advocate for Mali to establish a universal form of healthcare.

items.title: Incarcerated Worker Co-ops in Puerto Rico
items.body:
*2003–Present, Puerto Rico*

In most countries around the world, penitentiary systems are centered around punishment, not rehabilitation. That focus means that the people released from prison often re-enter society with few marketable skills, little money, and trauma from the years lost and the dehumanizing treatment they sustained while locked away. For those coming home to poverty, the likelihood of re-entering prison increases considerably.

Millions of people are incarcerated around the world, and many of them are subject to prison slave labor. This is a form of exploitation in which prisoners work grueling or dangerous jobs for corporate clients or the government. It is common for incarcerated workers to earn almost nothing, or a small fraction of the minimum wage, for their labor.

Incarcerated worker co-ops offer an alternative. Unlike prevailing systems of justice based on retribution, which expect a prisoner to suffer for their crime, incarcerated worker co-ops “return economic agency to those who are caged, giving them control over their livelihood and work experience,” says Jessica Gordon Nembhard, a US Cooperative Hall of Fame inductee and professor at John Jay College in New York City. Engagement in a cooperative enables incarcerated people to regain their dignity, while contributing to their families and communities in multiple ways. It also reduces recidivism, or the likelihood of a person returning to the criminal-justice system after leaving.

There are incarcerated worker co-ops in Italy, Canada, and Ethiopia, among others. On the Caribbean island of Puerto Rico, it was incarcerated people who started lobbying in 1999 for co-op education and the right to operate their own businesses in prison. They teamed up with the Puerto Rican League of Cooperatives and petitioned to change the law that had long barred them from running a co-op. After winning the right in 2003, they formed the artist’s cooperative Cooperativa ARIGOS. ARIGOS secured a contract with the Puerto Rican Department of Corrections, whereby the business pays 15 percent of its profits in exchange for production space and utilities in prisons such as electricity and internet. In addition, the co-op covers all costs for security and travel whenever its members need to go offsite to sell their art, especially at other co-op events around the island. After ARIGOS, more co-ops have formed in Puerto Rican prisons.

Through a co-op, incarcerated workers can gain some control over their working conditions and an ability to improve the dignity of their work. Income earned can be distributed as remittances to family members back home. The remainder is then paid out upon their release from prison, to help get their lives on track. By the time they are released from prison, co-op members will have developed employment-ready trade skills in carpentry, pottery, sewing, horticulture, or even solar technology. They also pick up other skills like problem solving, teamwork, and decision making, along with general knowledge of cooperative business practices. As a result, they are better prepared to either seek traditional jobs or collaborate with others to establish new co-op enterprises outside prison.

Of the dozens of men who have participated in Cooperativa ARIGOS and then been released from prison, only around 5 percent have been rearrested. The average recidivism rate in Puerto Rico, on the other hand, exceeds 50 percent. (For context, the United States has one of the highest recidivism rates in the world, at about 76 percent, and Norway has one of the lowest rates at 20 percent.) Equipped with new skills, social connections, and funds, co-op members have a better chance of succeeding upon their release. The ARIGOS model—and other programs that champion the dignity of prisoners—can be applied to existing prisons to aid in the transition away from punitive systems and toward prison abolition.

“When you’re in jail, the correctional department doesn’t care whether you’re doing better, whether you’re learning. They don’t care what you do. Just do your time and go home,” said Alan Vicéns, a former prison co-op member in Puerto Rico. “But this beautiful co-op system gave me theory and practice. It made me a better person,” he continued.

Despite the many benefits of such a system, there exist various barriers to its expansion. Certain laws, including those that prohibit entrepreneurship among incarcerated people or prevent the mere formation of co-ops in prisons, need to be changed. Prison administrators are constantly rotated in and out, often corresponding to each election cycle, so they need to be educated about—and convinced to endorse—the cooperative system. Though some of the public has yet to be convinced, the positive results of incarcerated-worker co-ops demonstrate the importance of efforts to enhance prisoner autonomy and dignity.

items.title: Islamic Finance
items.body:
*Seventh century–Present, Muslim communities worldwide*

1,400 years ago, Islamic scholars recognized the fragility of economic systems built on interest and categorically forbade it. They reasoned that money alone is not productive, so simply lending it should not produce more of it. Instead, value should increase or decrease according to people’s real-world productivity. At this time, Judaism and Christianity also opposed the charging of interest, but only in Islam has this legacy survived to the contemporary world in any widespread fashion.

Increasingly, people are realizing the global economy needs alternatives to dominant practices of interest-charging and debt. Economists have found that as people and businesses take on more and more debt they don’t invest as much in people, innovation, and other things essential to a healthy economy. Despite this evidence, policies and business practices around the world still favor debt-based financing and the interest that comes with it. But the longstanding tradition of Islamic finance reminds us that other ways of doing finance are possible.

While Islam welcomes loans, it uses debt as a form of redistributive finance, rather than as a profit-making tool for the already-wealthy. Islamic economics puts emphasis on mechanisms that foster widespread ownership through shareholding and risk-sharing. It encourages partners who take on some risk to share in the profits and losses. Mudaraba, for instance, is an Islamic finance instrument dating back to when Islam’s founder, Muhammad (peace be upon him), entered a partnership with his later-wife Khadija; she provided the capital and he provided the skill and labor, and they both shared the risk. When investors and participants share both risk and return, there is no incentive for dangerous financial projects such as the exchange of a debt for a debt or “shorting”—which helped produce the 2007–2008 global financial crisis by enabling investors to profit when borrowers don’t pay back their loans.

Fair trade, socially responsible enterprises, and shared investments make up the backbone of contemporary Islamic economics. Islamic tradition also recommends a wealth tax known as zakat on idle assets—those not generating revenue but requiring maintenance costs—which reflects an expectation that rich individuals and companies should circulate wealth in the economy rather than putting the burden on those dependent on an income. This tax then becomes a source of interest-free capital for future entrepreneurs.

Much of what is practiced in global financial markets today contradicts the values of Islamic finance. In the predominant forms of capitalist economics, interest-bearing debt is an integral feature. For most individuals and businesses, the only way to access capital is by taking on an interest-bearing debt. This makes borrowers beholden to lenders who, rather than sharing risk, profit from the interest on the loans and take possession of collateral offered against them. This allows lenders to increase their wealth regardless of the outcome and pushes borrowers into financial turmoil. Today, usury—the practice of lending money at extremely high interest rates—is a major contributor to wealth inequality.

It is difficult for alternative financial practices to function alongside and compete with dominant financial practices of today’s global capitalist system. Most of the Islamic financial sphere has side-stepped fundamental Islamic principles in order to maximize profits. This means there aren’t many working examples that can demonstrate the true potential of an Islamic finance model. But some entrepreneurs are working to change this.

After civil war broke out in Yemen in 2015, a London-born Yemeni named Faris Sheibani opened Qima Coffee to introduce Yemen’s specialty coffees to the world, using the company as a vehicle to improve the livelihoods of local rural communities sustainably. Modest loans played a vital role in Qima Coffee’s growth. With the help of flexible three-year payment terms, Qima Coffee became the largest specialty coffee exporter in Yemen, now working with 2,500 farmers across the country and selling to 26 countries globally. Sheibani went on to set up the Qima Foundation to direct the success of the coffee business toward serving Yemeni communities by making loans to local enterprises. In the spirit of Islamic finance, instead of imposing fixed repayment terms, Qima encourages entrepreneurs to move toward profitability before a 12-to-36month repayment period begins.

One could compare Qima Foundation’s interest-free loans with microfinance—small loans extended to unbanked communities. But most microfinance initiatives that have arisen in recent decades are rooted in conventional capitalism and interest-based practices. Qima offers an innovative approach through an incubator program based on the same age-old forms of support and financing that Qima Coffee received on its own journey.

There are aspects of the internet economy that are well-suited to be managed according to the principles of Islamic finance. Rewards- and equity-based crowdfunding, for instance, is a financial tool centered on communities pooling money rather than interest. But currently the model is rife with abuse. Most crowdfunding platforms don’t hold their campaigns to any ethical standards. As many as 9 percent of Kickstarter campaigns fail to deliver a single reward to supporters, enabling the campaigners to pocket their crowdfunding wins. The absence of guidance or education has resulted in a 64 percent failure rate for crowdfunding campaigns across the various platforms that host them. Since large crowdfunding platforms are financed by venture-capitalists, their business models privilege creators who can raise large sums at lower cost, through ripe access to resources, capital, and networks. This is a disservice to social enterprises led by women and people of color who are more likely to lack such privilege.

Inspired by the tradition of Islamic finance, UpEffect emerged in London in 2016 to address the failures of modern finance to empower and equip entrepreneurs addressing today’s most pressing problems. Through rewards-based crowdfunding, campaign management, and strategic consulting, UpEffect helps enterprises engage in real economic activity, avoid misaligned investors, and raise capital directly from customers to grow revenue. In contrast to the average industry success rate, UpEffect’s crowdfunding coaching model has led to a formidable 95 percent campaign success rate for social entrepreneurs. 70 percent of UpEffect campaigns have been female-owned and 65 percent have been led by people of color.

In 2017, actuarial practitioner Raza Ullah co-founded Primary Finance in London, a cooperative reinventing home buying by creating ethical alternatives to traditional mortgages. Its product enables home buyers and investors to enter into equitable partnership arrangements that form a virtuous cycle of risk-sharing and shared ownership. Home buyers are able to purchase a home by making monthly payments similar in cost to a traditional mortgage, but without any burden of debt. Meanwhile in Chicago, Muslim community organizer Hoda Katebi co-founded Blue Tin Production, a sewing cooperative run by refugee and immigrant women to address the fashion industry’s reliance on sweatshops, which, in turn, normalizes violence and exploitation. Profits are shared and distributed equally among the members every quarter, and all the members (minus one) are stitchers. Through organizations like Primary Finance and Blue Tin Production, the long tradition of Islamic finance converges with other traditions to promote inclusivity and solidarity in our economies.

Projects like the above demonstrate how financing instruments can enable shared ownership and equitable capital distribution on the path toward a more just economy. Alongside other global traditions, Islamic finance shows that efforts to imagine alternatives to economic exploitation go back a long, long time.

learn_more.title: House of Debt
The Economic System of Islam
The Season of the Dazzle: Islamic Finance and the New Economy

items.title: La Coperacha
items.body:
*2012–Present, Mexico*

In 2005, a group of independent journalists collaboratively produced a magazine entitled El Coyote Itinerante (The Traveling Coyote in English). The magazine explored local and regional issues of identity, culture, and community values. Through constant interaction with their communities—particularly in Coyoacán, a village south of Mexico City—the journalists discovered a trend. People throughout the country were working to transform their economic realities through business models such as cooperatives and collectives. Most of these initiatives did not receive media coverage, though, and seemed absent from public knowledge.

What they uncovered led them to form a digital media cooperative, La Coperacha, in 2012. The cooperative reports full time on Mexico’s grassroots democratic economic and social agenda. Its goal is to publicize successful local and regional efforts toward social transformation and gain both media attention and formal recognition for such efforts. The material La Coperacha covers is diverse and interconnected, documenting collective artmaking, free and cooperative technologies, efforts to defend land from unsustainable exploitation of natural resources, and the political and environmental impact of these topics and others. The cooperative’s website features written articles, video, audio, and other media.

As a cooperative, La Coperacha is democratically governed by its journalists, whose cohesion and discipline leads to solidarity and trust within the group. The cooperative model allows them to work in an environment governed by values like democracy and participation, which closely mirrors the values that guide the content the group produces. A core team of regular journalists executes daily administrative tasks like project management and finances, in addition to their own reporting, while contributors occasionally supply additional content.

La Coperacha receives funding from a few different sources. Other media and communication co-op projects provide some financial support while advertisements from social enterprises in La Coperacha’s publication provide additional revenue. The group also draws funds from awards and collaborations with local governments or organizations to cover certain issues. As with any media organization, though, financial sustainability is one of the greatest challenges and La Coperacha is always seeking new opportunities for funding partnerships.

La Coperacha is prolific. The worker-owners have produced over 2,500 pieces of journalism, 185 radio episodes on public radio, and five radio series. They have won the National Prize for Journalism twice—first in 2011, before officially organizing as a cooperative, and again in 2018 for the radio series Manantiales en Resistencia, which documented local and regional efforts to challenge problematic policies of the National Water Commission.

Manantiales en Resistencia is a prime example of the stories La Coperacha creates. The series uplifts the stories of Zapotec, Cucapás, and Totocanas communities in Guanajuato and Tecámac who fight for the right to water and its sustainable management. La Coperacha’s reporting makes space for stories that profit-driven media companies won’t or don’t normally cover. They both practice and write stories about democratic innovation, popularizing collective processes and community sovereignty through both their organization and their journalism.

La Coperacha also provides accessible resources about collectives and cooperatives throughout Mexico, from artisans to coffee co-ops to medical groups. Their efforts to disseminate this information began long before the media group organized into a cooperative. In 2007, La Coperacha had a webpage offering information about local cooperatives for conscious consumers and “cooperation among cooperatives.” With the formation of the G50 Network of Cooperatives, La Coperacha created an official digital directory of Mexico’s co-ops.

The organizations that make up the G50 network are an important part of La Coperacha’s mission. Groups must apply for certification as a G50, but once they are approved, they receive recognition and a profile with their mission, services, and contact information on La Coperacha’s website.

La Coperacha is working to expand reporting in isolated areas of Mexico that receive little to no media coverage. This commitment to inclusion and focus on community-based solutions defines La Coperacha as it continues to publicize efforts for social and environmental justice, cooperatives, and the solidarity economy.

Cooperatives as Sustainable Livelihood Strategies in Rural Mexico
Manantiales en Resistencia radio show

items.title: Landless Workers' Movement
items.body:
*1984–Present, Brazil*

The Landless Workers’ Movement (Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra, or MST) began to build its power in Brazil during a period of military dictatorship. Though officially founded in 1984, the group’s formation began in the early 1980s, as the rural poor came together to fight back against displacement from their land by powerful landowners and the rampant human rights violations that came with it.

The tumultuous political landscape of Brazil following the 1964 military coup (backed by both the US government and the Catholic Church) paved the way for extreme concentration of wealth—in particular, by perpetuating the concentration of land ownership which had marked Brazil since colonial times. This made Brazil a frontier for the growth of global capitalism, growth that excluded, displaced, and further impoverished rural people. Modernization of agricultural practices through widespread mechanization put farmers out of work and prevented them from renting land or even participating in sharecropping. The rural poor, now landless, began organizing throughout southern states of Brazil to demonstrate their right to work on the land. They occupied lands that sat unused, building tents and cultivating crops and livestock. Eventually, through pressure and negotiation with the government, many of these occupations became “agrarian reform settlements” in which the peasant families received formal rights to remain on the land. As the occupations spread and participation grew, their power increased to assert the ideals of democracy and push against the military dictatorship.

Occupying unproductive land has become the MST’s trademark. Its efforts led to the amendment of the Brazilian constitution in 1988 to say that land must be used to fulfill a social function. This means that the land must not only be used for the private interest of its owners, but also for the public interest, including being reasonably productive, making fair use of natural resources, and observing labor laws. This gave the MST an historic and transformative legal basis for its occupations.

The movement’s structure enables the direct and collective participation of everyone involved. Through delegating tasks and encouraging participation in collective decision-making processes (which are open to all families in the MST), the movement ensures strong bonds among its members. MST activities also help shift agricultural production toward agroecology, which is practiced in many agrarian reform settlements secured by the movement; in fact, the movement has become the largest producer of organic rice in Latin America. The MST estimates that it has helped 450,000 families secure formal land rights in agrarian reform settlements. Hundreds of thousands of families have participated in its more than 2,500 occupations.

Despite legal protections, the MST’s land claims continue to be threatened. The mid- to late-90s and early 2000s were particularly violent. In Pará in 1996, military police killed 19 landless workers in the Eldorado dos Carajás Massacre. An additional 69 people were wounded, with two dying from their injuries. Later, between 2020 and 2022, Brazil hit new historic records of violence in rural areas. State violence against the movement is ongoing as the MST faces continued displacement and human rights violations.

The MST is not the only movement in Brazil with goals of land reform. Other groups such as the National Confederacy of Agrarian Workers held a similar vision but implemented different strategies in their approach, such as forming labor unions. The MST, though, is set apart by its on-the-ground mobilization of farmers. The MST’s ideology is based largely on the idea that participants’ struggles and experiences—not the concessions of governments— are the path to progress.

Though land reform is still the MST’s focus, the movement has expanded to include a wider range of activities. These include interventions in education, health, human rights, and international relations. Local chapters gain support from their communities through educational projects, selling farming goods they produce, and reporting on human rights violations. More recently, the MST started promoting the so-called “Agrarian Reform Markets,” which give peasant families a chance to showcase their products to large urban audiences who are encouraged to support the movement. The MST rejects the uncritical consumerism and exploitation of Brazil’s capitalist class, particularly the exclusion and oppression of rural people. The movement advocates for a new agricultural model that finds balance and harmony between the needs of the people and the need to protect the environment. It challenges big agribusiness and proposes replacing capitalism’s social, economic, and political failures with a model that better serves the needs of the people and of the earth.

items.title: Mutual Aid Finance in Montreal
items.body:
*1990–Present, Montreal, Canada*

Some people face difficulties getting loans because they are written off for being in debt, having bad credit, or lacking collateral. This is often tied to discrimination on the basis on their race, class, or immigration status. Instead of getting loans to help them build a business or return to school, they are denied and sent home empty handed.

Borrowers need access to lenders that understand their loan history, financial products that meet their needs, and repayment schedules that don’t punish them for having unpredictable income. Communities left out by banks and lenders need mission-aligned investors who understand that value is more than just profits and are willing to trust the borrowers and their communities.

Finance needs to be controlled by the people it is supposed to serve—or it can exploit them, as many “microlending” initiatives around the world have. Community-controlled finance is about building power. Consider an example from Quebec, a province known for its long history of cooperative entrepreneurship and innovation around social finance. MicroCrédit Montréal puts into practice the original ideals of the movement that shares its name. Aware of the potential risks of microlending, they have developed measures to avoid the cycles of extraction and exploitation into which some other microlending has fallen.

MicroCrédit Montréal emerged in 1990 from the Milton Park neighborhood, the site of important housing rights organizing that led to the creation of a multi-unit housing cooperative in the early 1980s. Organizers noticed the lack of investment in this mixed-income area, where affluent blocks are in close proximity to poverty. A committee studied this issue and created a local loan fund inspired by the 1977 Community Reinvestment Act in the United States, which outlawed certain discriminatory credit practices (like redlining) in low-income areas. Listening to the needs of the community, the organization now manages a business-loan fund for new entrepreneurs, and offers loan products for immigrants seeking local recognition of their foreign credentials. In both cases, MCM prioritizes lending to women.

Currently, over 70 percent of MCM’s business loans are extended to entrepreneurs of color, many of whom encounter barriers to loan approval, because they might lack local credit history, assets for collateral, or people to act as guarantors.

MCM’s Foreign Credential Recognition loans aim to end the common assumption that first generation immigrants must work low-wage jobs and hope that their children might do better. New immigrants to Quebec need to demonstrate their credentials to the Ministry of Education and professional associations. It can cost the equivalent of tens of thousands of US dollars to obtain official licensure. This type of loan helps fast-track the credential-transfer process so new immigrants don’t have to fall behind or sustain gaps in their professional work experience.

MCM analyzes every business project and meets with each potential borrower to listen to their needs and approach their venture from an informed perspective.

Marc Nisbet, who served as a loan analyst and business development coach at MCM, explains that applicants often express that it is refreshing to show up somewhere and be treated in a way that is aligned with their self-image, as entrepreneurs. “We could see it in their body language,” says Nisbet, “They would arrive with a defensive posture, that changed after we spoke with them for half an hour.”

MCM’s loan fund is financed by a mix of large and small investors, from the cooperative Desjardins Group to individuals willing to contribute at least $500 CAD. Anyone can support the program—the youngest investor was only eight years old. Investors receive interest payments of up to two percent and are updated about their investments and the capital pool twice per year.

MCM’s loans are repaid with ten percent interest—a rate far preferable to those of predatory lenders or credit cards, which on average charge 22 percent. MCM’s average loan is $6,000, up to a maximum of $20,000. All the fund’s earned interest is returned to the capital pool, which covers the interest paid to investors, as well as any losses. Then, that growing capital pool can go out into the community as new loans.

MCM’s employees, whose wages come from outside fundraising, support prospective borrowers throughout the entire loan-application process. A committee composed of volunteers and a member of the board of directors reviews completed applications; investors do not have a voice in that process. The majority-immigrant staff uses its knowledge of cultural practices around money to guide applicants. The board determines whether to approve or deny the loan, but entrepreneurs who have been denied can request an appeal to better understand the reasoning behind the rejection.

Although loans officially last up to three years, loan officers are flexible about life’s uncertainties and have the power to postpone loan repayments in some situations, in order to avoid placing borrowers in a situation where they are unable to repay.

What began as a local project has created spin-offs across the province, with 17 agencies under the umbrella of Micro Entreprendre. This is a model that depends on local knowledge and local power, but it can be replicated in many contexts.

items.title: Muungano Slum Dwellers
items.body:
*1996–Present, Nairobi, Kenya*

Kenya is a country of 54 million people, with roughly one in two living on less than $5.50 a day, according to World Bank data. The capital, Nairobi, has a population of over four million and is a hub for economic migrants, young people, and displaced people from across the country who are looking for jobs and better opportunities. Urban population growth has expanded industry and education, but it has also created a need for housing and infrastructure that the country is not prepared to meet. The outdated system of urban planning employed in Nairobi is a holdover from British colonization, which continued into the 1960s. Today, over 50 percent of Nairobi’s population lives in informal settlements—or housing that is not recognized by the government—which make up less than two percent of the land mass.

Muungano Wa Wanavijiji—Swahili for “united slum dwellers”—is a Nairobi-based movement that emerged in 1996 in response to demolitions and evictions occurring in slums as a result of private development. Community members organized together and, through years of militant struggle, were able to stop the evictions and spark a movement that spread throughout Nairobi and then Kenya. Today, Muungano comprises over 100,000 people in 1,000 groups across Kenya. The movement has two main demands: secure tenure and access. “Secure tenure” means that every slum dweller, informal trader, and squatter should have a title and deed that recognizes their right to use the land. “Access” means every slum dweller should have access to clean water, health, basic services, and housing, among other human rights described in the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals.

Muungano reflects communities’ power to protect their rights, lands, and livelihoods as well as pushing for recognition of slums as important spaces not only for their inhabitants’ survival but also for the functioning of the city itself. The movement does not depend on external support. Instead, it emphasizes slum residents organizing themselves into networks that become part of city-wide federations.

In order to avoid stagnation within the movement, leaders are chosen at a community level rather than elected. This also keeps the movement from being used as a stepping stone for individuals seeking political power. In addition, Muungano intentionally develops women’s leadership, as women are at the center of communities and families and also suffer disproportionately from poor conditions in the slums. In Muungano, women are the leaders of data collection, savings, negotiating, and training.

In 2001, Muungano joined Slum Dwellers International, a global network of community-based organizations that mobilize urban poor people and slum dwellers. Through this connection, Muungano leaders learned the importance of data collection and mapping, and the need to strategically partner with the government. Although Muungano’s decision to work with the government has sometimes created tension, the movement has been able to leverage this relationship to access the services and information it needs. City officials have technical expertise and power to approve plans, and cities often own the utility companies, making them crucial partners in establishing both secure tenure and access to necessary services for slum dwellers.

Since its inception in 1996, Muungano has successfully shifted national policies around land and housing, gaining recognition for informal settlements, securing tenure in various parts of Kenya, creating housing projects, and securing access to services for thousands of slum dwellers. In 2003, Muungano established a finance vehicle, the Akiba Mashinani Trust (AMT), that can manage and hold assets for communities until those communities have the ability to manage them themselves. AMT also offers financial services like loans and savings for groups that might otherwise be excluded from the banking system and provides non-financial services like training, consultation, and technical assistance for Muungano members.

Thanks to the organizing of Muungano, more than 40,000 people have improved access to water and sanitation, and 7,000 homes and land rights to more than 140 hectares have been secured for Kenyan slum dwellers.

items.title: NDN Fund
items.body:
*2017–Present, Indian country across turtle island*

NDN Fund is an indigenous-led organization which provides loans and investments to large-scale community and national development projects. The fund is unique in scope and in structure: it seeks to invest in Indigenous communities while building Indigenous political power with the rallying cry: “Defend, Develop, and Decolonize.”

Starting in 2017, NDN Fund began with a vision to indigenize large-scale development, regenerative agriculture, food sovereignty, and equitable economic growth. Its parent organization, NDN Collective, is an advocacy organization for building Indigenous power. Creating the fund was a fundamental part of a strategy for transforming colonial economic practices through the application of Indigenous worldviews, knowledge, and perspectives.

NDN Fund is an emerging community development financial institution (CDFI), of which there are over a thousand across the United States. The community development sector has often played a paternalistic and colonizing role—or no role at all—in Native communities. There is a long and painful history of non-Indigenous populations seizing Native lands and imposing development models (including cooperative business models) on Indigenous communities across North America.

More recently, a dependence on federal funds has led to what former Managing Director Nikki Pieratos, a citizen of the Bois Forte Band of Chippewa, calls a scarcity mindset. Native Nations end up competing for scarce resources from the bureaucracy of the federal government—which throughout history has opposed and undermined Indigenous sovereignty and self-determination. The federal government’s investments often don’t align with the long-term vision of Indigenous communities; non-Native lenders, and the stakeholders they answer to, often fail to understand—and actively disregard—what is actually needed on the ground. When Indigenous communities look beyond government funding to commercial lenders, they encounter a predatory industry with high-interest rates and collateral requirements that exclude those who are not already wealthy. This industry has a history of extracting what little wealth remains in Native communities, which has led to community distrust of most outside lenders and funders.

The Fund provides an alternative route for Indigenous entrepreneurs by turning those extractive and paternalistic practices on their heads: it is run by Indigenous leadership, it gives decision-making power to Indigenous borrowers, and it practices an economics that aligns with Indigenous values.

What does an Indigenous economy look like in practice? The answers differ, of course, by community and context. The Minnesota Indigenous Business Alliance names eight values as being fundamental to building its understanding of an Indigenous economy: wisdom, humility, social responsibility, honesty, respect, equality, reciprocity, and love.

Guided by values like these, NDN Fund’s approach to project-based lending seeks to decolonize conventional financial practices. Firstly, tribal leadership has power over money, and the ability to control its own development—as opposed to the conventional model of top-down nonNative-led development. Secondly, lending is relationship-based, moving at the speed of trust—as opposed to transactional, volume-based operations. Next, NDN Fund practices a mindset of abundance over scarcity and incorporates this into its decisions. Finally, NDN Fund works to make its investments with nature and the wisdom of the land its ultimate guide, centering circular—as opposed to linear or extractive—economic relationships. All of these practices build on an Indigenous history of pre-colonial economics on Turtle Island, before capitalism dominated the continent.

This type of approach to development is rare for a financial institution. At NDN Fund, there is an ongoing practice of decolonizing “traditional” (read: colonized) underwriting and financing standards. According to Pieratos, “When we think of wellbeing, economic development is the cornerstone. But economic development for who? One of the most important and impactful things for Native communities is generational impact. To have a generational impact, we need to shift the way capital is flowing into communities.”

NDN Fund has already financed a number of projects through this decolonized lens: an eel aquaculture business in Maine, a Navajo-owned solar project in the Southwest United States, and a boat building company in Cordova, Alaska to support kelp harvesting. NDN Fund does not always require traditional collateral from the borrower and is creative in terms of what it requires to secure the loan. For instance, it has used equity shares and revenue sharing instead of requiring personal guarantees or asking borrowers to stake their homes or assets.

Another means by which NDN Fund seeks to “shift the way that capital flows” is through its sourcing of investment. Recognizing the restrictions that come with accepting federal dollars, NDN Fund has focused on bringing in flexible capital from private foundations, impact investors, and individuals. This has allowed it freedom in how it lends and who it lends to. With less red tape, it can structure project-based deals more creatively, create terms that work better for communities, and scale up the size of investments in a culturally responsive manner.

Defending Indigenous land rights is key to Indigenous sovereignty and, therefore, to developing strong Native economies through a decolonized approach. So, in addition to its development work, NDN Fund also builds Indigenous political power through supporting the return of Indigenous land with landback loans, such as the loan to Tzicatl Community Development Corporation for the purchase of land in Los Angeles to expand their language revitalization school.

That’s the power of “Defend, Develop, and Decolonize.” The three are interconnected, and one cannot happen without the others. NDN’s efforts in these three areas should be compelling not just for Indigenous peoples, but for everyone; as NDN President and CEO Nick Tilsen argues: “The liberation of Indigenous people is directly connected to the liberation of all people.” For NDN, to fight for Indigenous land sovereignty is to fight for collective liberation through movement building across all communities and generations.
